docs.title: Gradient Descent
docs.text:
TL;DR

Gradient descent is how almost every AI model learns. You measure how wrong the model is (the loss), work out which direction makes it less wrong (the gradient), and take a small step that way. Repeat thousands of times, and the model gets good.

Level: beginner · Prerequisites: basic algebra; knowing that a derivative is "the slope" helps but is not required.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text: When people say a neural network "learns", what is really happening is gradient descent (or one of its close relatives, such as Adam). ChatGPT, image classifiers and medical-image segmentation models are all trained this way. Once you understand this lesson, "training a model" stops being magic.

docs.title: Step 1 — The intuition: walking down a foggy mountain
docs.text:
Imagine you are standing on a mountain in thick fog. You want to reach the lowest point of the valley, but you can only see the ground right under your feet. What do you do?

  1. Feel which way the ground slopes.
  2. Take a step downhill.
  3. Repeat until the ground is flat.

That is the whole algorithm. In AI:

Mountain Machine learning Your position The model's parameters (its adjustable numbers, also called weights) Height of the ground The loss: how wrong the model is Slope under your feet The gradient Size of your step The learning rate Bottom of the valley The best parameters (lowest loss)

docs.title: Step 2 — What are we trying to make small? The loss
docs.text:
Let's use a tiny example. We have 7 data points (blue dots) and want to fit a straight line through the origin:

\[ \hat{y} = w \cdot x \]

There is only one parameter, the slope \(w\). For each point the model makes an error \(\hat{y}_i - y_i\) (the dashed red lines). We square the errors (so negative and positive errors don't cancel out, and big errors count extra) and take their average. This is the mean squared error (MSE) loss:

\[ L(w) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(w\,x_i - y_i\right)^2 \]

Try it: drag the slider. Watch the line on the left and the orange dot on the right. The right plot shows the loss for every possible value of \(w\). It is a bowl, and we want the bottom of it.

🎚️ Interactive: find a good w by hand

What to notice

  • When the line fits the dots well, the dashed error lines are short and the orange dot is near the bottom of the bowl.
  • You found the minimum by looking at the whole curve. A real model has millions of parameters, so we can never draw the whole curve. We need a method that only uses local information. That method is gradient descent.

docs.title: Step 3 — Which way is downhill? The gradient
docs.text:
Look at the red line touching the curve in the widget above. That is the slope of the loss at your current \(w\), written \(\frac{dL}{dw}\). It is the "feel the ground under your feet" step.

  • Slope positive → loss goes up as \(w\) increases → move \(w\) left (decrease it).
  • Slope negative → loss goes down as \(w\) increases → move \(w\) right (increase it).
  • Slope ≈ 0 → the ground is flat → you're at the bottom.

So the rule is simple: always move opposite to the slope.

For our loss, calculus gives the slope directly:

\[ \frac{dL}{dw} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} 2\,x_i\left(w\,x_i - y_i\right) \]

You don't need to derive this yourself. In practice libraries like PyTorch compute it automatically (this is called automatic differentiation, and backpropagation in neural networks). What matters is the meaning: it tells us which way is uphill, and how steep it is.

Gradient vs. derivative

With one parameter we call it the derivative or slope. With many parameters we get one slope per parameter. That list of slopes is called the gradient, written \(\nabla L\). It points in the direction of steepest ascent, so we walk the opposite way.

docs.title: Step 4 — Taking the step: the update rule
docs.text:
Now combine everything into one line, the heart of gradient descent:

\[ w_{\text{new}} = w_{\text{old}} - \eta \cdot \frac{dL}{dw} \]
  • The minus sign means "go opposite to the slope", i.e. downhill.
  • \(\eta\) (Greek letter eta) is the learning rate: how big a step to take.
  • Steep slope → big step; gentle slope → small step. The algorithm slows down by itself as it nears the bottom.

Try it: press Run 30 steps, then try the preset learning rates. The green ring marks the true minimum.

🏃 Interactive: gradient descent in action

What to notice: the learning rate matters a lot

Learning rate What happens Too small (0.01) Safe but slow: after 30 steps it still hasn't arrived. Good (0.05) Gets to the bottom quickly and smoothly. Big (0.18) Overshoots and bounces from side to side, but slowly settles. Too big (0.22) Every jump lands higher than the last one, and the loss explodes. This is called divergence.

Choosing the learning rate is one of the most important practical decisions when training a model.

docs.title: Step 5 — More parameters: a landscape instead of a curve
docs.text:
Real models have more than one parameter. Let's add an intercept \(b\), so the line no longer has to pass through the origin:

\[ \hat{y} = w \cdot x + b \]

Now the loss depends on two numbers, \(L(w, b)\). Instead of a curve, it is a surface, like a real valley. Below, we view it from above as a contour map: the stronger the purple, the lower the loss. The green ring marks the minimum. The gradient now has two parts, one per parameter:

\[ \nabla L = \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial w},\; \frac{\partial L}{\partial b}\right), \qquad \begin{aligned} w &\leftarrow w - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}\\ b &\leftarrow b - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial b} \end{aligned} \]

Exactly the same rule, applied to each parameter at the same time.

🗺️ Interactive: descending a 2-D loss landscape

What to notice

  • Click different starting points. Every path ends at the green ring, because this bowl has only one bottom.
  • The valley is long and narrow. With a learning rate around 0.15 the path zig-zags across the narrow direction while crawling along the long one. This exact problem is what improved optimizers like Momentum and Adam were invented to fix (a future lesson).
  • Push the learning rate to 0.2 and the path diverges, just as in 1-D.

docs.title: Step 6 — Real data is big: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)
docs.text:
To compute the exact gradient we averaged over all data points. With 7 points that's easy. With 10 million images it is far too slow to do for every single step.

The trick is to estimate the gradient from a small random subset of the data, called a mini-batch, at every step:

Variant Gradient computed from Each step is… Batch gradient descent all \(N\) examples accurate but slow Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) 1 random example very cheap but noisy Mini-batch gradient descent e.g. 32–512 examples the practical sweet spot, used almost everywhere

Try it: in the 2-D widget above, switch gradient from to 1 random point (SGD) and press Run. The path becomes wobbly, because each step only "sees" one point. It still heads towards the minimum on average. That noise is not all bad: in deep learning it can even help the model escape poor regions.

Vocabulary: epoch

One epoch is one full pass over the training data. With 10,000 examples and a mini-batch of 100, one epoch is 100 steps.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is the full algorithm from the 2-D widget, in a few lines of NumPy:

import numpy as np

x = np.array([0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5])
y = np.array([1.3, 1.6, 3.2, 4.5, 4.7, 6.1, 6.8])

w, b = -0.5, 5.0        # starting point
lr = 0.1                # learning rate (η)

for step in range(200):
    y_hat = w * x + b                     # 1. predict
    error = y_hat - y
    loss = np.mean(error ** 2)            # 2. measure loss (MSE)
    grad_w = np.mean(2 * error * x)       # 3. gradient
    grad_b = np.mean(2 * error)
    w -= lr * grad_w                      # 4. step downhill
    b -= lr * grad_b

print(f"w = {w:.3f}, b = {b:.3f}, loss = {loss:.4f}")

And the same thing in PyTorch, which computes the gradient for you:

import torch

x = torch.tensor([0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5])
y = torch.tensor([1.3, 1.6, 3.2, 4.5, 4.7, 6.1, 6.8])
w = torch.tensor(-0.5, requires_grad=True)
b = torch.tensor(5.0, requires_grad=True)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD([w, b], lr=0.1)

for step in range(200):
    loss = ((w * x + b - y) ** 2).mean()
    optimizer.zero_grad()   # clear old gradients
    loss.backward()         # compute gradients automatically
    optimizer.step()        # w ← w − lr · grad

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"Gradient descent always finds the best possible answer.\"

Only for bowl-shaped (convex) losses like the ones in this lesson. Neural-network loss landscapes have many hills, valleys and flat regions. Gradient descent finds a low point, not necessarily the lowest. In practice, these low points are usually good enough.

\"A bigger learning rate means faster training.\"

Only up to a point. Past it, training oscillates or diverges (you saw this in Step 4). That's why practitioners often use learning-rate schedules that start larger and shrink over time.

\"The gradient points towards the minimum.\"

It points in the direction of steepest local descent, which is not necessarily straight at the minimum. The zig-zag in the 2-D widget shows this clearly.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. At the current w, the slope dL/dw = +3. Should w increase or decrease?

Decrease. A positive slope means the loss rises as \(w\) grows, so we move the opposite way: \(w_{\text{new}} = w - \eta \cdot 3\).

2. Your training loss gets bigger every step and eventually becomes NaN. What is the most likely cause?

The learning rate is too large, so gradient descent is diverging. Try reducing it by a factor of 10.

3. Why does gradient descent automatically take smaller steps near the minimum, even with a fixed learning rate?

Because the step is \(\eta \times\) gradient, and the gradient (the slope) gets close to zero near the bottom of the bowl.

4. What is the difference between batch GD and SGD?

Batch GD computes the gradient from all training examples: it is accurate but slow per step. SGD uses one (or a small mini-batch of) random examples: each step is cheap and noisy, but on average it still points downhill.

5. With 50,000 training images and a mini-batch size of 250, how many update steps are in one epoch?

$50{,}000 / 250 = $ 200 steps.

docs.title: Hierarchical and Graph Tsetlin Machines
docs.text:
TL;DR

A standard Tsetlin machine reads a flat list of Boolean features, so it cannot say "an atom with property A, bonded to an atom with property B": the list says what is there, not what is connected to what. A graph Tsetlin machine takes a graph as input: nodes with properties (symbols such as "N" or "O"), joined by edges that may have types (such as "left" and "right"). Each rule is split into parts, one per layer. Part 0 checks a node's own properties, exactly like a convolutional rule checks a patch. Wherever a rule's part matches, the node sends a message (the rule's name) to its neighbours, and part 1 of every rule can then ask "did a neighbour send me R1?". More layers see further: after \(D-1\) rounds of messages, a rule can describe a node's surroundings up to \(D-1\) steps away, built from rules over rules. That is the hierarchy: small patterns (an O) feed bigger ones (a C next to an O), which feed bigger ones again. A rule is True for the graph if it matches at some node (OR over nodes), and learning is the same Recognize, Erase and Reject Feedback as before, applied at one matching node, picked at random. In our toy molecules, flat features and depth-1 rules stay at chance level (about 51%), while depth-2 rules reach 100% and read like chemistry: "an N bonded to an O".

Level: intermediate–advanced · Prerequisites: Convolutional Tsetlin machines (patches, the OR over positions, feedback on one random matching patch). It builds on Classification by voting (the vote sum \(v\) and the Voting Margin \(T\)). The math needs nothing beyond AND, OR and counting steps along a path.

Beyond the book

Granmo's book An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines announces Ch. 8, "Hierarchical Representation", and Ch. 9, "Graphs", but they are not published yet. This lesson is therefore based on the research papers listed in Further reading, mainly Granmo et al. (2025), The Tsetlin Machine Goes Deep, and the GraphTsetlinMachine code it describes. We use the book's vocabulary (rules, Memorize/Forget, Recognize/Erase/Reject Feedback) and give the research term once, in brackets. All experiments are our own toy runs; numbers that come from the papers are marked as quotes.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
Much of the data in medicine is about relations, not just lists of facts:

  • Molecules. Whether a drug is toxic often depends on which atoms are bonded to which, not on how many atoms of each element it contains. Two molecules with exactly the same atoms can behave very differently.
  • Sequences. In DNA or in an ECG, order matters: "three A's in a row" is not the same as "three A's somewhere".
  • Patient records. A hospital record links a patient to tests, diagnoses, drugs and notes. The README of the GraphTsetlinMachine code sketches exactly this use case: nodes for ECGs and clinical notes, and edges of different types, such as Measurement edges from tests to a patient and Condition edges from diseases to patients.

A flat feature list loses the links. You could add one feature per possible link ("atom 3 is bonded to atom 5"), but then a rule must name exact slots, and you need one rule per slot combination, the same problem the convolutional lesson had with positions. A graph Tsetlin machine solves it the same way convolution did: rules look at one node at a time, and the node's neighbours tell it what they are through messages.

docs.title: Step 1 — What flat features cannot say
docs.text:
Take two small toy "molecules" (tree-shaped, made up for this lesson; not real chemistry). Both have four carbons, one nitrogen and one oxygen. In molecule A, the N is bonded to the O. In molecule B, the N and the O sit three bonds apart.

A standard Tsetlin machine needs a fixed list of Boolean features. The natural ones are "contains N", "contains at least 2 C", and so on (thermometer-coded counts, as in the classification lesson). For A and B these features are identical, so every rule, and therefore the whole machine, must give A and B the same answer. If the question is "is the N bonded to the O?", it is bound to be wrong on one of them.

Try it: click atoms to change their element, or press Random pair.

🧪 Interactive: same atoms, different bonds

What to notice

  • In the starting pair, the counts are C × 4, N × 1, O × 1 for both molecules, yet the graph rule "an N with an O neighbour" is True for A and False for B.
  • Change an atom and the counts may differ, but then a flat rule can only tell the molecules apart by counting, never by looking at the bonds.
  • You could give a standard machine one feature per pair of atom slots ("slot 3 is N, slot 5 is O, and they are bonded"). With up to 8 atoms, "N bonded to O" alone then needs a rule for each ordered pair of slots: \(8 \times 7 = 56\) rules, and the slot numbers mean nothing chemically. The graph rule says it once.

docs.title: Step 2 — Inputs as graphs: nodes, properties and typed edges
docs.text:
A graph Tsetlin machine takes as input a graph (Granmo et al. 2025, §2):

  • Nodes, each with a set of properties: symbols such as "C", "A", "pixel (3, 5) is white" or "the word pain". A property is a Boolean feature of the node, so the node's literals are its properties and their negations, exactly as before.
  • Edges between nodes, each with a type: "bond", "left", "right", "Measurement", … Edges are directed; an undirected bond is two edges, one each way.

The same input format covers many kinds of data:

Data Nodes Properties Edges (types) Our toy molecules atoms the element: C, N or O bonds (one type) A sequence such as BAAAE positions the letter to the neighbour on the left / right (two types) An image, split into patches patches the pixels and the patch position none A tabular patient record one node all the features none A hospital record patient, tests, notes, diagnoses values, words, codes Measurement, Condition, …

The last two rows show that the earlier machines are special cases. A graph with one node is a standard Tsetlin machine. A graph of patches without edges is a convolutional Tsetlin machine: the paper checks this and reports test accuracies close to those of a convolutional machine on MNIST (98.42% vs 98.93%) and Fashion-MNIST (89.49% vs 91.05%) (Granmo et al. 2025, Table 3, quoted).

Hypervectors: how the real code stores symbols

With thousands of possible symbols (all the words of a language, say), one Boolean feature per symbol becomes large. The GraphTsetlinMachine code therefore stores each node's properties in a hypervector: a fixed-length bit vector in which every symbol is given a few random bit positions, and a node's bits are the OR of its symbols' bits. Its README example uses vectors of 32 bits with 2 bits per symbol, which gives \(32 \cdot 31 / 2 = 496\) different bit pairs (quoted from the README). Rules then memorize bits, and a learned rule is read back by checking which symbols' bits it contains. Two symbols can share a bit by accident, which adds a little noise. This lesson skips hypervectors and gives every symbol its own feature (the code also has such a one-hot option). Nothing else changes.

What to notice

  • Edge types matter. In the sequence BAAAE, a node that only knows "a neighbour is an A" can't tell left from right; with left and right edges it can (the README makes this remark for its sequence demo).
  • The graph can have any size. A rule never names a node number, so molecules of 6 atoms and of 8 atoms are handled by the same rules.

docs.title: Step 3 — Rules that look at one node: part 0
docs.text:
Start with the simplest graph rule: an AND of property literals, checked at every node, with an OR over the nodes. "O" matches every oxygen atom; "¬C" matches every atom that isn't carbon. The rule is True for the molecule if it matches at one node or more.

This is word for word the convolutional machine, with nodes in place of patches:

\[ C_j(\text{graph}) \;=\; \bigvee_{v \in \text{nodes}} \; \bigwedge_{k \in I_j} l_k^{(v)} , \]

where \(I_j\) is the set of literals rule \(C_j\) has memorized and \(l_k^{(v)}\) is the truth value of literal \(l_k\) at node \(v\). A rule like this can say "there is an N" and "there is an O", but not "the N is next to the O": it sees one node at a time, and the OR throws away which nodes matched. That is why, in Step 7, a graph machine with only this one part (depth 1) is stuck at chance level on the bonding task, just like the flat machine.

In the paper's terms, this is the layer-0 component \(C^0_j\) of a clause (Granmo et al. 2025, §2). To see more than one node, the rule needs more parts, and the parts need a way to talk.

What to notice

  • Part 0 of a rule is a pattern detector for single nodes: "an O", "an N", "an atom that is N or O".
  • On its own it is a convolutional machine whose "patches" are nodes. Everything new in this lesson is about what happens between nodes.

docs.title: Step 4 — Messages: rules tell the neighbours what they found
docs.text:
Here is the key idea of the graph Tsetlin machine (Granmo et al. 2025, §2, "Messages" and "Message Submission"):

  1. Evaluate part 0 of every rule at every node.
  2. Wherever part 0 of rule \(R_k\) matches, the node sends the message "\(R_k\)" along all its outgoing edges (bound to the edge's type, when there are several types).
  3. Every node collects what it receives in its inbox. The inbox gives the node new Boolean features: "a neighbour sent \(R_k\)", one per rule (and per edge type).
  4. Part 1 of each rule is an AND of these message literals. A rule matches at a node in layer 1 only if part 0 and part 1 both match there.
  5. Finally, OR over the nodes, and vote, exactly as before.

So the "bonded" rule from Step 1 is two rules working together:

\[ \begin{aligned} R_1 &: \quad \text{O} \\ R_2 &: \quad \underbrace{\text{N}}_{\text{part 0}} \;\wedge\; \underbrace{\text{a neighbour sent } R_1}_{\text{part 1}} . \end{aligned} \]

\(R_2\) reads as "an N with an O neighbour". Its part 1 does not mention O at all; it mentions another rule. That is what the paper calls a deep or nested clause: rules built from rules. To read it, you trace each message back to the rule that sent it (the paper does exactly this in its Table 1).

Try it: step through the evaluation. The widget starts on the N atom (dashed ring); its inbox is shown in the readout.

📨 Interactive: rules send messages to their neighbours

What to notice

  • Layer 0: R1 matches at the O; R2 and R4 match at the N (their part 0 is "N"); R3 matches at every C.
  • Round 1: only the O's neighbour (the C in the middle) receives R1. The N's inbox gets R3 (from its C neighbours) and nothing else, so R2 fails: this N is not bonded to an O.
  • Layer 1: R3 ("a C next to an O") now matches only at the middle C. Round 2 carries that fact one bond further, so in layer 2, R4 ("an N next to a C that is next to an O") matches at the N.
  • Faded atoms are the ones that cannot have influenced the selected atom yet. After layer 0 the N sees only itself, after layer 1 its neighbours, after layer 2 everything within two bonds.
  • Click the O's neighbour twice to turn it into an N: now R2 fires in layer 1, and R4 no longer does.

docs.title: Step 5 — Depth is hierarchy: seeing further, one round at a time
docs.text:
With \(D\) layers (the paper's depth \(D\)), a rule has parts \(0, 1, \dots, D-1\), and there are \(D - 1\) rounds of messages. In round \(i\), a node sends \(R_k\) if rule \(R_k\) matched all its parts up to layer \(i-1\) at that node (Granmo et al. 2025, Algorithm in §2 and Appendix A.3). So messages get richer every round:

Round A message "\(R_k\)" from a neighbour means … What a rule can see from a node — (part 0) — the node itself 1 the neighbour matches part 0 of \(R_k\) its neighbours 2 the neighbour matches parts 0–1 of \(R_k\), which already looked at its neighbours everything up to 2 edges away \(D-1\) … everything up to \(D-1\) edges away

This growing receptive field is the same idea as stacking convolution layers in a convolutional neural network, and it is where the hierarchy comes from: R1 (an O) is used by R3 (a C next to an O), which is used by R4 (an N next to a C next to an O). Each level is a readable rule, and it can be traced back to atoms.

Two details make the rules shorter than you might expect:

  • The receptive field is a radius, not a path length. "N and O two bonds apart" (N–X–O) needs only depth 2, if the rule is centred on the middle atom: "any atom, with a neighbour that sent R(N) and a neighbour that sent R(O)".
  • Reasoning by elimination. A rule may describe a node by what it is not. In the paper's Figure 1, a part that memorized ¬1 ∧ ¬3 ∧ ¬5 ∧ ¬7 ∧ ¬9 matches every even number. In our molecules (one N and one O each), "an N-or-O atom next to an N-or-O atom" can only be the N–O bond. The paper argues that this kind of sharing, rules reusing other rules, lets the machine recognise sub-graph patterns "with exponentially fewer clauses" (quoted from its abstract).

The paper's sequence example

Granmo et al. (2025, §3.1) classify 5-letter sequences by whether they contain three A's in a row. Each letter is a node, with left and right edges. A depth-2 machine with only four rules reaches 100% test accuracy after four epochs (quoted), and its rules read as, for example, "an A whose left and right neighbours match the A-rules": three A's centred on the middle one.

What to notice

  • More layers = a wider view, built from rules about neighbours of neighbours. The paper reports that depth matters on real data: on IMDB sentiment, 86.43% test accuracy at depth 1 vs 88.15% at depth 2, and on 5-class viral genome sequences, 59.81% at depth 1 vs 95.14% at depth 2 (Granmo et al. 2025, Tables 5 and 8, quoted).
  • Depth also makes learning harder: a deep rule only works once the rules it relies on have learned something useful. Step 7 shows this in our toy runs.

docs.title: Step 6 — Learning: same feedback, at one matching node
docs.text:
Nothing in the learning rule is new; it is the convolutional machine's procedure with nodes in place of patches (Granmo et al. 2025, §2, step 5; the code picks the node at random among the nodes where the clause is True):

  • Compute every rule's output for the graph (all layers, then OR over nodes), and the vote sum \(v\) for the true class, clipped to \([-T, T]\).
  • Select each rule for feedback with probability \((T - v)/2T\), as in the classification lesson.
  • A selected rule of the true class that is True gets Recognize Feedback at one node where it matched, picked at random. A selected rule of the other class that is True gets Reject Feedback at one random matching node. A selected rule of the true class that is False gets Erase Feedback (no node needed).
  • At the chosen node, the rule's literal vector is everything the node had: its properties (for part 0) and its inboxes (for parts 1, 2, …). Message literals are simply more literals, learned with the same memory, Memorize Value and Forget Value.

One thing is new in spirit: a message literal means "a neighbour sent \(R_k\)", and what \(R_k\) matches changes while \(R_k\) learns. Rules are learning on top of each other's moving results. It works because a rule that is useful to others keeps being reinforced, so its meaning settles, and the rules built on it settle with it.

Our simplifications (what this lesson's code does differently from the paper)

  • One feature per symbol, no hypervectors (Step 2), and one edge type (bonds).
  • Votes for and against with equal weight, as in the classification lesson. The paper's machine is built on the Coalesced Tsetlin machine (Glimsdal & Granmo 2021): one shared pool of rules, each with a learned integer weight per class.
  • Only positive message literals ("a neighbour sent \(R_k\)"). The paper's rules can also use negated ones ("no neighbour sent \(R_k\)"; its Table 1 shows several). In our small runs with negated message literals, Reject Feedback quickly taught rules "no neighbour sent \(R_k\)" for some \(R_k\) that matches everywhere. That literal is False at every node, so the rule never fired again, and the machine never got above 51.0% test accuracy (seed 1, the Step 7 task, 15 epochs). With thousands of rules and the full update scheme this is presumably not a problem in the paper, but we could not check it at toy scale, so our toy drops the negations.
  • Small and slow: 8 rules per class, plain Python and JavaScript, no GPU. The paper's code runs on GPUs with thousands of rules.

What to notice

  • The only new ingredient compared with the convolutional machine is where the literals come from: a node's own properties and its inbox. "Pick one matching node at random" is the convolutional machine's "pick one matching patch at random".
  • Erase Feedback lowers message literals too, so a rule that fails everywhere loosens both what it asks of the node and what it asks of the neighbours.

docs.title: Step 7 — Training a graph Tsetlin machine on toy molecules
docs.text:
The task: random tree-shaped molecules of 6 to 8 atoms, all carbon except exactly one N and one O, and the question "is the N bonded to the O?". Every molecule has the same element counts (apart from the number of carbons), so flat features carry almost no information. There are 300 training and 300 test molecules, half of each class. The machine has 8 rules per class, Voting Margin \(T = 4\), Forget Value 0.8 (Memorize Value 0.2), and a memory depth of 10 positions per literal, as in the convolutional lesson. Everything is seeded; the widget runs a line-by-line port of our Python check script with the same random numbers, so it shows exactly the numbers below.

Try it: press Train to 15 epochs for each model. Then click rules in the list to see where they match.

🧠 Interactive: train a graph Tsetlin machine on "is the N bonded to the O?"

What to notice

  • Flat features fail. The standard machine sees thermometer-coded element counts. It ends at 51.0% test accuracy (seed 1), and 50.9% on average over seeds 1 to 10: a coin flip, because the counts say nothing about bonds.
  • Depth 1 fails too. Rules that see one node at a time end at 51.0% (seed 1; 51.8% on average). This is the convolutional machine of Step 3.
  • Depth 2 solves it. With one round of messages, the machine reaches 100% test accuracy after the first epoch (seed 1), and every seed from 1 to 10 is at 100% after 15 epochs (reached within 1 to 4 epochs). Depth 3 also ends at 100% for all ten seeds.
  • The rules read like chemistry. With seed 1 and depth 2, all eight "yes" rules fire on all 147 test molecules where the N is bonded to the O, and on none of the other 153. Their descriptions say it in different words, for example "N, next to [O], next to [N or O]", "O, next to [N], next to [N or O]", and, by elimination, "N or O, next to [N or O]". One "no" rule found a pattern that rules out a bond: "C, next to [N], next to [O], next to [N or O]", i.e. N–C–O, which fires on 78 of the 153 "no" molecules and on none of the "yes" ones.
  • A harder question exposes the learning problem. Switch the task to "N within 2 bonds of O?". Depth 2 can express the answer (Step 5), and with seed 1 it does reach 100% test accuracy at epoch 5, but then loses it and ends at 50.7%. Over seeds 1 to 10 the final accuracy averages 56.2% (49.3% to 69.3%); three seeds touched 100% at some epoch. Depth 3 does no better (49.6% on average). The "no" class is the hard part: "the N has no O within 2 bonds" is a statement about every path, and a rule that is an OR over nodes can only find something that exists. The "yes" rules have to carry the whole decision, and in our small runs they don't settle. Bigger machines, weighted rules and more data are what the paper uses.

docs.title: Step 8 — Another kind of depth: stacking Tsetlin machines
docs.text:
Message passing builds a hierarchy over the graph: rules about neighbours of neighbours. There is a second, older idea for hierarchy that works on ordinary flat inputs: stack whole Tsetlin machines, so that the rule outputs of one machine become the Boolean features of the next.

  • Granmo's original Tsetlin machine paper (2018, §6.2) sketches a "Fully Connected Deep Tsetlin Machine": the clause outputs of one machine are the input of the next, and each layer is trained on its own, directly from the class label, similar to how deep belief networks were trained layer by layer. If one layer has learned \(P \wedge \lnot Q\) and \(\lnot P \wedge Q\), the next layer can combine them into larger formulas.
  • Tarasyuk, Gorbenko, Yakovlev and Shafik (2024) built and tested such a multi-layer Tsetlin machine. They train the layers one after another: train layer 1 until its accuracy levels off, freeze its rules, then use their outputs as inputs for layer 2, and so on. On Digits-MNIST with 100 rules per class, they report validation accuracy 96.58% with one layer, 97.42% with two and 96.90% with five, while training accuracy keeps rising (97.72% to 99.93%). They conclude that two layers were best and that more layers overfit (quoted from their Tables II and III).
Stacked (multi-layer) Tsetlin machine Graph Tsetlin machine Input a flat feature list a graph of nodes, properties and typed edges What a higher layer reads the outputs of all rules of the layer below, for the whole input messages from neighbouring nodes: which rules matched next door Hierarchy means formulas made of formulas patterns made of neighbouring patterns, wider each layer Training layer by layer, earlier layers frozen (Tarasyuk et al.) all parts of all rules at once, with the usual feedback

What to notice

  • Both kinds of depth build rules over rules, and both keep every level readable: a higher-level rule is an AND of lower-level rules, each of which is an AND of literals.
  • Both papers find that depth helps up to a point, and both show that it is not free: the multi-layer machine overfits beyond two layers, and our toy graph machine struggles to learn deeper patterns.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
The complete learning loop is the convolutional loop with layers of messages in the middle.

Here is a complete (simplified) graph Tsetlin machine in numpy, on the Step 7 task. It uses numpy's random numbers, so its exact numbers differ from the widget's.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
ELEMENTS = "CNO"


def make_molecule():
    """A random tree of 6-8 atoms: all C except one N and one O; at most 3 bonds per atom."""
    n = rng.integers(6, 9)
    nbr = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for k in range(1, n):
        p = rng.integers(0, k)
        while len(nbr[p]) >= 3:
            p = rng.integers(0, k)
        nbr[p].append(k)
        nbr[k].append(p)
    el = np.zeros(n, int)
    el[rng.choice(n, 2, replace=False)] = [1, 2]                     # one N, one O
    return el, nbr


def make_data(size):
    """Balanced data: label 1 if the N is bonded to the O."""
    X, y = [], []
    for i in range(size):
        while True:
            el, nbr = make_molecule()
            bonded = any(el[u] == 2 for u in nbr[int(np.flatnonzero(el == 1)[0])])
            if bonded == i % 2:
                break
        props = np.eye(3, dtype=bool)[el]                              # one-hot element per atom
        X.append((np.hstack([props, ~props]), nbr))
        y.append(i % 2)
    return X, np.array(y)


class GraphTM:
    def __init__(self, rules_per_class=8, depth=2, T=4, forget=0.8, mem=10):
        self.m, self.D, self.T, self.F, self.mem = 2 * rules_per_class, depth, T, forget, mem
        self.cls = np.repeat([0, 1], rules_per_class)
        self.L = [6] + [self.m] * (depth - 1)                         # literals per layer: properties, then messages
        self.state = [np.full((self.m, L), mem // 2) for L in self.L]  # start just below Memorized

    def evaluate(self, graph):
        """Literals of every node, layer by layer, and M[j, v] = rule j matches (all layers) at node v."""
        lits, nbr = [graph[0]], graph[1]
        M = ~((self.state[0] > self.mem // 2)[:, None, :] & ~lits[0][None]).any(2)
        for i in range(1, self.D):
            inbox = np.array([M[:, u].any(1) if u else np.zeros(self.m, bool) for u in nbr])  # a neighbour sent R_k
            lits.append(inbox)
            M = M & ~((self.state[i] > self.mem // 2)[:, None, :] & ~inbox[None]).any(2)
        return lits, M

    def predict(self, graph):
        fires = self.evaluate(graph)[1].any(1)                             # OR over nodes
        return 0 if fires[self.cls == 0].sum() >= fires[self.cls == 1].sum() else 1

    def update(self, graph, y):
        lits, M = self.evaluate(graph)
        fires = M.any(1)
        v = np.clip(fires[self.cls == y].sum() - fires[self.cls != y].sum(), -self.T, self.T)
        for j in np.flatnonzero(rng.random(self.m) <= (self.T - v) / (2 * self.T)):
            node = rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(M[j])) if fires[j] else None  # ONE matching node, at random
            for i, s in enumerate(self.state):
                if node is None:
                    if self.cls[j] == y:                                   # Erase Feedback
                        s[j] -= (rng.random(self.L[i]) <= self.F) & (s[j] > 1)
                    continue
                p = lits[i][node]
                if self.cls[j] == y:                                       # Recognize Feedback
                    s[j] += p & (rng.random(self.L[i]) <= 1 - self.F) & (s[j] < self.mem)
                    s[j] -= ~p & (rng.random(self.L[i]) <= self.F) & (s[j] > 1)
                else:                                                      # Reject Feedback
                    s[j] += ~p & (s[j] <= self.mem // 2)


Xtr, ytr = make_data(300)
Xte, yte = make_data(300)
for depth in (1, 2):
    tm = GraphTM(depth=depth)
    for epoch in range(15):
        for i in rng.permutation(len(Xtr)):
            tm.update(Xtr[i], ytr[i])
    acc = np.mean([tm.predict(g) == y for g, y in zip(Xte, yte)])
    print(f"depth {depth}: test accuracy {acc:.3f}")


def atom(j):
    """Which elements rule j's layer-0 part allows (x_e memorized: must be e; NOT x_e memorized: must not be e)."""
    mem = tm.state[0][j] > tm.mem // 2
    ok = [e for e in range(3) if not mem[3 + e] and not any(mem[q] for q in range(3) if q != e)]
    return "any" if len(ok) == 3 else "/".join(ELEMENTS[e] for e in ok) if ok else "nothing"


for j in range(tm.m):                                                      # read the rules back to atoms
    sent = sorted({atom(k) for k in np.flatnonzero(tm.state[1][j] > tm.mem // 2)})
    vote = "bonded" if tm.cls[j] else "not bonded"
    print(f"R{j + 1:<2} votes {vote:10}: atom {atom(j):5} next to " + (", ".join(f"[{t}]" for t in sent) or "anything"))

depth 1: test accuracy 0.500
depth 2: test accuracy 1.000
R1  votes not bonded: atom C     next to anything
R2  votes not bonded: atom C     next to [N], [O]
R3  votes not bonded: atom any   next to [N]
R4  votes not bonded: atom nothing next to [any]
R5  votes not bonded: atom N     next to [N]
R6  votes not bonded: atom N     next to anything
R7  votes not bonded: atom O     next to anything
R8  votes not bonded: atom any   next to [N], [O]
R9  votes bonded    : atom N     next to [N/O]
R10 votes bonded    : atom N/O   next to [N/O], [O], [any]
R11 votes bonded    : atom O     next to [N], [N/O], [any]
R12 votes bonded    : atom any   next to [O]
R13 votes bonded    : atom any   next to anything
R14 votes bonded    : atom N/O   next to [N/O], [any]
R15 votes bonded    : atom any   next to [N/O], [O], [any]
R16 votes bonded    : atom N/O   next to [N/O], [O], [any]

Each message literal is printed as the part 0 of the rule that sends it ("next to [O]" = "a neighbour sent a rule whose part 0 is O"). Depth 1 is at chance level and depth 2 is perfect, as in the widget. The "bonded" rules again say "an N, or an N/O atom, next to an O or N/O atom". R2 is the N–C–O pattern that rules out a bond. Some rules are vague or empty ("any atom next to anything" fires on every molecule) and some can never fire (R4: "nothing"); the clean rules outvote them. To go deeper, give a rule a third state array and read the second inbox, which is built from M after layer 1, exactly as the loop in evaluate does.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"A graph Tsetlin machine is a graph neural network with Boolean weights.\"

Both pass messages along edges, but what is passed is different. A graph neural network passes vectors of real numbers and mixes them with learned weights. A graph Tsetlin machine passes rule names: "rule \(R_k\) matched here". Every message literal can be traced back to a readable rule about the neighbour.

\"More layers always help.\"

More layers let a rule see further, but each layer adds rules that depend on other rules' moving results. In our toy runs, depth 2 solved "N bonded to O", while neither depth 2 nor depth 3 settled on "N within 2 bonds of O". The multi-layer Tsetlin machine paper also found that validation accuracy peaks at two layers and then drops (Tarasyuk et al. 2024).

\"To find a pattern two bonds away you need three layers.\"

The receptive field is a radius around the node where the rule matches. A depth-2 rule centred on the middle atom sees both ends of N–X–O. You need more layers only for patterns that are wide in every direction from their centre.

\"Messages are extra input features you have to design.\"

You only design the graph: the nodes, their properties and the edges. The message literals are created by the machine itself, one per rule (and edge type), and their meaning is learned along with the rules.

\"The convolutional Tsetlin machine is something different.\"

It is the special case of a graph with no edges: one node per patch, with the patch's pixels and position as properties. The paper reports similar accuracy for the two on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST (Step 2).

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. A molecule has 7 atoms. Molecule A has its N bonded to its O; molecule B has the same atoms but the N and O are 3 bonds apart. Why can no standard Tsetlin machine on element counts tell them apart?

The counts (and any thermometer features made from them) are the same for A and B, so every rule has the same truth value on both, every vote is the same, and so is the prediction. Bonds are not in the input at all. In Step 7 this showed up as 51.0% test accuracy (seed 1).

2. Write the rule \"a C bonded to an O\" as a two-part graph rule. Which rule must exist alongside it?

You need a rule whose part 0 matches O, say \(R_1\): O. Then \(R_3\): part 0 = C, part 1 = "a neighbour sent \(R_1\)". The widget in Step 4 uses exactly this \(R_3\).

3. A graph Tsetlin machine has depth 3. Which atoms can influence whether a rule matches at atom v?

All atoms at most 2 bonds from v: part 0 sees v itself, part 1 sees messages from v's neighbours (about themselves), and part 2 sees messages that the neighbours sent after reading their neighbours. Depth \(D\) gives a radius of \(D - 1\).

4. During training, a \"bonded\" rule is True on a bonded molecule at two atoms (the N and the O), and is selected for feedback. What happens?

It belongs to the true class and is True, so it gets Recognize Feedback. One of the two matching atoms is picked at random. The rule's literals are then compared with that atom's properties (part 0) and its inbox (part 1): True literals move towards Memorized with the Memorize Value, False ones towards Forgotten with the Forget Value.

5. Why is \"the N has no O within 2 bonds\" harder for a Tsetlin machine than \"the N has an O within 2 bonds\"?

A rule is an OR over nodes of an AND, so it says "there exists a node where this local pattern holds". The positive statement is exactly that kind of claim. The negative one says something about all paths from the N, which a single existential rule can't express; the machine has to rely on the "yes" rules not firing, and in our runs that was hard to learn (56.2% average at depth 2).

docs.text:

Clarke, Kunal Dumbre, Ylva Grønningsæter, Vojtech Halenka, Runar Helin, Lei Jiao, Ahmed Khalid, Rebekka Omslandseter, Rupsa Saha, Mayur Shende and Xuan Zhang, The Tsetlin Machine Goes Deep: Logical Learning and Reasoning With Graphs (arXiv 2507.14874, 2025; v2 2026). The graph Tsetlin machine: graph input, deep clauses, messages and depth (§2), the three-A sequence example (§3.1, Appendix A.3), results on images, text, action coreference, recommendation and viral genomes. Our main source for Steps 2 to 6.
  • The cair/GraphTsetlinMachine repository and its README: the tutorial (nodes, edges, properties, hypervector sizes), the sequence and hospital examples, and the CUDA code in which feedback goes to one random node where the clause is True.
  • Vojtech Halenka, Ahmed K. Kadhim, Paul F. A. Clarke, Bimal Bhattarai, Rupsa Saha, Ole-Christoffer Granmo, Lei Jiao and Per-Arne Andersen, Exploring Effects of Hyperdimensional Vectors for Tsetlin Machines (ISTM 2024; arXiv 2406.02648). Hypervector inputs for Tsetlin machines, the representation the graph machine uses for its symbols.
  • Sondre Glimsdal and Ole-Christoffer Granmo, Coalesced Multi-Output Tsetlin Machines with Clause Sharing (arXiv 2108.07594, 2021). The shared, weighted pool of rules that the graph machine is built on.
  • Olga Tarasyuk, Anatoliy Gorbenko, Alex Yakovlev and Rishad Shafik, Multi-Layer Tsetlin Machine: Architecture and Performance Evaluation (ISTM 2024; open accepted version at Leeds Beckett). Stacked Tsetlin machines trained layer by layer (Step 8).
  • Ole-Christoffer Granmo, The Tsetlin Machine – A Game Theoretic Bandit Driven Approach to Optimal Pattern Recognition with Propositional Logic (arXiv 1804.01508, 2018). §6.2 sketches the Fully Connected Deep Tsetlin Machine.
  • Ole-Christoffer Granmo, Sondre Glimsdal, Lei Jiao, Morten Goodwin, Christian W. Omlin and Geir Thore Berge, The Convolutional Tsetlin Machine (2019): the special case of a graph without edges.

docs.title: The Ising model
docs.text:
TL;DR

The Ising model is a grid of tiny arrows (spins) that each point up or down. Neighbours prefer to agree, and temperature adds random flips that fight this preference. Below a critical temperature the whole grid lines up by itself; above it, the order melts. The same three ingredients (binary units, pairwise links, an energy to minimise) are the basis of Hopfield networks, Boltzmann machines and every "temperature" knob in AI.

Level: beginner · Prerequisites: none. Knowing what \(e^{x}\) looks like helps from Step 3 on.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
A piece of iron is a magnet at room temperature. Heat it above 770 °C and the magnetism disappears. Cool it and it comes back. No atom "decides" this. Each atom only feels its nearest neighbours. So how do billions of atoms agree on one direction, and why does that agreement break at one sharp temperature?

The Ising model (also called the Lenz–Ising model: Wilhelm Lenz proposed it in 1920, his student Ernst Ising solved the first case in 1924) is the simplest model that answers this. It is worth learning for AI because:

  • Hopfield networks and Boltzmann machines are Ising models whose links are learned. They earned John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics.
  • The Metropolis algorithm, invented to simulate models like this one, is the ancestor of the sampling methods (MCMC) used across statistics and machine learning.
  • The temperature setting of a language model comes from the same formula you will meet in Step 3.

docs.title: Step 1 — Tiny magnets on a grid
docs.text:
Take a grid. Put one arrow on every square. Each arrow is called a spin and has only two options:

  • up, written \(s_i = +1\)
  • down, written \(s_i = -1\)

That is the whole state of the model: a list of \(+1\)s and \(-1\)s. A 4×4 grid has 16 spins and therefore \(2^{16} = 65{,}536\) possible patterns.

One number summarises a pattern: the magnetisation \(m\), the average of all spins.

\[ m = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} s_i \]

\(m = +1\) means every spin is up, \(m = -1\) means every spin is down, and \(m = 0\) means half and half. A real magnet is a piece of material with \(m\) far from 0.

Try it: click spins to flip them and watch \(m\) in the readout. Ignore the right-hand panel for a moment; Step 2 explains it.

🧲 Interactive: flip spins, watch the energy

What to notice

  • All up gives \(m = +1\). Two halves and Checkerboard both give \(m = 0\), although they look very different. Magnetisation alone doesn't tell them apart. Energy will.
  • The model has no idea what "up" means physically. A spin can stand for an atom's magnetic moment, a pixel (black or white), a neuron (firing or silent), or a voter (yes or no).

docs.title: Step 2 — Energy: neighbours want to agree
docs.text:
Every pair of neighbouring spins shares a link (physicists say bond). The rule is:

  • the two spins agree → the link contributes \(-1\) to the energy (good, stable)
  • the two spins disagree → the link contributes \(+1\) (bad, tense)

The smallest possible example is two spins with one link:

Pattern \(s_1 s_2\) Energy ↑ ↑ \(+1\) \(-1\) ↓ ↓ \(+1\) \(-1\) ↑ ↓ \(-1\) \(+1\) ↓ ↑ \(-1\) \(+1\)

The product \(s_1 s_2\) is \(+1\) when the spins agree and \(-1\) when they don't, so the energy of one link is simply \(-s_1 s_2\). For a whole grid, add up all links:

\[ E(s) = -J \sum_{\langle i,j \rangle} s_i s_j \;-\; h \sum_i s_i \]
  • \(\langle i,j \rangle\) means "every pair of neighbours, counted once".
  • \(J\) is the coupling: how strongly neighbours want to agree. We use \(J = 1\) throughout.
  • \(h\) is an external field: a push that makes every spin prefer up (\(h > 0\)) or down (\(h < 0\)), like holding a big magnet nearby. It is 0 until Step 5.

Systems drift towards low energy, like a ball rolling downhill. So this formula says: patterns in which neighbours agree are preferred.

Go back to the widget above. The 4×4 grid has 24 links. Green links agree, red links disagree, and the purple marker shows the total energy.

What to notice

  • All up (and all down) is the lowest possible energy, \(-24\): every link agrees. Checkerboard is the highest, \(+24\).
  • Two halves has \(m = 0\) but energy \(-16\). Only the 4 links on the border between the halves disagree. Energy lives on the borders between regions.
  • Start from All up and flip one spin in the middle: 4 links turn red and the energy rises by 8. Flip a 2×2 block: 8 links are red, the energy rises by 16. An island of flipped spins costs energy in proportion to its perimeter. Remember this for Step 6.

What if neighbours want to disagree?

With \(J < 0\) the signs swap: the checkerboard becomes the lowest-energy pattern. That is an antiferromagnet. With a different random \(J\) on every link you get a spin glass, which is the starting point for Hopfield networks (Step 8).

docs.title: Step 3 — Temperature: order against chance
docs.text:
If energy were the whole story, every grid would end up all up or all down. But a warm material jiggles. Heat keeps knocking spins into random directions.

Physics gives an exact rule for how often each pattern \(s\) shows up at temperature \(T\), the Boltzmann distribution:

\[ P(s) = \frac{e^{-E(s)/T}}{Z}, \qquad Z = \sum_{\text{all patterns } s'} e^{-E(s')/T} \]
  • Lower energy → larger \(e^{-E/T}\) → more likely.
  • \(T\) decides how much energy matters. Small \(T\): energy differences are huge, so only the lowest-energy patterns appear. Large \(T\): every pattern is almost equally likely.
  • \(Z\), the partition function, is just the sum that makes the probabilities add up to 1.

(We measure \(T\) in units where Boltzmann's constant \(k_B\) is 1, so \(T\) and \(E\) can be divided directly.)

A 2×2 grid is small enough to list everything. It has 4 links and \(2^4 = 16\) patterns:

Patterns How many Energy all four spins agree 2 \(-4\) mixed (one or two spins differ) 12 \(0\) checkerboard 2 \(+4\)

So \(Z = 2e^{4/T} + 12 + 2e^{-4/T}\). At \(T = 2\) this is \(27.05\), and each all-agree pattern has probability \(e^{2}/27.05 = 27.3\%\).

Try it: drag the temperature. Each column is one of the 16 patterns with its probability bar.

🌡️ Interactive: all 16 patterns of a 2×2 grid

What to notice

  • Cold (T = 0.5): the two aligned patterns take 99.8% of the probability. Energy wins.
  • Warm (T = 2): each aligned pattern (27.3%) is still far more likely than each mixed pattern (3.7%). But there are 12 mixed patterns and only 2 aligned ones, so together the mixed ones already hold 44.4%.
  • Hot (T = 10): the bars are nearly level and the mixed patterns hold 73.5%, close to their share by pure counting (\(12/16 = 75\%\)). Numbers win.
  • This is the key trade-off of the whole lesson: low energy (few ordered patterns) against large numbers (many disordered patterns, which physicists call entropy). Temperature sets the exchange rate.

docs.title: Step 4 — One flip at a time: the Metropolis rule
docs.text:
Listing all patterns worked for 4 spins. A 64×64 grid has \(2^{4096}\) patterns, a number with 1,234 digits. We can never compute \(Z\).

The Metropolis algorithm (1953) avoids \(Z\) completely. It walks from pattern to pattern by trying to flip one spin at a time, and it only needs the energy change \(\Delta E\) of that single flip:

\[ \Delta E = 2\, s_i \Big( J \sum_{j \,\in\, \text{neighbours of } i} s_j + h \Big) \]

Only the spin's own links change, so only its four neighbours matter. The rule is then:

  • \(\Delta E \le 0\) (downhill or flat): always flip.
  • \(\Delta E > 0\) (uphill): flip anyway with probability \(e^{-\Delta E / T}\).

The second line is where temperature comes in. Uphill moves are how heat creates disorder: rare when it's cold, common when it's hot.

Try it: build a situation by clicking the spins, then change \(T\).

🎲 Interactive: should this spin flip?

What to notice

  • The starting situation (3 neighbours agree, 1 disagrees) is uphill by \(\Delta E = +4\). At \(T = 2\) the flip still happens 13.5% of the time.
  • Make all four neighbours agree with the centre: \(\Delta E = +8\) and the chance drops to 1.8%. A spin surrounded by friends almost never flips.
  • Make most neighbours disagree: \(\Delta E\) is negative and the flip is certain, whatever the temperature.
  • With \(h = 0\) only five values are possible: \(\Delta E \in \{-8, -4, 0, +4, +8\}\).

Repeating this rule many times makes the grid visit patterns exactly as often as the Boltzmann distribution says. One sweep means as many attempted flips as there are spins.

docs.title: Step 5 — Watch 4,096 spins at once
docs.text:
Here is the Metropolis loop running on a 64×64 grid. The edges wrap around (the left column is a neighbour of the right column), so no spin sits on a border. The grid starts with random spins.

Try it: press ▶ Play and watch for about 20 seconds. Then try the three temperature buttons, and Random start to begin again.

🔥 Interactive: a live Ising model

What to notice

  • Cold (T = 1.5): small patches form at once and then slowly eat each other. From this random start, \(m\) climbs to \(+0.37\) after 100 sweeps, \(+0.89\) after 300 and \(+0.98\) after 500. Nobody told the grid to choose "up". It was a tie, and chance broke it.
  • Hot (T = 3.5): fine-grained noise. \(m\) stays within a few hundredths of 0, and no patch survives.
  • Critical (T = 2.27): patches of every size, from single spins to blobs as wide as the grid, and \(m\) wanders slowly without settling. This is the most interesting temperature, and Step 6 is about it.
  • The field breaks the tie. At \(T = 3.5\), slide \(h\) to \(+0.50\): \(m\) jumps to about \(+0.6\) within ten sweeps. Slide it back to 0 and the magnetisation is forgotten. Now do the same at \(T = 1.5\): the grid stays magnetised after you remove the field. That memory is what makes a permanent magnet.
  • A cold grid sometimes gets stuck in two broad stripes. Their straight borders have no corners to shrink from, so the stripes can last a long time. It is an early taste of "stuck in a local minimum".

docs.title: Step 6 — The phase transition
docs.text:
Let's turn what you just watched into a measurement. For each temperature, run the simulation, wait for it to settle, and record the average of \(|m|\) (the absolute value, because up and down are equally good).

Try it: press Run. The green curve is the exact answer for an infinitely large grid.

📉 Interactive: magnetisation against temperature

What to notice

  • On the 32×32 grid the dots follow the exact curve closely while the grid is ordered: 0.986 at \(T = 1.5\) (exact: 0.986) and 0.908 at \(T = 2.0\) (exact: 0.911).
  • Between \(T = 2.2\) and \(T = 2.5\) the magnetisation collapses from 0.815 to 0.252. The order does not fade gradually; it breaks over a narrow range. This is a phase transition, like ice melting.
  • Switch to the 8 × 8 grid: the drop is smeared out, and at \(T = 4\) you still measure 0.191 (against 0.044 on the 32×32 grid). A small grid can't average its random spins away. The transition is only perfectly sharp for an infinite grid.

The exact position of the break is the critical temperature, found by Lars Onsager in 1944:

\[ T_c = \frac{2J}{\ln\!\left(1 + \sqrt{2}\right)} \approx 2.269 \]

Below it, the exact magnetisation of an infinite grid is

\[ m = \left[\,1 - \sinh^{-4}\!\left(\frac{2J}{T}\right)\right]^{1/8} \]

and above it, \(m = 0\). That is the green curve.

Why is there a sharp temperature? Go back to Step 2: a flipped island costs energy in proportion to its perimeter. When it's cold, large islands are too expensive, so one colour dominates. But the number of possible island shapes also grows with the perimeter. At \(T_c\) the two effects balance, islands of every size appear, and the dominant colour is lost.

Who solved what: Lenz, Ising, Onsager

Ernst Ising solved the one-dimensional model, a single chain of spins, in his 1924 thesis. He found no phase transition: a chain is disordered at every temperature above zero. The reason is the island argument again. In a chain, flipping a block of any length breaks just 2 links (its two ends), so large islands are cheap and they always destroy the order. Ising guessed that the same would happen in higher dimensions. He was wrong: Rudolf Peierls showed in 1936 that the 2-D model must order, and Onsager's 1944 solution gave the exact numbers above. The 3-D model still has no exact solution, only simulations like yours.

docs.title: Step 7 — An AI example: cleaning a noisy picture
docs.text:
The Ising model is also a tool. Take a black-and-white picture where some pixels have been flipped by noise. Two facts help us repair it:

  1. Most pixels are correct, so the answer should stay close to what we observe.
  2. Real pictures are smooth, so a pixel usually agrees with its neighbours.

Fact 2 is the Ising link term. Fact 1 is a field, but a different one for every pixel: it pulls pixel \(i\) towards its observed value \(y_i\).

\[ E(s) = -J \sum_{\langle i,j \rangle} s_i s_j \;-\; \sum_i s_i\, y_i \]

Here \(s\) is our guess for the clean picture and \(y\) is the noisy one (\(+1\) = ink, \(-1\) = paper). We look for a low-energy \(s\) in the simplest way: start from \(s = y\) and flip any pixel whose flip lowers the energy, until nothing changes. This is the Metropolis rule at \(T = 0\) (no uphill moves).

🧹 Interactive: denoising with an Ising energy

What to notice

  • With 10% noise, 152 of the 1,600 pixels are wrong. With J = 1 only 15 remain wrong (0.9%).
  • J = 0 ignores the neighbours, so the energy is lowest at \(s = y\) and nothing is repaired.
  • J = 0.3 is cautious: a pixel flips only when all four neighbours disagree with it. That leaves 76 wrong pixels, mostly where two noisy pixels touch.
  • Raise the noise to 30%: J = 1 still more than halves the errors (478 → 224), but clumps of noise now look like real shapes, and the model keeps them.

The general idea

A model like this, where each variable interacts only with its neighbours, is called a Markov random field. Geman and Geman introduced this picture-restoration recipe in 1984, using exactly the Ising analogy.

docs.title: Step 8 — From magnets to neural networks
docs.text:
So far \(J\) was the same on every link and fixed in advance. The step to machine learning is one sentence long: let every pair of units have its own weight \(w_{ij}\), and learn the weights.

\[ E(s) = -\sum_{i<j} w_{ij}\, s_i s_j \;-\; \sum_i b_i\, s_i \] Ising model Machine learning spin \(s_i = \pm 1\) a binary neuron, pixel or other variable coupling \(J\) a weight \(w_{ij}\) between two units field \(h\) a bias \(b_i\) energy \(E(s)\) the energy function of an energy-based model Boltzmann distribution the model's probability of a pattern; a softmax is the same formula temperature \(T\) sampling temperature (for example in a language model) Metropolis sweeps MCMC sampling (Gibbs sampling is a close relative) lowest-energy patterns stored memories (Hopfield) or likely data (Boltzmann machine)

What to notice: the temperature of a language model

A language model gives every possible next word a score \(z_k\) (a logit) and samples from

\[ P(k) = \frac{e^{z_k / T}}{\sum_{k'} e^{z_{k'}/T}} \]

This is the Boltzmann distribution with energy \(E_k = -z_k\). Low \(T\): the model almost always picks the top word (ordered, repetitive). High \(T\): all words become similar in probability (disordered, random). It is the same trade-off as in Step 3.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
The whole simulation fits in a few lines of NumPy:

import numpy as np

def simulate(T, L=32, sweeps=600, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    s = np.ones((L, L), dtype=int)                 # start with every spin up
    m = []
    for sweep in range(sweeps):
        for _ in range(L * L):                     # one sweep = L*L attempted flips
            i, j = rng.integers(L, size=2)         # 1. pick a random spin
            nb = (s[(i + 1) % L, j] + s[(i - 1) % L, j] +
                  s[i, (j + 1) % L] + s[i, (j - 1) % L])
            dE = 2 * s[i, j] * nb                  # 2. energy change if it flipped (J = 1, h = 0)
            if dE <= 0 or rng.random() < np.exp(-dE / T):
                s[i, j] *= -1                      # 3. Metropolis rule: flip
        if sweep >= 200:                           # skip the first 200 sweeps (settling in)
            m.append(abs(s.mean()))                # 4. measure
    return np.mean(m)

for T in [1.5, 2.27, 3.5]:
    print(f"T = {T}: average |m| = {simulate(T):.3f}")

T = 1.5: average |m| = 0.987
T = 2.27: average |m| = 0.573
T = 3.5: average |m| = 0.061

Ordered, in between, disordered. The plain Python loop takes about 25 seconds; real codes update half of the spins at once in a checkerboard pattern.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"The Ising model is only about magnets.\"

It is a model of any set of two-state things that influence their neighbours: atoms in an alloy, molecules in a gas (occupied / empty), neurons, pixels, opinions. Magnetism is just where it was born.

\"When it's hot, high-energy patterns are more likely than low-energy ones.\"

Never. At every temperature a single low-energy pattern is more likely than a single high-energy one (27.3% against 3.7% in the 2×2 grid at \(T = 2\)). Disorder wins when it's hot only because there are so many more disordered patterns.

\"Below the critical temperature the spins point up.\"

Up and down have exactly the same energy when \(h = 0\). The grid picks one of the two at random and then sticks with it. This is called spontaneous symmetry breaking. Only a field \(h \ne 0\) makes one direction better.

\"The Metropolis animation shows how a real magnet moves in time.\"

Metropolis is a sampling method. It is built so that the patterns it visits have the right probabilities, not so that the path between them is physically realistic. The pictures at each temperature are trustworthy; the "movie" is only a rough guide.

\"Ising discovered the phase transition.\"

Ising solved the 1-D chain, found no transition, and wrongly concluded that the model could not explain magnets. The 2-D transition was proved by Peierls (1936) and solved exactly by Onsager (1944).

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. A chain of three spins is ↑ ↑ ↓ (two links, J = 1, h = 0). What is its energy?

The first link agrees (\(-1\)), the second disagrees (\(+1\)), so \(E = -1 + 1 = 0\).

2. A spin points up and all four of its neighbours point up. At T = 1.5, how likely is Metropolis to flip it?

\(\Delta E = 2 \cdot (+1) \cdot (+4) = +8\), so the probability is \(e^{-8/1.5} = 0.48\%\). About one attempt in 200.

3. In the 2×2 grid at T = 2, which is more likely: finding the grid all up, or finding it in some mixed pattern?

Some mixed pattern. All up has probability 27.3%. Each mixed pattern has only 3.7%, but there are 12 of them, so together they have 44.4%.

4. Why does a chain of spins (1-D) never order, while a grid (2-D) does?

In a chain, flipping a block of any length breaks only 2 links, so big disordering islands are cheap at any temperature above zero. In a grid, an island costs energy in proportion to its perimeter, so big islands are rare when it's cold.

5. A model scores two words with logits 2 and 0. What is the probability of the first word at T = 1 and at T = 0.5?

At \(T = 1\): \(e^{2}/(e^{2} + e^{0}) = 88.1\%\). At \(T = 0.5\): \(e^{4}/(e^{4} + 1) = 98.2\%\). Lowering the temperature sharpens the choice, exactly as it orders the spins.

6. In the denoising energy, what plays the role of the field h, and why is it different for every pixel?

The observed pixel \(y_i\). It pulls each pixel of the answer towards the value that was actually seen at that position, so it must be local. A single global \(h\) would only make the whole picture darker or lighter.

docs.text:

  • Nicholas Metropolis, Arianna Rosenbluth, Marshall Rosenbluth, Augusta Teller and Edward Teller, Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines, Journal of Chemical Physics 21 (1953), 1087–1092. The Metropolis algorithm.
