docs.title: Tsetlin Machine Autoencoders and Word Embeddings
docs.text:
TL;DR

Most text and clinical records come without labels. A Tsetlin machine autoencoder still learns from them: it hides one word of a document and tries to predict it from the words that are left. Every word is an output, and all outputs share one pool of rules. Each rule has a signed integer weight per output word: positive means "when this rule fires, the hidden word is probably there", negative means "probably not". Training uses the same Recognize, Erase and Reject Feedback as classification. The hidden word is masked: it counts as True and its memory is frozen. Training examples are balanced (the hidden word is present in half of them), and each one is the OR of a few documents. After training, a word's row of positive weights is its embedding: a short list of readable rules such as "fever AND sputum" or "breathless AND wheeze" for cough. Words with similar rows are used in similar contexts. On 600 generated clinical notes, the nearest neighbour of every one of 18 findings came from the same condition (17.5 of 18 on average over 10 seeds).

Level: intermediate · Prerequisites: Classification by voting (rules voting for and against, the vote sum \(v\), the Voting Margin \(T\)) and Weighted clauses and clause sharing (rules with integer weights, a pool of rules shared by several outputs). You need nothing beyond AND, OR, counting, and a cosine.

Beyond the book

The book chapter on this topic, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines, Ch. 6 "Auto-Encoding", is not published yet. This lesson is based on the research papers listed in Further reading, mainly Bhattarai et al. (2024), and on the TMAutoEncoder in the CAIR group's TMU library. It uses the book's vocabulary. The clinical notes, the code and every number not attributed to a paper come from our own runs, made for this lesson.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
Labels are expensive. Someone has to read each note or image and write down the answer. Unlabelled text is everywhere: discharge letters, referral notes, radiology reports, the scientific literature. A model that can learn something useful from the text alone is very valuable.

  • Words get their meaning from their company. "Words that occur in the same contexts tend to have similar meanings" (the distributional hypothesis, Harris 1954). Cough keeps company with fever and sputum in some notes and with wheeze in others. A model that learns this company has learned something about what cough means, without anyone defining it.
  • Embeddings power modern NLP, but you can't read them. Word2Vec and GloVe turn each word into about 300 decimal numbers. Similar words get similar vectors, but no single number means anything to a person.
  • A Tsetlin machine embedding is made of rules. Bhattarai et al. (2024) represent each word by the logical rules that predict it, for example coffee by rules over hot, cup and black. You can read why two words are similar: they are predicted by the same rules.

This lesson builds that autoencoder step by step and trains it on a small set of generated clinical notes, where you know the truth and can check what it learns.

docs.title: Step 1 — Learning without labels: hide a word, predict it
docs.text:
Take a short clinical note and treat it as a set of words, ignoring order and repeats:

fever, cough, sputum, chest pain

Each word of the vocabulary becomes a Boolean feature \(x_k\): True if the note mentions it. This is the usual bag-of-words Booleanisation, as in the first lesson.

Now hide one word, say cough, and ask: given the rest of the note, was cough there? The answer is in the note itself, so you can make as many training examples as you have notes, without asking anyone for labels. This is self-supervised learning: the data supplies its own targets. Hiding part of the input and predicting it is the same trick as the "masked word" task used to pre-train BERT, here with logic instead of a neural network.

To get the hidden word right, the model has to learn what cough usually comes with. If fever and sputum are there, cough is likely. If sneezing and runny nose are there, it is less likely. These co-occurrence patterns are exactly what an AND-rule can express.

An autoencoder does this for every word at once: its output has one slot \(\hat x_k\) per input word, and \(\hat x_k\) is predicted from all the other inputs. A neural autoencoder squeezes the input through a small hidden layer. The Tsetlin machine version squeezes it through a small pool of rules instead.

What to notice

  • No labels are needed: the target is a word the note already contains (or doesn't).
  • The task is a means to an end. What we want is not a perfect predictor of hidden words, but the rules the machine has to learn in order to predict them.

docs.title: Step 2 — One pool of rules, one weight per word
docs.text:
A separate Tsetlin machine for each of the 18 words would learn 18 separate rule sets, and fever AND sputum would have to be discovered again for cough, for chest pain and for fatigue. The autoencoder of Bhattarai et al. (2024) instead builds on the coalesced Tsetlin machine (Glimsdal & Granmo, 2021; the weighted lesson covers it): one pool of \(n\) rules shared by all outputs, and a signed integer weight \(w_{kj}\) that connects rule \(j\) to output word \(k\).

In symbols, with rules \(C_1, \dots, C_n\) (in the papers: clauses), each an AND of words, the prediction for word \(k\) is

\[ v_k = \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_{kj}\, C_j(x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}, 1, x_{k+1}, \dots, x_m), \qquad \hat x_k = \begin{cases} 1 & v_k \ge 0 \\ 0 & v_k < 0. \end{cases} \]

The \(1\) in position \(k\) is the mask. It replaces the real value of \(x_k\), so a rule like "fever AND cough AND sputum" acts as "fever AND sputum" when it predicts cough. That is how the same rule can serve as context for cough and, unmasked, for fatigue.

Two details differ from the classification lessons:

  • No rules "for" and "against". The sign of the weight says which way a rule votes, and it can change during training. The same rule can vote for one word and against another.
  • No negated literals in Bhattarai et al.'s version: a rule only says which words must be present. TMU's implementation can add the negations (\(\lnot x_k\), "the note does not mention …"), and Kadhim et al. (2024) study that variant. We stick to the paper.

What to notice

  • One rule, many words. With \(n = 24\) rules and 18 words there are \(18 \times 24 = 432\) weights but only 24 rules to learn. A useful context such as "fever AND sputum" is learned once and reused by every word it predicts.
  • A tie (\(v_k = 0\), for example when no rule fires) counts as "present", following the paper's \(\hat x_k = [0 \le v_k]\). The classification lesson sent ties the other way; this choice doesn't matter for the embeddings, which come from the weights.

docs.title: Step 3 — Building a training example: a coin flip and a handful of notes
docs.text:
Bhattarai et al. make each training example in a particular way (their Algorithm 1). For a target word \(k\):

  1. Flip a fair coin for the target value \(q\). With \(q = 1\) the example will contain word \(k\); with \(q = 0\) it won't. Rare words are therefore present in half of their examples, however rare they are in the data. (TMU calls this output_balancing = 0.5.)
  2. Pick \(u\) notes at random that mention word \(k\) (if \(q = 1\)) or don't (if \(q = 0\)). The paper calls \(u\) the accumulation.
  3. OR them together: the example contains every word that appears in any of the \(u\) notes. Combining several notes makes rare context words show up more often, which helps the rules pick them up.
  4. Mask word \(k\) and train output \(k\) to answer \(q\).

One round of training makes one such example for every word of the vocabulary, in random order.

Our toy data are 600 generated clinical notes (plus 300 held out for testing), using 18 findings. Each note comes from one condition (sometimes two) chosen at random, and each condition mentions its typical findings with fixed probabilities: pneumonia (fever, cough, sputum, chest pain, breathless, fatigue), asthma (wheeze, breathless, cough), hay fever (sneezing, runny nose, itchy eyes), gastroenteritis (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, stomach ache, sometimes fever), diabetes (thirst, frequent urination, weight loss, fatigue) and migraine (headache, often nausea). Every other finding turns up by chance 3% of the time. 125 of the 600 notes come from two conditions, and a note mentions 3.71 findings on average. Some findings belong to two conditions on purpose (cough, fever, fatigue, nausea, breathless), like a word with two meanings. The conditions are never shown to the machine; we use them only to check its answers.

🎲 Interactive: build one training example

What to notice

  • The coin flip balances the classes. Chest pain is in 76 of the 600 notes (12.7%), yet it is present in half of its training examples. Without balancing, "never there" would be right 87% of the time and the rules would have little reason to learn.
  • Accumulation adds context, and noise. Averaged over all 18 target words, an example built from \(u = 1\) note has 3.63 context words when the target is present; with \(u = 2\) it has 5.73, with \(u = 3\) 7.12, and with \(u = 5\) 9.36 (more when the target is absent: 3.53, 6.20, 8.21 and 11.14). With only 18 words, a few notes already switch on half the vocabulary. In a corpus with tens of thousands of words, the paper's \(u = 25\) is what makes rare context words visible at all.
  • Try headache with \(u = 1\). Of its 114 training notes, 38 mention nothing else or only nausea; its other companions depend on whatever second condition a note happens to have. A word with little steady company has little context to be predicted from.

docs.title: Step 4 — Feedback: the weight's sign decides the role
docs.text:
Training an output word \(k\) on an example \((x, q)\) is the familiar recipe from the feedback lesson and classification, with the weight's sign deciding which way each rule is trained.

1. How much feedback? Compute the vote sum \(v_k\) on the masked example (empty rules count as True while training) and clip it to \([-T, T]\). Each rule is picked for feedback independently with probability

\[ p = \frac{T - v_k}{2T} \;\text{ if } q = 1, \qquad p = \frac{T + v_k}{2T} \;\text{ if } q = 0. \]

This is the Voting Margin \(T\) again: the target is \(v_k \ge T\) when the word is there and \(v_k \le -T\) when it is not.

2. Which feedback? A rule with \(w_{kj} \ge 0\) is trying to fire when the word is present; a rule with \(w_{kj} < 0\) is trying to fire when it is absent. So, for a picked rule:

rule fires (\(C_j = 1\)) rule does not fire its weight's sign matches the target (\(w \ge 0\) and \(q = 1\), or \(w < 0\) and \(q = 0\)) Recognize Feedback, then the weight moves towards \(q\) Erase Feedback its weight's sign does not match Reject Feedback, then the weight moves towards \(q\) nothing

"The weight moves towards \(q\)" means \(w_{kj} \mathrel{+}= 1\) if \(q = 1\) and \(w_{kj} \mathrel{-}= 1\) if \(q = 0\). So a rule that fires on notes with the word is rewarded with a larger weight, and a rule that fires on notes without it loses weight. A rule that keeps firing on the wrong side can cross zero and change its role: the paper notes that it then trains to recognise the word's absence instead.

3. The masked word is frozen. Recognize, Erase and Reject Feedback skip word \(k\) itself: its memory position in every rule stays where it is. Otherwise a rule would learn "cough" as context for predicting cough, which is useless (and the mask makes it always True anyway).

As in the paper, Recognize Feedback memorizes present words with Memorize Value 1 and forgets absent ones with Forget Value \(1/s\). In the research papers: Recognize = Type Ia, Erase = Type Ib, Reject = Type II.

One extra detail from the TMU code

TMU's TMAutoEncoder adds a brake that the paper does not describe. At the start of each round, a rule takes part (votes and learns) only with probability \((T - \bar w_j)/T\), where \(\bar w_j\) is the rule's average absolute weight over all output words, capped at \(T\). A rule that has collected large weights has found its role and is rarely disturbed. Without the brake, our rules sometimes drifted to new words while keeping weights earned by their old words. We use the brake. TMU's demo also caps every rule at 3 words (a "literal budget"); we don't.

What to notice

  • Nothing here is new machinery. An autoencoder is a multi-output, weighted Tsetlin machine with two twists: the input it sees is masked, and the training examples are sampled in a balanced way.
  • The weights are integers that only ever move by ±1, so a weight of +12 means "this rule fired on examples with the word, 12 more times than on examples without it, when it was picked for feedback".

docs.title: Step 5 — What the rules learn
docs.text:
We trained the autoencoder on the 600 notes with 24 rules, Voting Margin \(T = 24\), Forget Value \(1/s\) with \(s = 4\), memory depth 100 (positions 1–100, Memorized above 50), \(u = 2\) notes per example, and 300 rounds (each round one example per word, so 5,400 examples). It takes about two seconds in plain Python, and the widget below runs the same seeded code (seed 7), so its numbers match ours exactly.

Hide a word, build a note, and see which rules vote:

🙈 Interactive: hide a word, let the rules vote

What to notice

  • Cough has two contexts. Its strongest rules are R16 "fever AND sputum" (+12), the pneumonia context, and R13 "breathless AND wheeze" (+7), the asthma context. A single average vector can't show this; a list of rules can. Bhattarai et al. see the same with real words: heart and surgery share the rules went ∧ hospital and old ∧ disease ∧ patient, while heart also has woman ∧ love.
  • Rules can contain the hidden word. R7 is "fever AND cough AND sputum" (+5). For cough the mask makes it "fever AND sputum"; the rule is shared, and for fatigue (+11) it really does need cough.
  • Negative weights are the "unlikely" contexts. For cough: −11 for "thirst AND frequent urination" and −10 for "sneezing AND runny nose AND itchy eyes".
  • Try the presets. fever + sputum + chest pain: R7 (+5) and R16 (+12) fire, \(v = +17\), cough predicted present. breathless + wheeze: only R13 fires, \(v = +7\). sneezing + runny nose: no rule fires (the hay-fever rules also want itchy eyes), so \(v = 0\), a tie, which the paper's rule counts as "present". Hide fatigue and use thirst + frequent urination: three diabetes rules fire, \(v = 9 + 8 + 10 = +27\).
  • Not every rule is clean. Fatigue has weight +8 on R1 "wheeze AND frequent urination", a rule that matches only 16 of the 600 training notes (9 with fatigue, 7 without). Compare R16 for cough: 74 notes, 65 of them with cough. Check how often a rule fires before you read much into it.
  • Headache has no strong rules for it. In migraine notes it comes with nothing but (sometimes) nausea, and nausea is more often a gastroenteritis word (77 of its 162 notes also mention vomiting, 58 mention headache). Little steady context, no strong rule.

docs.title: Step 6 — From rules to embeddings
docs.text:
After training, the weight matrix \(W\) (18 words × 24 rules) holds everything the machine learned about each word's company. Bhattarai et al. turn it into embeddings in two ways:

  • the weighted logical embedding \(E = \operatorname{clip}(W, 0, T)\): keep the positive weights, set negative ones to zero, cap at \(T\);
  • the purely logical embedding \(B = [W > 0]\): just which rules vote for the word.

Row \(k\) of \(E\) is the embedding of word \(k\): a vector with one entry per rule. Two words are compared with the cosine similarity of their rows,

\[ \cos(\mathbf e_k, \mathbf e_l) = \frac{\mathbf e_k \cdot \mathbf e_l}{\lVert \mathbf e_k \rVert \, \lVert \mathbf e_l \rVert}, \]

which is 1 when two words put their weight on the same rules in the same proportions, and 0 when they share no rule. Unlike a Word2Vec vector, every coordinate has a name: it is a rule you can read.

🗺️ Interactive: train the autoencoder and explore the embedding

What to notice

  • The blocks on the diagonal are the conditions. With the defaults, the nearest neighbour of every one of the 18 words comes from a condition it belongs to: sneezing → itchy eyes (0.93), nausea → stomach ache, thirst → frequent urination.
  • Two-context words sit between their groups. Cough is close to sputum (0.55) and less close to wheeze (0.32), and far from sneezing (0.07). Fatigue is closest to thirst (0.72) but also related to fever (0.40), and unrelated to itchy eyes (0.01).
  • The embedding is sparse. Each word puts positive weight on only 3 to 9 of the 24 rules (6.7 on average). Bhattarai et al. report that with 600 rules, a word links to at most 10% of them.
  • Compare with plain counting. Switch "similarity from" to co-occurrence counts (PPMI): cosine similarity of positive pointwise mutual information, a classic count-based embedding computed from the same 600 notes. It gets 16 of 18 nearest neighbours right. On this toy data counting works almost as well; what the rules add is that you can read why two words are similar.
  • Change \(u\). With \(u = 5\), almost every example contains half the vocabulary and the rules get long and vague. Change the seed to see how much a single run varies.

docs.title: Step 7 — How good is it, honestly?
docs.text:
Our nearest-neighbour check is crude, and the data are generated. Still, it shows the trade-offs. We repeated the training with 10 seeds (1–10) for several values of \(u\), and also scored each model as a hidden-word predictor on the 300 held-out notes. Because most words are absent from most notes, we use balanced accuracy: the average of the hit rate on notes with the word and on notes without it (a coin scores 50%).

notes per example \(u\) nearest neighbour from the same condition (of 18) hidden-word balanced accuracy, mean ± sd 1 16.8 (16–17) 76.2% ± 1.3 2 (our default) 17.5 (17–18) 72.8% ± 2.4 3 16.6 (16–17) 64.3% ± 2.5 5 16.2 (15–17) 53.8% ± 1.6 baselines on the same notes raw co-occurrence counts: 13; PPMI: 16 logistic regression per word: 84.3%
  • It is not the best predictor of hidden words. A logistic regression for each word (scikit-learn, balanced class weights) predicts the hidden word better: 84.3% against 72.8%. The autoencoder's 24 shared rules, trained on ORs of several notes, are tuned for describing contexts, not for predicting single notes. The bigger \(u\), the further the training examples are from a single note, and the worse the prediction.
  • The embedding is good on this toy, but so is counting. PPMI gets 16 of 18. The point of the Tsetlin machine embedding is that each similarity can be explained by rules.
  • Single runs vary. The default run (seed 7) is one of the better ones (18 of 18) and scores 69.9% balanced accuracy.

What the papers report (on real text, not our toy). Bhattarai et al. (2024) trained on the One Billion Word benchmark with 600 rules, \(T = 1200\), \(s = 5\), \(u = 25\) and 2,000 examples per word. On six word-similarity benchmarks, the average Spearman correlation with human similarity scores was 0.52 for the TM embedding, against 0.58 for Word2Vec, 0.57 for GloVe and 0.54 for FastText (trained on the same data), so slightly behind. Used as input features to a BiLSTM classifier, their purely logical embedding was close to pre-trained GloVe on six text-classification tasks, e.g. 96.40% vs 95.20% accuracy on TREC and 75.61% vs 76.38% on SST-2. Kadhim et al. (2024) add negated words to the rules ("reasoning by elimination") and report 90.62% accuracy on IMDB sentiment. Kadhim et al. (2025, preprint) build the embedding from the whole memory of every rule, including forgotten words, so that one training run gives reusable embeddings for all words.

What our toy data can and can't show

The notes were generated from six conditions with fixed probabilities, so the "right answer" is known and clean. Real clinical notes have negation ("no fever"), synonyms, abbreviations, and thousands of words. Don't read our numbers as evidence about real records; read them as a demonstration of the mechanism.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is a complete autoencoder in numpy, about 80 lines including the data generator. It follows Steps 2–6 line by line, vectorised over rules and words, and includes TMU's brake from Step 4. It uses numpy's random numbers and its own copy of the notes, so its rules and numbers differ a little from the widgets'.

import numpy as np

# ---- 1. Toy clinical notes: each note is the SET of findings it mentions (no labels are used)
WORDS = ["fever", "cough", "sputum", "chest pain", "breathless", "wheeze", "sneezing", "runny nose",
         "itchy eyes", "nausea", "vomiting", "diarrhoea", "stomach ache", "thirst", "frequent urination",
         "weight loss", "fatigue", "headache"]
CONDITIONS = [{"fever": .9, "cough": .9, "sputum": .7, "chest pain": .5, "breathless": .5, "fatigue": .5},
              {"wheeze": .9, "breathless": .8, "cough": .6},
              {"sneezing": .9, "runny nose": .9, "itchy eyes": .7},
              {"nausea": .8, "vomiting": .7, "diarrhoea": .8, "stomach ache": .7, "fever": .3},
              {"thirst": .8, "frequent urination": .8, "weight loss": .5, "fatigue": .7},
              {"headache": .95, "nausea": .5}]
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
P = np.array([[c.get(w, 0.03) for w in WORDS] for c in CONDITIONS])     # 3% noise for every other word
notes = []
while len(notes) < 600:
    cs = rng.choice(6, size=1 + (rng.random() < 0.2), replace=False)    # one condition, sometimes two
    x = rng.random(len(WORDS)) < P[cs].max(axis=0)
    if x.any():
        notes.append(x)
X = np.array(notes)
m = len(WORDS)


class TMAutoEncoder:
    """Shared pool of rules; W[k, j] = signed integer weight of rule j for output word k."""

    def __init__(self, n_rules=24, T=24, s=4.0, depth=100, u=2, seed=7):
        self.T, self.s, self.depth, self.half, self.u = T, s, depth, depth // 2, u
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.memory = np.full((n_rules, m), depth // 2)                     # top of Forgotten
        self.W = self.rng.choice([-1, 1], size=(m, n_rules))

    def fires(self, x, k, training=False):
        x = x.copy(); x[k] = True                                           # mask: the hidden word counts as True
        memorized = self.memory > self.half
        ok = ~np.any(memorized & ~x, axis=1)
        return ok if training else ok & memorized.any(axis=1)               # empty rules: silent when predicting

    def predict(self, x, k):
        return int(self.W[k] @ self.fires(x, k) >= 0)                       # x̂_k = 1 if v ≥ 0

    def update(self, k, x, q, active):
        C = self.fires(x, k, training=True) & active                        # inactive rules sit this round out
        v = np.clip(self.W[k] @ C, -self.T, self.T)
        p = (self.T - v) / (2 * self.T) if q else (self.T + v) / (2 * self.T)
        picked = (self.rng.random(len(C)) <= p) & active
        recog = (self.W[k] >= 0) == bool(q)                                 # rules that want to fire for this q
        u = self.rng.random(self.memory.shape) <= 1 / self.s                # Forget Value 1/s
        not_k = np.arange(m) != k                                           # the masked word is frozen
        mem = self.memory
        rec = (picked & recog & C)[:, None] & not_k                         # Recognize: memorize present, forget absent
        mem += rec & x & (mem < self.depth)
        mem -= rec & ~x & u & (mem > 1)
        era = (picked & recog & ~C)[:, None] & not_k                        # Erase: forget everything
        mem -= era & u & (mem > 1)
        rej = (picked & ~recog & C)[:, None] & not_k                        # Reject: memorize absent forgotten words
        mem += rej & ~x & (mem <= self.half)
        self.W[k] += np.where(picked & C, 1 if q else -1, 0)                # weights follow the target value

    def fit(self, X, rounds=300):
        for _ in range(rounds):
            # TMU detail: a rule whose weights are already large (on average) is rarely updated
            avg = np.abs(self.W).mean(axis=0)
            active = self.rng.random(len(avg)) <= (self.T - np.minimum(avg, self.T)) / self.T
            for k in self.rng.permutation(m):
                q = self.rng.random() < 0.5                                 # balanced: present or absent
                pool = np.flatnonzero(X[:, k] == q)
                x = X[self.rng.choice(pool, size=self.u)].any(axis=0)       # OR of u notes
                self.update(k, x, q, active)
        return self

    def rule(self, j, k):
        lits = [f"[{w}]" if i == k else w for i, (w, mm) in enumerate(zip(WORDS, self.memory[j])) if mm > self.half]
        return " AND ".join(lits) or "(empty)"


tm = TMAutoEncoder().fit(X)
E = np.clip(tm.W, 0, tm.T)                                                 # the embedding: one row per word
unit = E / np.linalg.norm(E, axis=1, keepdims=True)
S = unit @ unit.T
for w in ["cough", "fatigue", "sneezing"]:
    k = WORDS.index(w)
    best = np.argsort(-tm.W[k])[:3]
    print(f"{w}: " + " | ".join(f"{tm.W[k, j]:+d} IF {tm.rule(j, k)}" for j in best))
    print("   nearest:", ", ".join(f"{WORDS[b]} {S[k, b]:.2f}" for b in np.argsort(-S[k])[1:4]))

cough: +12 IF fever AND [cough] AND sputum AND breathless | +12 IF breathless AND wheeze | +10 IF sputum AND fatigue
   nearest: sputum 0.87, fever 0.84, breathless 0.82
fatigue: +10 IF thirst | +9 IF thirst AND frequent urination AND [fatigue] | +6 IF sputum AND [fatigue]
   nearest: frequent urination 0.72, thirst 0.68, weight loss 0.63
sneezing: +16 IF [sneezing] AND runny nose AND itchy eyes | +14 IF runny nose AND itchy eyes | +10 IF [sneezing] AND runny nose AND itchy eyes
   nearest: runny nose 0.86, itchy eyes 0.80, fatigue 0.06

The square brackets mark the masked word. The same story appears with different random numbers: cough is described by a pneumonia rule and an asthma rule, fatigue by diabetes rules and a pneumonia rule. Sneezing has two copies of the same rule, which act like one rule with a bigger weight. It runs in under two seconds.

Piece What it does Book term (research term) Hidden word \(x_k\) the output to predict; counts as True and is frozen (masked input variable) Shared pool of rules every output word uses the same rules rules (clauses of a coalesced TM) Weight \(w_{kj}\) signed integer; its sign says which way rule \(j\) votes for word \(k\) weight (clause weight) Vote sum \(v_k\) \(\sum_j w_{kj} C_j\); word present if \(v_k \ge 0\) vote sum (weighted clause sum) Voting Margin \(T\) feedback probability \((T \mp v_k)/2T\) Voting Margin (target \(T\)) Coin flip \(q\), accumulation \(u\) balanced examples built from \(u\) notes ORed together (output balancing, accumulation) Embedding \(\operatorname{clip}(W, 0, T)\) a word = its positive weights on readable rules (weighted logical embedding \(E\))

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"An autoencoder needs labels, like any Tsetlin machine.\"

No. The targets come from the data: each example asks whether a word that the notes do or don't contain was there. The only "label" is the hidden word itself. That is why it can learn from unlabelled text.

\"Each word gets its own rules.\"

All words share one pool of rules. What a word owns is a row of weights. In our run, R7 "fever AND cough AND sputum" has weight +5 for cough (where cough is masked) and +11 for fatigue, where all three words are real context.

\"The embedding is just co-occurrence counts in disguise.\"

It is built from co-occurrence, like every embedding, and on our toy data PPMI counts give similar neighbours (16 of 18, against 17.5 on average for the autoencoder). But each coordinate of the TM embedding is an AND-rule over several words, such as "breathless AND wheeze". That separates the asthma context of cough from its pneumonia context, and you can read it.

\"A bigger accumulation u is always better.\"

Not on a small vocabulary. With 18 words, \(u = 5\) notes already switch on about 9 to 11 context words per example, so rules get long and vague: our hidden-word balanced accuracy fell from 76.2% (\(u = 1\)) to 53.8% (\(u = 5\)). The paper's \(u = 25\) suits a corpus with tens of thousands of words, where most words are rare.

\"Logical embeddings beat neural embeddings.\"

The paper's results are mixed: slightly behind Word2Vec and GloVe on word-similarity correlations, close to GloVe as input to a text classifier. The selling points are sparsity and readability, not accuracy.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. The note is {fever, sputum, chest pain} and the hidden word is cough. Rule R7 is \"fever AND cough AND sputum\". Does it fire?

Yes. The hidden word counts as True, so for predicting cough the rule only needs fever and sputum, which are both there. In our trained model R7 has weight +5 for cough and R16 "fever AND sputum" has +12, so \(v = +17\) and cough is predicted present.

2. T = 24, the hidden word is present (q = 1) and v = −8. What is the feedback probability? What happens to a picked rule with weight −3 that fires?

\(p = (24 - (-8))/48 = 32/48 \approx 0.67\). The rule's weight is negative (it votes "absent"), but the word is present, so its sign doesn't match: it gets Reject Feedback (an absent, Forgotten word is pushed towards its memory, to stop it firing on such notes), and because it fired, its weight moves towards \(q = 1\): from −3 to −2.

3. Why flip a coin for the target value instead of using notes as they come?

Most words are absent from most notes (chest pain is in only 12.7% of ours). Unbalanced, the easiest answer would be "absent" every time, the vote sums would sit near \(-T\), and there would be little feedback to learn the contexts in which the word does appear. The coin flip makes present and absent equally common for every word, rare or not.

4. Two words have cosine similarity 0 between their embeddings. What does that mean in terms of rules?

No rule has a positive weight for both words: they share no context rule. In our run fatigue and itchy eyes score 0.01, almost no overlap. Since every coordinate is a rule, you can list the rules each word uses and see exactly what they don't share.

5. Why is the hidden word frozen during feedback, and not just masked?

The mask makes it True, so it would look like a present word in every example. Recognize Feedback would then keep memorizing it into the rules for this output, and the rule would end up "predicting" the word from itself. Freezing its memory position keeps the rule's content about the other words. (The word can still enter a rule through feedback for other outputs, where it is real context.)

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Bimal Bhattarai, Ole-Christoffer Granmo, Lei Jiao, Rohan Yadav & Jivitesh Sharma, Tsetlin Machine Embedding: Representing Words Using Logical Expressions, Findings of EACL 2024, pp. 1512–1522 (preprint arXiv:2301.00709). The Tsetlin machine autoencoder, masking and freezing, the balanced sampling with accumulation (Algorithm 1), and the logical embeddings \(E\) and \(B\). This lesson follows it.
  • Sondre Glimsdal & Ole-Christoffer Granmo, Coalesced Multi-Output Tsetlin Machines with Clause Sharing (2021). The shared pool of rules with signed weights per output that the autoencoder is built on.
  • Ahmed K. Kadhim, Ole-Christoffer Granmo, Lei Jiao & Rishad Shafik, Exploring State Space and Reasoning by Elimination in Tsetlin Machines (2024). The autoencoder with negated words in the rules, and how \(T\) and \(s\) shape them.
  • Ahmed K. Kadhim, Lei Jiao, Rishad Shafik & Ole-Christoffer Granmo, Omni TM-AE: A Scalable and Interpretable Embedding Model Using the Full Tsetlin Machine State Space (2025, preprint). Embeddings from the whole memory of each rule, in one training run.
  • The TMU library (CAIR, University of Agder): TMAutoEncoder in tmu/models/autoencoder/autoencoder.py, and the IMDb word-embedding demo in examples/autoencoder/, which learns which words keep company with targets such as awful, brilliant and scary.
  • Ole-Christoffer Granmo, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines (free online). Chapter 6, "Auto-Encoding", is announced but not yet published.
  • Zellig S. Harris, Distributional Structure, Word 10 (1954). The distributional hypothesis behind every word embedding.

docs.title: Many Rules Voting: Classification with a Tsetlin Machine
docs.text:
TL;DR

One AND-rule can describe only one kind of patient. A Tsetlin machine therefore uses a whole team of rules: some vote for a class, some vote against it. Each rule whose condition is True casts one vote, and the vote sum \(v\) (votes for minus votes against) decides the class. During training, a single number, the Voting Margin \(T\), decides how much feedback each example hands out: examples the team already gets right by a margin of \(T\) votes give no feedback at all, and examples it gets wrong give a lot. That simple rule makes the rules spread out over different sub-patterns instead of all learning the same one. This lesson builds the complete machine, extends it to many classes, and runs it end to end on the breast-cancer recurrence data, with an honest look at the accuracy.

Level: beginner–intermediate · Prerequisites: Recognize, Erase & Reject feedback (how a single rule learns). Fractions and a sum are all the math you need.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
In the last lesson a single rule learned a single pattern, such as "if Deg-malig 3 and not Menopause lt40 then Recurrence". Real classes are rarely that tidy:

  • Patients recur for different reasons. In the breast-cancer data, some recurrences come with a highly malignant tumour, others with many affected lymph nodes, and a rule demanding both misses everyone who has only one of them.
  • Evidence should add up. A clinician weighs several findings, some pointing towards recurrence and some away from it. A sum of votes does the same thing, and you can still read every vote as a plain rule.
  • This is the whole machine. Everything from the earlier lessons (literals, the graded memory, the three kinds of feedback) comes together here. After this lesson you can write a working Tsetlin machine in about 70 lines of numpy and read what it learned.

The ideas follow Granmo, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines, Ch. 1, §1.5–1.7, and Ch. 2, §2.3. The visuals and code are redrawn and rewritten for this site.

docs.title: Step 1 — One rule is not enough
docs.text:
A rule in a Tsetlin machine is an AND of literals: every memorized literal must be True for the rule to fire. That makes each rule a description of one kind of object. But a class often contains several kinds.

Look at the 85 patients with a recurrence in the UCI breast-cancer data (286 patients in total; we count "3 or more involved lymph nodes" as not Inv-nodes 0-2):

Recurrence patients (85) how many Deg-malig 3 and 3+ involved nodes 27 Deg-malig 3 only 18 3+ involved nodes only 12 neither 28

And how often patients with each profile recur, out of everyone with that profile:

Profile recurred Deg-malig 3 and 3+ nodes 27 of 37 (73%) Deg-malig 3 only 18 of 48 (38%) 3+ nodes only 12 of 36 (33%) neither 28 of 165 (17%)

There are (at least) two recurrence profiles: a highly malignant tumour, and spread to the lymph nodes. The single rule "Deg-malig 3 AND not Inv-nodes 0-2" only catches the 27 patients who have both. To also catch the 18 + 12 who have just one of them, you need an OR: "Deg-malig 3" or "not Inv-nodes 0-2". An AND-rule cannot express an OR, but two rules can: one for each profile.

This is the general recipe. Any yes/no pattern can be written as an OR of AND-rules (logicians call it disjunctive normal form), so a team of AND-rules can describe any class, as long as the team is big enough and its members learn different things. Making them learn different things is the main topic of this lesson.

What to notice

  • One AND-rule = one sub-pattern (one "profile"). Several sub-patterns need several rules.
  • None of the profiles is certain: even the strongest one recurs in only 73% of cases, and 28 of the 85 recurrences fit neither profile. Keep this in mind when we measure accuracy in Step 6.

docs.title: Step 2 — Rules vote: the vote sum v
docs.text:
A Tsetlin machine for two classes has two groups of rules:

  • rules that vote for the class (here: Recurrence),
  • rules that vote against it (they vote for No recurrence).

To classify a patient, every rule checks its condition on the patient's literals. Each rule whose condition is True casts one vote. Then

\[ v \;=\; \underbrace{\#\{\text{rules for Recurrence that fire}\}}_{\text{votes for}} \;-\; \underbrace{\#\{\text{rules against that fire}\}}_{\text{votes against}} \]

and the machine predicts Recurrence if \(v > 0\) and No recurrence otherwise. A tie (\(v = 0\)) has to go one way or the other; here it goes to the more common class, No recurrence (the book's notebook sends ties to the first class instead, and the convolutional lesson follows the notebook). (In the research papers the two groups are the positive and negative polarity clauses \(C^+_j\) and \(C^-_j\), and \(v = \sum_j C^+_j - \sum_j C^-_j\).) An empty rule, one with no literals memorized, stays silent when classifying.

The book's first example uses the six patients from the earlier lessons and three rules: R1 and R2 are the same rule, "Deg-malig 3 and not Menopause lt40", voting for Recurrence, and R3, "Inv-nodes 0-2", votes against. Pick the book's patients in the widget below:

🗳️ Interactive: rules vote on a patient

What to notice

  • Patient #1 (ge40, 3-5 nodes, Deg-malig 3): R1 and R2 fire, R3 does not, so \(v = +2\) → Recurrence. Correct.
  • Patient #5 (premeno, 0-2 nodes, Deg-malig 3) fires all three rules: R3 votes against because of the 0-2 nodes. The duplicate R1 + R2 still win, \(v = 2 - 1 = +1\). A lone rule would have been out-voted to a tie. Duplicated rules act as a weight.
  • The vote sums for the six patients are \(+2, -1, +2, -1, +1, -1\): all six correct.
  • Switch to "learned from 200 patients" to see the 20 rules the machine learns in Step 6, written in plain English. Hover a rule to see its raw literals.

This is what the book means by unifying rule-based and summation-based decisions: each vote is a readable rule, like a branch of a decision tree, and the decision is a sum, like logistic regression with all weights equal to 1.

docs.title: Step 3 — The Voting Margin T: how much feedback does an example get?
docs.text:
Training has to decide, for every example, which rules learn from it. A naive answer is "all of them, every time". Then every rule for Recurrence sees the same stream of examples and the same feedback, and they all drift towards the same, most frequent pattern. You get ten copies of one rule.

The Tsetlin machine instead asks: how far is this example from being safely classified? You choose a Voting Margin \(T\), a whole number of votes. For a training example:

  1. Compute the vote sum from the example's own point of view: votes for its true class minus votes for the other class. (Empty rules count as True during training, so a fresh machine has something to work on.)
  2. Clip it to the range \([-T, T]\).
  3. Give each rule, independently, feedback with probability
\[ p \;=\; \frac{T - v}{2T}. \]

The book's example uses \(T = 2\), so \(p = (2 - v)/4\):

vote sum \(v\) (own class − other) \(-2\) or less \(-1\) \(0\) \(+1\) \(+2\) or more feedback probability \(p\) 1 0.75 0.5 0.25 0

If the team already wins by \(T\) votes, nobody learns from this example: the job is done, and those rules are free to work on other examples. If the team is losing badly, every rule gets feedback.

The kind of feedback is the same as in the previous lesson. A rule of the example's own class gets Recognize Feedback if it fired and Erase Feedback if it did not. A rule of the other class gets Reject Feedback if it fired (it voted wrongly) and nothing otherwise.

🎚️ Interactive: how the Voting Margin hands out feedback

What to notice

  • Two mirror-image lines. The chart's \(v\) counts votes for Recurrence. For a patient with recurrence that is "own minus other"; for a patient without, it is the reverse. So the two kinds of patients want \(v\) pushed in opposite directions.
  • Outside the purple band nothing changes. Once \(v \ge T\) for a recurrence patient (or \(v \le -T\) for a non-recurrence patient), the probability is 0. Raising \(T\) widens the band: the team must win by more votes before it stops learning.
  • The book's prioritisation example (\(T = 2\), rules "Deg-malig 3 and not lt40" and "Deg-malig 3" for, "Inv-nodes 0-2" against): patients #1 and #3 reach \(v = +2\) and give no feedback; #4, #5 and #6 are one vote short and give feedback a quarter of the time; patient #2 (no recurrence, but both rules for Recurrence fire) ends in a tie, \(v = 0\), and gives feedback half of the time. The examples that need it most get the most attention.

docs.title: Step 4 — The complete learning algorithm
docs.text:
Put the pieces together and you have the whole training procedure. Every rule starts empty, with all its literals at the top of the Forgotten half of its memory. Then, for each training example in turn:

That is the entire algorithm. There is no gradient, no loss function and no global optimiser. Each rule only ever sees its own condition, the example, and one coin flip. The coordination between rules comes entirely from the shared vote sum inside \(p\).

Why it coordinates the rules (the book's argument)

  • Reject Feedback is targeted. Only rules that fired and voted for the wrong class receive it. Rules that voted correctly are shielded.
  • Useful rules learn fastest. A rule that matches many examples of its class and never votes wrongly gets the most Recognize Feedback and no Reject Feedback, so its literals sink deepest into memory.
  • Satisfied examples stop pulling. Once a sub-pattern is covered by enough votes, its examples hand out no more feedback. The remaining feedback comes from examples that are not yet covered, so idle or weak rules drift towards those. The book calls this a resource-allocation effect.

docs.title: Step 5 — Why the margin matters: two rules, one OR pattern
docs.text:
Chapter 2 of the book makes this precise with the smallest interesting case. The class is \(Y = x_1 \text{ OR } x_2\) (with 10% of the labels flipped as noise). There are two rules, both voting for \(Y\), and each rule can memorize \(x_1\), \(x_2\), both, or neither. Of the 16 possible pairs of rules, only two solve the problem: one rule "if \(x_1\) then Y" and the other "if \(x_2\) then Y".

A tempting wrong answer is "if \(x_1\) AND \(x_2\) then Y": it is very precise when it fires, but it misses every example where only one of them is True. Two copies of it are a sub-optimal configuration (a local optimum): no single rule can improve things by changing alone.

In this game there are no rules voting against \(Y\), so \(v\) is just the number of firing rules. With margin \(T\), a \(Y\) example gives each rule feedback with probability \((T - v)/T\), and a not-\(Y\) example with probability \(v/T\) (with \(v\) capped at \(T\)). With \(T = 2\): a \(Y\) example with one rule firing gives feedback half of the time; with both firing, never.

🤝 Interactive: two rules learning x1 OR x2

What to notice

  • Without a margin (every rule gets feedback every time), fast-forward to 200,000 steps: the pair spends 60.7% of the time as two copies of "x1 AND x2", and only 7.1% in the correct OR solution. Both rules chase the same, most precise pattern.
  • With \(T = 2\) the picture flips: 81.4% of the time in the OR solution, and only 0.3% as two AND-copies. As soon as one rule covers \(x_1\), examples it handles no longer push the other rule, which is left to pick up \(x_2\).
  • \(T\) must fit the team. With \(T = 1\) (one vote is "enough") the second rule rarely gets feedback and only 28.6% of the time is spent in the solution. With \(T = 3\) or \(T = 4\) the team can never reach the margin (two rules give at most two votes), so feedback never fully stops: 26.4% and 18.1%, and with \(T = 4\) the two AND-copies are back at 25.4%.
  • These are time shares from one seeded run (seed 42, Forget Value \(1/s\) with \(s = 4\), Memorize Value 1.0, memory depth 4), computed in Python and reproduced exactly by the widget. The book computes the exact long-run probabilities with a Markov chain instead and finds the same story: without the margin the AND-copies are the most likely outcome; with \(T = 2\) any configuration involving them has essentially zero probability.

The lesson generalises: the Voting Margin should be roughly the number of votes you expect a well-covered example to collect. Too small, and rules stop learning before every sub-pattern has a rule. Too large, and feedback never switches off, so rules keep crowding onto the most common pattern.

docs.title: Step 6 — The full run: breast-cancer recurrence
docs.text:
Now the real thing. The data is the public UCI Breast Cancer dataset (University Medical Centre, Ljubljana, donated by M. Zwitter and M. Soklic): 286 patients, 85 of whom (29.7%) had a recurrence. Like the book's chapter, we use three properties, Menopause, Inv-nodes and Deg-malig, and Booleanize them with one feature per value: 3 + 7 + 3 = 13 Boolean features, so 26 literals.

The setup, fixed in advance:

  • shuffle the patients with seed 1; 200 for training, 86 for testing (23 of the test patients had a recurrence);
  • 10 rules for and 10 rules against Recurrence, Voting Margin \(T = 10\);
  • Forget Value \(1/s\) with \(s = 3\) (so Memorize Value \(2/3\));
  • memory depth 200 (positions 1–200; Memorized above 100). The book's toy examples use depth 10; a deeper memory makes the rules steadier on noisy data;
  • 60 epochs; a tie (\(v = 0\)) is predicted as No recurrence.

The widget trains exactly this machine in your browser. Change the knobs and it retrains in a second or two.

🏋️ Interactive: train a Tsetlin machine on breast-cancer data

What to notice

  • With the defaults the machine ends at 75.0% training and 74.4% test accuracy (64 of 86 test patients right). That sounds fine until you see the dashed line: always answering "no recurrence" scores 73.3% on the same test set. The machine is one patient better than the trivial answer.
  • It catches some recurrences. It flags 15 test patients, 8 of them correctly, so it finds 8 of the 23 recurrences, with 7 false alarms among the 63 others. The trivial answer finds none.
  • The test curve jumps around. Between epochs 11 and 60 the test accuracy moves between 68.6% and 76.7%. With 86 test patients, one patient is 1.2 percentage points, so a single lucky or unlucky epoch says little.
  • The rules for Recurrence spread out. Look at the learned rules: one broad rule, "Inv-nodes is not 0-2", matches 29 recurrence and 26 non-recurrence training patients; the rest specialise on small groups (6-8, 12-14, 15-17 or 24-26 nodes, or Menopause lt40). That is the resource allocation of Step 4 at work: once the common cases are covered, idle rules move to patients nobody has covered yet. On noisy data that also means chasing rare individuals: four identical rules memorized "Inv-nodes 24-26", which matches a single training patient.
  • Try \(T = 1\) or \(T = 2\), or 1 rule per class. With one rule per class and \(T = 1\) the machine never predicts Recurrence on this split. Change the seed to get a different train/test split and watch the accuracy move by several points.

docs.title: How good is that, honestly?
docs.text:
One split is not enough to judge a model on 86 test patients. So we repeated the run on 10 different random splits (seeds 1–10, same settings) and compared with simple baselines on the same splits and the same 13 features:

Method (10 random 200/86 splits) test accuracy, mean ± sd Always "no recurrence" 70.7% ± 3.1 The book's single rule "Deg-malig 3 and not Menopause lt40" 71.2% ± 3.8 Tsetlin machine (10 + 10 rules, \(T = 10\), \(s = 3\)) 71.3% ± 3.7 (range 64.0–75.6%) Logistic regression (scikit-learn defaults) 72.7% ± 3.5 Decision tree, depth 3 72.9% ± 3.7

All of these are within about one standard deviation of each other and of the trivial baseline. Using all nine properties of the dataset instead of three gave the same Tsetlin-machine accuracy (71.3% ± 2.9). Sweeping the margin over the same 10 splits: \(T = 1\) and \(T = 2\) were worse (69.1% each, with larger spread), and \(T = 5\), 10, 20, 50 and 10000 all landed between 70.8% and 72.4%.

What this tells you about the data, not just the model

These three properties (and even all nine) simply do not contain enough information to predict recurrence well: remember from Step 1 that 28 of the 85 recurrences fit neither risk profile. No method in the table escapes that. What the Tsetlin machine adds is not accuracy but transparency: every vote it casts is a rule you can read and check against clinical knowledge. With a test set of 86 patients, a difference of a few points between methods, or between one split and another, is noise. Lesson 1 of this series reports 76.7% against a 70.9% baseline on a different split (seed 42) with a different set of 11 features; our 10-split range of 64.0–75.6% shows how much a single split can move.

docs.title: Step 7 — Reading the model as plain English
docs.text:
A learned rule is a list of memorized literals, for example (from the default run above):

NOT Inv-nodes 6-8 AND NOT Inv-nodes 24-26 AND NOT Deg-malig 3 → against Recurrence

Literals that mention the same property can be merged, the way the book simplifies "Deg-malig 3 and not Deg-malig 1 and not Deg-malig 2" to "Deg-malig 3":

IF Inv-nodes is not 6-8 or 24-26 AND Deg-malig is not 3 then vote against Recurrence.

This rule matches 108 of the 138 non-recurrence training patients and 25 of the 62 recurrence patients. The widgets in Step 2 and Step 6 do this merging automatically. A few habits make a learned model easy to read:

  • Count duplicates. Rules that say the same thing are one rule with a bigger weight: +4 means four votes. (Two rules can list slightly different literals and still be equivalent, such as "Deg-malig 2" and "Deg-malig 2 AND NOT Deg-malig 1"; the widgets merge them.)
  • Check each rule's coverage, the number of training patients of each class it matches. A rule matching 1 patient is an anecdote, not a pattern.
  • Spot rules that can never fire. Reject Feedback sometimes leaves a rule demanding two values of the same property at once ("Inv-nodes 9-11 AND Inv-nodes 12-14"). It is harmless dead weight.
  • Read the vote for one patient. In the Step 2 widget, pick book patient #5 with the learned rules: no rule fires on either side, \(v = 0\), so it is predicted as No recurrence even though it recurred. You can see exactly why the model got it wrong: no learned rule describes "premeno, 0-2 nodes, Deg-malig 3".

Interpretable is not the same as correct

Readable rules let you audit a model: you can see that four rules memorized a single patient with 24-26 nodes, and decide that this is overfitting. They do not make the model right. The breast-cancer machine above is honest about its uncertainty only because you can look inside it.

docs.title: Step 8 — More than two classes
docs.text:
So far one team of rules decided between two classes. For \(m\) classes (say Car, Plane and Boat), the standard Tsetlin machine (Granmo, 2018) gives every class its own team, each with rules voting for and against that class. Each team computes its own vote sum \(v_i\), and the class with the highest vote sum wins.

Training each example updates two teams: its own team, exactly as in Step 4 with the example counted as "own class", and one other team chosen at random, with the example counted as "other class" for that team. Updating just one other team, rather than all of them, keeps the cost the same however many classes there are. The two-class machine of this lesson is the special case with a single team: rules for Recurrence and rules against it.

What to notice

  • Each team is a two-class Tsetlin machine of its own: "this class" against "everything else".
  • The output is still readable: for any prediction you can list the firing rules in the winning team and in its closest rival.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is the complete two-class machine in numpy, about 70 lines, trained on the same three properties. It follows the algorithm of Step 4 line by line, but vectorised over rules and literals. It uses numpy's random numbers and its own train/test shuffle, so its numbers differ a little from the widget's.

from collections import Counter

import numpy as np

# ---- 1. Booleanize: one feature per value of Menopause, Inv-nodes and Deg-malig (UCI Breast Cancer data)
VALUES = {"menopause": (1, ["lt40", "ge40", "premeno"]),             # (column after the label, values)
          "inv-nodes": (3, ["0-2", "3-5", "6-8", "9-11", "12-14", "15-17", "24-26"]),
          "deg-malig": (5, ["1", "2", "3"])}
rows = [line.strip().split(",") for line in open("data/breast-cancer.data") if line.strip()]
X = np.array([[r[c + 1] == v for c, vals in VALUES.values() for v in vals] for r in rows], dtype=np.int8)
y = np.array([r[0] == "recurrence-events" for r in rows], dtype=np.int8)
names = [f"{p} {v}" for p, (c, vals) in VALUES.items() for v in vals]


class TsetlinMachine:
    """Two classes. memory[c, j, k] = position (1 … depth) of literal k in rule j of class c."""

    def __init__(self, n_features, rules_per_class=10, T=10, s=3.0, depth=200, seed=1):
        self.T, self.s, self.depth, self.half = T, s, depth, depth // 2
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.memory = np.full((2, rules_per_class, 2 * n_features), depth // 2)  # top of Forgotten

    def fires(self, lits, training=False):
        """Which rules fire? A rule fires when every memorized literal is True."""
        memorized = self.memory > self.half                        # (2, rules, literals)
        ok = ~np.any(memorized & (lits == 0), axis=2)
        if not training:
            ok &= memorized.any(axis=2)                            # empty rules stay silent when classifying
        return ok

    def predict(self, x):
        f = self.fires(np.concatenate([x, 1 - x]))
        return int(f[1].sum() - f[0].sum() > 0)                    # vote sum v > 0 → class 1

    def update(self, x, y):
        lits = np.concatenate([x, 1 - x])                          # literals: x_k, then NOT x_k
        f = self.fires(lits, training=True)
        v = f[y].sum() - f[1 - y].sum()                            # votes for own class − votes against
        v = np.clip(v, -self.T, self.T)
        p = (self.T - v) / (2 * self.T)                            # Voting Margin: feedback probability
        _, n_rules, n_lits = self.memory.shape
        chosen = self.rng.random((2, n_rules)) <= p                # which rules get feedback this time
        u = self.rng.random((n_rules, n_lits))
        own, other = self.memory[y], self.memory[1 - y]            # views: changes go into self.memory

        # Recognize Feedback (own-class rules that fire): memorize True literals, forget False ones
        rec = (chosen[y] & f[y])[:, None]
        own += rec & (lits == 1) & (u <= (self.s - 1) / self.s) & (own < self.depth)
        own -= rec & (lits == 0) & (u <= 1 / self.s) & (own > 1)
        # Erase Feedback (own-class rules that don't fire): forget every literal
        era = (chosen[y] & ~f[y])[:, None]
        own -= era & (u <= 1 / self.s) & (own > 1)
        # Reject Feedback (other-class rules that fire): memorize Forgotten False literals
        rej = (chosen[1 - y] & f[1 - y])[:, None]
        other += rej & (lits == 0) & (other <= self.half)

    def fit(self, X, y, epochs):
        for _ in range(epochs):
            for i in self.rng.permutation(len(X)):
                self.update(X[i], y[i])
        return self

    def rules(self, c, names):
        lits = names + ["NOT " + n for n in names]
        return [" AND ".join(l for l, m in zip(lits, rule) if m > self.half) or "(empty)" for rule in self.memory[c]]


order = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(X))              # 200 patients to train on, 86 to test
train, test = order[:200], order[200:]
tm = TsetlinMachine(X.shape[1], rules_per_class=10, T=10, s=3.0, depth=200, seed=1).fit(X[train], y[train], epochs=60)
acc = lambda idx: np.mean([tm.predict(X[i]) == y[i] for i in idx])
print(f"train accuracy {acc(train):.3f} · test accuracy {acc(test):.3f} · always 'no recurrence' on test {1 - y[test].mean():.3f}")
for c, label in ((1, "Recurrence"), (0, "No recurrence")):
    for rule, count in Counter(tm.rules(c, names)).most_common(2):
        print(f"{count} × IF {rule} THEN {label}")

train accuracy 0.775 · test accuracy 0.744 · always 'no recurrence' on test 0.698
5 × IF inv-nodes 24-26 THEN Recurrence
2 × IF inv-nodes 9-11 THEN Recurrence
3 × IF inv-nodes 0-2 AND NOT menopause lt40 AND NOT inv-nodes 3-5 AND NOT inv-nodes 6-8 AND NOT inv-nodes 9-11 AND NOT inv-nodes 12-14 AND NOT inv-nodes 15-17 AND NOT inv-nodes 24-26 AND NOT deg-malig 3 THEN No recurrence
1 × IF inv-nodes 0-2 AND NOT menopause lt40 AND NOT inv-nodes 6-8 AND NOT inv-nodes 9-11 AND NOT inv-nodes 12-14 AND NOT deg-malig 1 AND NOT deg-malig 2 THEN No recurrence

Download breast-cancer.data from the UCI repository first. On this split the machine beats the trivial answer by more (74.4% vs 69.8%), and again five rules spent themselves on the only patient in the whole dataset with 24-26 nodes. The first No-recurrence rule simplifies to "Inv-nodes 0-2 and Menopause is not lt40 and Deg-malig is 1 or 2".

Piece What it does Book term (research term) Rule AND of memorized literals; votes when True rule (clause \(C_j\)) Rules for / against +1 / −1 votes for the class (positive / negative polarity clauses) Vote sum \(v\) votes for − votes against; the sign is the prediction vote sum (\(\sum C^+_j - \sum C^-_j\)) Voting Margin \(T\) feedback probability \((T - v)/2T\) during training Voting Margin (threshold / target \(T\)) Recognize, Erase, Reject how a picked rule changes its memory (Type Ia, Type Ib, Type II feedback) One team per class multi-class: the highest vote sum wins (multi-class Tsetlin machine)

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"The Voting Margin is a decision threshold.\"

No. Classification only looks at the sign of \(v\). The Voting Margin \(T\) is used only during training, to decide how likely each rule is to get feedback. A trained machine never looks at \(T\).

\"More feedback is better, so always give every rule feedback.\"

In the OR game, feedback on every step left the two rules as copies of "x1 AND x2" for 60.7% of the time, and in the correct OR solution only 7.1% of the time. With \(T = 2\) the solution held 81.4% of the time. Switching feedback off for examples that are already safe is what lets rules specialise.

\"Rules know about each other.\"

They don't. Each rule only sees its own condition, the example and one random number. The only shared quantity is the vote sum \(v\), which sets the feedback probability for everyone. Coordination emerges from that single number.

\"74% test accuracy means the model works.\"

On this dataset, answering "no recurrence" for everyone already scores 70.7% on average over 10 splits, and the Tsetlin machine averaged 71.3%. Always compare with the trivial baseline, use more than one split, and look at what the model gets right (here: 8 of 23 recurrences on the default split).

\"Duplicate rules are wasted.\"

Partly true and partly not. Duplicates act as weights: in the book's example, the duplicated R1 + R2 out-vote R3 for patient #5. But four copies of a rule that matches a single patient is wasted capacity, and a sign of overfitting.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. With T = 2, three rules for Recurrence fire and one rule against fires on a patient with recurrence. What is the feedback probability?

Own class minus other: \(v = 3 - 1 = 2\), which is already at the margin. $p = (2 - 2)/4 = $ 0: no rule learns from this patient.

2. Same rules, but the patient did NOT have a recurrence. What happens?

From the patient's point of view \(v = 1 - 3 = -2\), so $p = (2 - (-2))/4 = $ 1: every rule is picked. The rules against Recurrence get Recognize (the one that fired) or Erase (the others). The three rules for Recurrence that fired voted wrongly and get Reject Feedback, which pushes a False literal of this patient into each of them.

3. Why does a Tsetlin machine predict with the sign of v, but train with (T − v)/2T?

Prediction only needs to know which side wins. Training also wants a safety margin: an example won by a single vote is fragile, so it keeps asking for feedback until it wins by \(T\) votes. And examples won by \(T\) votes or more stop asking, which frees the rules to cover other sub-patterns.

4. You have 4 rules for a class whose examples come in 4 clearly different sub-patterns. Is T = 1 or T = 20 the better choice?

Neither. With \(T = 1\) one firing rule is enough, so a second sub-pattern covered by the "wrong" rule stops the learning early, and there is little pressure to fill every niche. With \(T = 20\) the margin can never be reached (4 rules give at most 4 votes), so feedback never switches off and the rules crowd onto the most frequent sub-pattern. A margin around the number of votes a well-covered example can collect (here a few) works best, as the OR game showed with \(T = 2\) for two rules.

5. The learned model predicts 'No recurrence' for book patient #5 (premeno, 0-2 nodes, Deg-malig 3), who did recur. How would you find out why?

Read the votes. In the Step 2 widget with the learned rules, no rule fires on either side, so \(v = 0\) and the tie goes to No recurrence. No learned rule describes this profile, and the data explains why: Deg-malig 3 without lymph-node spread recurred in only 38% of patients. A black-box model would give you the same wrong answer without the explanation.

docs.text:
• Ole-Christoffer Granmo, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines (free online), Ch. 1, §1.5–1.7 (voting, the Voting Margin and the complete algorithm) and Ch. 2, §2.3 (rule interaction and the OR example with its Markov-chain analysis). This lesson follows those sections.
  • Ole-Christoffer Granmo, The Tsetlin Machine – A Game Theoretic Bandit Driven Approach to Optimal Pattern Recognition with Propositional Logic (2018). The original paper, including the multi-class machine and the clause/threshold terminology.
  • M. Zwitter and M. Soklic, Breast Cancer dataset, UCI Machine Learning Repository. The data used in Step 6.
  • The Tsetlin automaton and Recognize, Erase & Reject feedback: the memory and the feedback this lesson builds on.
