docs.title: What Is a Tsetlin Machine?
docs.text:
TL;DR

A Tsetlin machine is a machine-learning model built from plain if-then rules. Its input is a list of yes/no facts (Boolean features). Each rule joins a few of those facts, or their opposites, with AND: "if Four Wheels and not Wings then Car". Many such rules vote, and the class with the most votes wins. Because the rules are ordinary logic, you can read every one of them, and because they only use bits, AND and counting, they can run very cheaply in hardware. This lesson shows what the rules look like and how data is turned into bits. How the rules are learned comes in the next lessons.

Level: beginner · Prerequisites: none. If you have read What is reinforcement learning?, you will spot a familiar idea in the next lesson, but it is not needed here.

This series follows Ole-Christoffer Granmo's free book An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines. This first lesson covers the start of Chapter 1 (the overview, §1.1 and §1.2).

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
Most of today's strong models, deep neural networks above all, are black boxes: millions of numbers multiplied together, with no human-readable reason behind each answer. In medicine that is a real problem. If a model says "high risk of recurrence", a clinician wants to know why, and a regulator wants to know whether the reason is sound.

A Tsetlin machine takes a different road. Its whole "knowledge" is a set of rules such as

if malignancy grade 3 and tumour through node capsule and premenopausal then vote Recurrence

which a person can read, check and argue with. Granmo's book (Ch. 1, box "Tsetlin Machines vs Black Boxes") sums up what the approach aims for:

The Tsetlin machine is… …like What that means a universal function approximator neural networks with enough rules it can represent any pattern in Boolean data rule-based decision trees its knowledge is a list of readable AND-rules summation-based logistic regression, Naive Bayes the final answer adds up votes from many rules hardware-near (digital logic) inputs are bits, rules are ANDs, votes are integer counts: a small energy and memory footprint

That last row is worth spelling out. Once a Tsetlin machine is trained, making a prediction needs no floating-point arithmetic at all: test some bits, AND them together, and count. That is why the book points to edge devices and low-energy chips as a natural home for it.

Be careful not to read more into this than it says. Being readable does not make a model accurate, and on hard problems a Tsetlin machine is not automatically better than other methods. You will see an honest example of that at the end of this lesson.

Where the name comes from

The machine is named after Michael Lvovitch Tsetlin (1924–1966), a Soviet mathematician and physicist. He invented a tiny learning device, now called a Tsetlin automaton, that improves its behaviour in a random environment while remembering its entire past experience as a single integer, and that can change its mind when the environment changes. He also studied how collectives of such devices can solve problems together. The Tsetlin machine (Granmo, 2018) builds on that idea: each rule's memory is a team of Tsetlin automata. (Granmo, Ch. 1, box "Tsetlin Machine Origins".) The next lesson is all about that one-integer memory.

docs.title: Step 1 — Objects described by yes/no facts
docs.text:
A Tsetlin machine looks at objects (a vehicle, a patient, an image) and describes each one with Boolean features: properties that are either True or False. A vehicle either has wings or it doesn't; it is either yellow or it isn't.

Here is the toy dataset that runs through the whole of Granmo's Chapter 1 (Table 1.1): three cars and three planes, each described by five Boolean features. ● means True and · means False.

# Four Wheels Transports People Wings Yellow Blue Type 1 ● ● · · ● Car 2 ● ● · ● · Car 3 ● ● · ● · Car 4 ● ● ● · ● Plane 5 ● · ● ● · Plane 6 · ● ● · ● Plane

We write the features of one object as \(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_o\), where \(o\) is the number of features (here \(o = 5\)) and each \(x_k\) is 1 (True) or 0 (False). Vehicle 1 is the list \((1, 1, 0, 0, 1)\).

Some features matter for telling cars from planes (Wings, Four Wheels). Others are noise (the colour). Part of what a Tsetlin machine learns is which is which.

What to notice

  • Plane 4 is awkward: it has four wheels and transports people, just like the cars. Any rule that only looks at those two features will mistake it for a car.
  • Plane 6 is the only vehicle without four wheels. A plane on a runway would be a different story, so don't expect real data to be this tidy.

docs.title: Step 2 — Booleanising real data
docs.text:
Real data is rarely yes/no. A tumour has a size in millimetres; menopausal status has three possible values. Before a Tsetlin machine can use such data you booleanise it: turn each property into one or more True/False features. Two recipes cover most cases.

Categories → one feature per value. Menopausal status takes the values lt40, ge40 and premeno, so it becomes three Boolean features, exactly one of which is True for each patient. This is how Granmo booleanises the breast-cancer data in Ch. 1 (Table 1.4). People in deep learning call it one-hot encoding.

Numbers → thresholds. For a number, pick some cut points \(t_1 < t_2 < \dots\) and make one feature per cut point: "size ≥ \(t_1\)", "size ≥ \(t_2\)", and so on. A bigger tumour switches on more of them, the way mercury fills a thermometer, so this is called thermometer encoding. The alternative, one feature per interval ("20–29 mm"), is just the category recipe again.

The playground below uses the public UCI Breast Cancer dataset (286 patients from the Institute of Oncology in Ljubljana, the same data as in the book). Each bar counts the patients whose tumour size was recorded in that 5 mm range; the red part had a recurrence of their cancer, the blue part did not.

🌡️ Interactive: turn tumour size into Boolean features

What to notice

  • With the default thresholds, size ≥ 20 mm is True for 216 patients. Their recurrence rate is 35.2%, against 12.9% for the 70 patients below 20 mm. One bit already carries a useful signal.
  • size ≥ 40 mm is nearly useless here: 30.3% recurrence if True and 29.6% if False. Where you put a threshold decides whether a feature is informative. Booleanising is a modelling choice, not a formality.
  • Move the patient slider. In thermometer mode the bits fill up from the left and never switch back off. In interval mode exactly one bit is on. Both describe the same patient; they just make different rules easy to write.

Why go to the trouble? The book (Ch. 1, §1.1) gives three reasons:

  1. Bits suit computers. Each feature is stored as a single bit, and whole groups of them can be tested at once with bitwise operations: fast, small and low-energy.
  2. Boolean algebra is the language of computers. If you have written if a and not b: in a program, you already know the operations a Tsetlin machine uses.
  3. Logic is readable. Boolean algebra is the same thing as propositional logic, the "True/False statements" kind of reasoning that people can follow step by step.

docs.title: Step 3 — Literals: a feature or its opposite
docs.text:
Rules often need to say what an object does not have. A car is something without wings. So for every feature \(x_k\) we also allow its negation \(\lnot x_k\) ("NOT \(x_k\)"), which is True exactly when \(x_k\) is False:

\[ \lnot x_k = 1 - x_k . \]

Together, the features and their negations are called literals, the usual name in Boolean algebra. With \(o\) features there are \(2o\) literals. For vehicle 1:

Literal Four Wheels Transports People Wings Yellow Blue \(x_k\) ● ● · · ● \(\lnot x_k\) · · ● ● ·

Exactly half of the ten literals are True for any object: one from each column. A Tsetlin machine treats a feature and its negation in exactly the same way. Each is simply one of the \(2o\) building blocks a rule can choose from.

docs.title: Step 4 — Rules: AND-ing literals together
docs.text:
A Tsetlin machine expresses patterns as rules of the form

\[ \textbf{if}\ \text{condition}\ \textbf{then}\ \text{class}, \]

where the condition is an AND of literals. In the research papers a rule's condition is called a clause (a conjunctive clause), written \(C_j\). For example

if Four Wheels and Transports People and not Wings then Car.

A rule matches an object only if every literal in its condition is True for that object. One False literal is enough to stop it. In symbols, if \(L_j\) is the set of literals in rule \(j\):

\[ C_j(\mathbf{x}) = \bigwedge_{l \in L_j} l \;=\; \prod_{l \in L_j} l , \]

the AND of the chosen literals, which for 0/1 values is the same as their product.

Try it: build rules for Car or Plane and see which vehicles they catch.

🧩 Interactive: build a rule and test it on the vehicles

Two numbers describe how good a rule is for its class:

  • coverage: of all the objects of that class, how many does the rule match? (Statisticians call this recall or sensitivity.)
  • precision: of all the objects the rule matches, how many really belong to its class?

What to notice

  1. Adding a literal can only shrink what a rule matches. Four Wheels matches 5 vehicles (precision 3/5). Adding Transports People leaves 4 (precision 3/4): plane 4 still slips through. Adding NOT Wings removes it: 3 matches, all cars, so coverage 3/3 and precision 3/3. This is the book's car rule.
  2. Too specific is also bad. Add Blue instead and the rule matches only car 1 and plane 4: coverage 1/3, precision 1/2. Colour is a detail of individual cars, not a property of cars in general.
  3. Shorter can be just as good. NOT Wings on its own also gets coverage 3/3 and precision 3/3 on this table. With only six vehicles many rules fit perfectly; with more data the extra literals start to earn their place.
  4. The empty rule matches everything (no literal can fail), and the contradiction Four Wheels AND NOT Four Wheels matches nothing, because one of the two is always False. The book points out that learning naturally avoids such contradictions (Ch. 1, §1.3).
  5. Wings → Plane is a one-literal rule that matches all three planes and nothing else.

Why only AND?

A Tsetlin machine never puts OR or nested logic inside a rule. Each rule is a plain AND-list, which keeps it easy to read (Granmo, Ch. 1, §1.2). "OR" appears one level up: when several rules vote for the same class, the class gets support if any of them matches. With enough AND-rules you can describe any pattern in Boolean data, so nothing is lost.

docs.title: Step 5 — From one rule to a machine: rules vote
docs.text:
One rule rarely captures a whole class. A Tsetlin machine therefore uses many rules, each assigned to a class. When an object arrives, every rule that matches casts one vote for its class, and the class with the most votes wins. Here is the book's example (Ch. 1, §1.5) with plane 4, the tricky one:

For two classes it is convenient to give each rule a sign: rules for a class vote \(+1\), rules against it vote \(-1\). Adding them up gives the vote sum \(v\), and its sign is the answer. (In the research papers these are rules of positive and negative polarity.) Lesson 4 works this out in full.

Where do the rules come from? Each rule has a memory: every one of the \(2o\) literals sits at a position on a scale from Maximally Forgotten to Maximally Memorized, and only literals in the upper half take part in the rule. Training nudges those positions up and down, one example at a time. That memory is the subject of the next lesson, and the nudges are lesson 3.

docs.title: Step 6 — A first look at a learned rule set
docs.text:
Here is what a trained Tsetlin machine looks like. We booleanised the UCI breast-cancer data into 11 features (tumour-size thresholds at 20, 30 and 40 mm, involved lymph nodes ≥ 3 and ≥ 6, malignancy grade 3 or 1, and a few yes/no facts), held back 86 patients for testing, and trained a small machine with 3 rules for Recurrence and 3 for No recurrence on the other 200. The code is a few dozen lines of numpy that follow the book's algorithm; lesson 4 builds it step by step.

The six rules below are the entire model. Step through the test patients, or click a feature to see which rules react.

📜 Interactive: read a learned rule set (breast-cancer recurrence)

What to notice

  • You can read every rule. Rule 2 says: grade 3, through the node capsule, premenopausal and no radiotherapy → Recurrence. It matches 8 of the 286 patients, and all 8 had a recurrence. Rule 6 (grade 1, fewer than 6 involved nodes, tumour under 20 mm → No recurrence) matches 27 patients, only 1 with a recurrence.
  • Rules can be broad and weak. Rule 4 says only "not premenopausal → No recurrence". It matches 136 patients, and 37 of them did have a recurrence. On its own it is a poor rule; it is useful only as one voice among several.
  • Readable is not the same as accurate. This rule set gets 66 of the 86 test patients right (76.7%), but always answering "No recurrence" gets 61 right (70.9%), and it catches only 6 of the 25 test patients who had a recurrence. Over five training runs with different random seeds, test accuracy ranged from 69.8% to 76.7% (mean 72.6%). This dataset is known to be hard. The point is that you can see why the model is weak: 255 of the 286 patients match none of the three Recurrence rules, so for them the model can never answer "Recurrence".
  • The negated literals ("not 20 mm or larger") are how the machine says "small". Thermometer features plus NOT give you intervals for free.

Not a clinical tool

These rules come from a tiny model trained on a small, decades-old dataset. They illustrate how a Tsetlin machine represents knowledge; they are not medical advice.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
The whole pipeline, from an object to an answer. Step through it; the last step shows where learning plugs in.

And the same thing as code: the vehicle table, the book's two rules, and voting. A rule is just a list of literal names.

FEATURES = ["Four Wheels", "Transports People", "Wings", "Yellow", "Blue"]

# Granmo's vehicle table (Ch. 1, Table 1.1): 1 = True, 0 = False
vehicles = [
    ([1, 1, 0, 0, 1], "Car"),
    ([1, 1, 0, 1, 0], "Car"),
    ([1, 1, 0, 1, 0], "Car"),
    ([1, 1, 1, 0, 1], "Plane"),
    ([1, 0, 1, 1, 0], "Plane"),
    ([0, 1, 1, 0, 1], "Plane"),
]


def literals(x):
    """Every feature, then every negated feature: 2 x 5 = 10 literals."""
    lits = {name: v for name, v in zip(FEATURES, x)}
    lits.update({"NOT " + name: 1 - v for name, v in zip(FEATURES, x)})
    return lits


def rule_matches(rule, x):
    """A rule is an AND of literals: it matches only if every one of them is True."""
    lits = literals(x)
    return all(lits[l] == 1 for l in rule)


# Two hand-written rules (the book's examples). A real Tsetlin machine learns these.
rules = [
    (["Four Wheels", "Transports People", "NOT Wings"], "Car"),
    (["Wings"], "Plane"),
]


def classify(x):
    votes = {"Car": 0, "Plane": 0}
    for condition, cls in rules:
        if rule_matches(condition, x):
            votes[cls] += 1                       # each matching rule casts one vote
    return max(votes, key=votes.get), votes


for i, (x, label) in enumerate(vehicles, start=1):
    pred, votes = classify(x)
    print(f"vehicle {i}: votes {votes} -> {pred:5s} (true: {label})")


# Booleanising a number with thresholds ("thermometer" encoding)
def thermometer(value, thresholds):
    return [int(value >= t) for t in thresholds]

print(thermometer(27, [20, 30, 40]))   # a 27 mm tumour

vehicle 1: votes {'Car': 1, 'Plane': 0} -> Car   (true: Car)
vehicle 2: votes {'Car': 1, 'Plane': 0} -> Car   (true: Car)
vehicle 3: votes {'Car': 1, 'Plane': 0} -> Car   (true: Car)
vehicle 4: votes {'Car': 0, 'Plane': 1} -> Plane (true: Plane)
vehicle 5: votes {'Car': 0, 'Plane': 1} -> Plane (true: Plane)
vehicle 6: votes {'Car': 0, 'Plane': 1} -> Plane (true: Plane)
[1, 0, 0]

Everything here was written by hand. The interesting part, how a machine finds good rules by itself from examples, starts in the next lesson.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"Interpretable means correct.\"

Being able to read a rule tells you what the model does, not whether it is right. The breast-cancer rule set above is perfectly readable and only a little better than always guessing "No recurrence". The benefit is that you can spot such weaknesses, and argue with them.

\"A Tsetlin machine is just a decision tree.\"

Both use readable conditions, but a decision tree follows one path to one leaf, so one rule decides. A Tsetlin machine lets many rules fire at once and adds up their votes. In the book's words it combines rule-based and summation-based decision making (Ch. 1, §1.5).

\"Booleanising is a harmless preprocessing step.\"

It decides what the machine can see. A threshold at 40 mm for tumour size produces a feature that carries almost no signal in this dataset; one at 20 mm produces a useful one. Too few thresholds hide detail, too many give the machine lots of near-duplicate features to sort through.

\"The rules are written by an expert.\"

In this lesson we wrote them by hand to see what they look like. In a real Tsetlin machine every rule is learned from labelled examples, and nobody tells it which literals to use.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. A dataset has 8 Boolean features. How many literals does a Tsetlin machine work with, and how many of them are True for any one object?

\(2 \times 8 = 16\) literals (each feature and its negation). Exactly 8 are True for any object: for every feature, either \(x_k\) or \(\lnot x_k\) is True, never both.

2. Does the rule \"if Yellow then Car\" work on the vehicle table? Give its coverage and precision.

It matches vehicles 2, 3 and 5. Two of those are cars, so coverage 2/3 (it misses blue car 1) and precision 2/3 (yellow plane 5 is a false positive). Colour is a poor basis for recognising cars.

3. Why can't adding a literal to a rule ever make it match more objects?

A rule is an AND: an object must make every literal True. Adding a literal adds one more requirement, so every object that matched before must still pass the new test, and some may fail it. The set of matches can only stay the same or shrink.

4. Booleanise a tumour of 33 mm with thermometer thresholds 20, 30 and 40 mm. Then write a single rule that means \"between 20 and 29 mm\".

Thermometer bits: size ≥ 20 → 1, size ≥ 30 → 1, size ≥ 40 → 0, so \((1, 1, 0)\). "Between 20 and 29 mm" is size ≥ 20 AND NOT size ≥ 30. Negated literals turn thresholds into intervals.

5. Name two reasons the book gives for using Boolean features.

Any two of: they are stored as single bits and processed with fast, low-energy bitwise operations (good for edge devices); they let you build patterns with Boolean algebra, the language of computers; and Boolean algebra is propositional logic, which people can follow, so the model stays transparent.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Ole-Christoffer Granmo, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines (free book), Ch. 1 introduction, §1.1 "Boolean Features" and §1.2 "Creating Patterns with AND and NOT", plus the boxes "Tsetlin Machine Origins" and "Tsetlin Machines vs Black Boxes". The vehicle table and the overview in this lesson are based on Ch. 1, Table 1.1 and Figure 1.1.
  • Ole-Christoffer Granmo, The Tsetlin Machine: A Game Theoretic Bandit Driven Approach to Optimal Pattern Recognition with Propositional Logic (2018), the original paper, using the research terms (clauses, Type I/II feedback).
  • M. Zwitter and M. Soklic, Breast Cancer dataset, UCI Machine Learning Repository (University Medical Centre, Institute of Oncology, Ljubljana), the data used in Steps 2 and 6.
  • Cynthia Rudin, Stop explaining black box machine learning models for high stakes decisions and use interpretable models instead, Nature Machine Intelligence (2019), the wider argument for readable models in medicine and other high-stakes fields.

docs.title: The series
docs.text:
This lesson is the first of eleven. Lessons 1–4, 6 and 9 follow the published chapters of Granmo's book; the others cover chapters that are only announced so far, and are based on the research papers instead:

  1. What is a Tsetlin machine? (this lesson): Boolean features, literals, AND-rules and voting at a glance.
  2. The Tsetlin automaton: a memory that learns: the graded memory behind every literal, and its roots in the two-armed bandit.
  3. Learning rules: Recognize, Erase and Reject feedback: how a rule learns frequent patterns, and how it learns to tell classes apart.
  4. Many rules voting: classification with a Tsetlin machine: the vote sum, the Voting Margin and the complete learning algorithm, on the breast-cancer data.
  5. Regression with Tsetlin machines: rules that vote for a number, and the staircase they build.
  6. Convolutional Tsetlin machines: finding patterns anywhere in an image or a sequence.
  7. Weighted clauses and clause sharing: one weighted rule instead of many copies, and one pool of rules for all classes.
  8. Autoencoders and word embeddings: learning without labels by predicting a hidden word from the others.
  9. Confidence, trustworthiness and composites: when to trust a Tsetlin machine, and how to combine several.
  10. Hierarchical and graph Tsetlin machines: rules that pass messages along a graph, and rules built from rules.
  11. Tsetlin machines for language and images: reading the rules of text and image classifiers.

Next lesson: The Tsetlin automaton: a memory that learns

docs.title: Tsetlin Machines for Language and Images
docs.text:
TL;DR

A Tsetlin machine only reads True/False features, so text and images must first be Booleanized. For text, the classic recipe is the set of words: pick a vocabulary, and give every sentence one feature per word, True if the word occurs in it. Rules are then ANDs of words and of negated words ("the note does NOT mention rash"). Because a sentence holds only a handful of the vocabulary's words, almost every negated literal is True, and learned text rules end up with many of them. For images, each pixel (or each colour channel, or each edge or gradient direction) becomes one or more features through a threshold, a thermometer or an adaptive threshold, and rules become little pictures of must-be-ink, must-be-blank and don't-care pixels. On a small restaurant-review task our numpy Tsetlin machine reaches 75.0% ± 1.9 test accuracy, close to logistic regression (76.7%) on the same words; on 8×8 handwritten digits it reaches 96.9% with a thermometer. The published results tell the same story at scale: competitive with classic methods and small neural networks, behind large modern ones, and readable all the way down.

Level: intermediate · Prerequisites: Classification by voting (rules voting for and against a class, the vote sum \(v\), the Voting Margin \(T\)) and Convolutional Tsetlin machines (windows, patches, thermometer encoding). Hierarchical & graph TMs is useful background but not needed.

Beyond the book

The chapter of Granmo's book on this topic (Ch. 10, Natural Language and Image Processing) has not been published yet. This lesson is therefore based on the research papers listed in Further reading, retold with the book's vocabulary (rules, memory, Recognize/Erase/Reject Feedback, Voting Margin). The text and digit experiments are our own small numpy runs, made for this lesson; they are toy-scale on purpose and are labelled as ours throughout.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
Most medical information is not a neat table. It is free text (admission notes, discharge letters, radiology reports) and images (X-rays, slides, photographs of the skin). The models that read them best today are large neural networks, and nobody can read their reasoning.

  • Clinical text. Berge et al. (2019) used a Tsetlin machine to find notes about drug allergies in real electronic health records from a Norwegian hospital, written in a mixture of Latin, English and the local language, full of jargon and misspellings. Their example rule is if "rash" and "reaction" and "penicillin" then Allergy: a clinician can check that in a second.
  • Images. A convolutional Tsetlin machine learns small pixel patterns you can draw and inspect, and colour images are now handled by teams of machines that each look at the image in a different way (Grønningsæter et al., 2024).
  • An honest trade. You give up some accuracy compared with the best neural networks, and in exchange every decision is a sum of rules you can list. This lesson shows both sides with numbers.

The learning algorithm doesn't change at all. Everything new in this lesson is about turning words and pixels into literals, and reading the rules that come out.

docs.title: Step 1 — Text as a set of words
docs.text:
The simplest way to Booleanize text (Berge et al., 2019) is:

  1. Build a vocabulary: a list of words, \(w_1, \dots, w_K\).
  2. Give every document one Boolean feature per vocabulary word: \(x_k\) is True if word \(w_k\) occurs in the document at least once, False otherwise.

That's it. Word order and word counts are thrown away; only "which words are present" survives. The literature calls this a set of words (or binary bag of words). Each feature brings two literals as always: \(x_{\text{good}}\) ("the text contains good") and \(\lnot x_{\text{good}}\) ("the text does NOT contain good").

Our running example is real data: the Yelp part of the UCI "Sentiment Labelled Sentences" dataset (Kotzias et al., 2015): 1,000 one-sentence restaurant reviews, 500 labelled Positive and 500 Negative. We split them once, 700 for training and 300 for testing. The training sentences contain 1,661 different words, far too many for a toy machine, so we keep a vocabulary of 150 words. To pick them, we drop words that appear in fewer than 2 training sentences and rank the rest by how unevenly they are spread over the two classes (a \(\chi^2\) score, the same feature selection the TMU library's IMDb example uses). The top of the list is not, great, good, amazing, delicious, friendly, bad, at, minutes, don't, …

Try it: type a sentence, or pick one of the buttons.

🔤 Interactive: a sentence becomes 150 True/False features

What to notice

  • Text is sparse. A training sentence contains on average only 3.05 of the 150 vocabulary words (at most 12). So a typical sentence has about 3 True features and 147 False ones, and 147 of its negated literals are True. Hold on to that; it explains Step 2.
  • Words outside the vocabulary are invisible. In "Never had anything to complain about here." only never and to are in the vocabulary. 15 of the 300 test sentences contain no vocabulary word at all.
  • The vote is the familiar one. "Crust is not good." fires 9 rules for Positive (all "good") and 10 for Negative (8 copies of "not" plus two refined "not" rules), so \(v = 9 - 10 = -1\): Negative, which is right. The machine never learned that not belongs to good; the "not" rules simply outvote the "good" rules here.

docs.title: Step 2 — What a text does NOT say: negated word literals
docs.text:
In a table of patient data, \(x\) and \(\lnot x\) are usually about equally common. In text they are not: any given word is absent from almost every sentence. That has two consequences.

Negation is a real, useful signal. "The note does not mention penicillin" is evidence too. Berge et al. stress that "even the absence of terms (negated features) can be used for categorization". Their worked example (Figure 4 of the paper) shows how a rule for Allergy grows document by document. Step through it:

Negated literals pile up. Recall Recognize Feedback: it memorizes the literals that are True in the example. In a sentence with 3 vocabulary words, 147 of the True literals are "NOT word". So every Recognize step nudges a rule towards "NOT this AND NOT that AND NOT …", and only Erase Feedback and the Voting Margin hold it back. Sharma et al. (2021) report exactly this on movie reviews: "for NLP, the majority of the features appear in negated form", and a well-trained machine explains a negative review with literals like NOT witty, NOT graceful, NOT terrific, NOT honest: the review lacks every sign of praise.

What to notice

  • In our run (Step 3's machine, seed 1), the 200 rules hold 182 memorized plain-word literals and 562 "NOT word" literals: 76% are negated, but they are very unevenly spread: 175 rules are a single plain word like "great", while 6 rules carry 10 or more NOTs each, and three Positive rules carry 140 to 144.
  • What such a rule means. One Positive rule is "NOT any of 144 words": every vocabulary word except great, good, i, is, another, being. In plain English: the sentence uses none of the warning words. It matches 61 Positive and 21 Negative training sentences. It is a description of what Positive reviews lack, the same thing Sharma et al. saw.
  • Medical notes have the same shape. "No rash", "denies chest pain", "no known drug allergies": clinical text is full of negation, and a set of words cannot tell which word a "no" belongs to. Berge et al.'s rule handles it with \(\lnot\)not; Step 4 shows where that breaks.

docs.title: Step 3 — Train a text Tsetlin machine
docs.text:
Nothing about the learning changes. It is the two-class machine from Classification by voting: rules voting for Positive and rules voting against it (for Negative), feedback probability \((T - v)/2T\), Recognize, Erase and Reject Feedback. The settings, chosen after a small search on this same split (so our test accuracy is slightly optimistic; the baselines below were not tuned at all):

  • 150 features → 300 literals; 100 rules per class, Voting Margin \(T = 15\);
  • specificity \(s = 8\): Forget Value \(1/8\), Memorize Value \(7/8\) (the research papers' version; the book's later chapters use Memorize Value 1);
  • memory depth 100 (positions 1–100, Memorized above 50); 40 epochs; a tie (\(v = 0\)) is predicted as Negative.

Text needs many more rules than the breast-cancer data did. Each sentence only touches 3 of the 150 words, so one rule built around one word only ever votes on the few sentences containing that word. You need rules for many words before most sentences get any votes at all.

Try it: press Train. The widget runs exactly the code of our Python check, with the same seeded random numbers, so with the defaults you will see the numbers below (it takes about 10 seconds).

🏋️ Interactive: train a Tsetlin machine on restaurant reviews

What to notice

  • With the defaults (seed 1) the test accuracy climbs from 59.7% after one epoch to 78.3% after 40 (training accuracy 83.7%). Seed 1 happens to be the best of ten: over seeds 1–10 the final test accuracy is 75.0% ± 1.9 (range 72.0–78.3%).
  • The baselines on the same 150 Boolean features: logistic regression 76.7%, Bernoulli naive Bayes 77.0%, a decision tree 75.0%, always answering Positive 51.0%. With 300 test sentences, one sentence is 0.33 percentage points, so the Tsetlin machine is roughly level with the classic methods, not ahead of them. That matches the literature: on the private clinical notes, Berge et al. report an F-measure of 69.3 for the Tsetlin machine, 69.9 for naive Bayes and 69.6 for logistic regression.
  • Too few rules hurt. With 20 rules per class and \(T = 5\) the test accuracy ends at 68.7%; with 50 rules per class and \(T = 10\), 72.7% (seed 1). Many sentences get no votes at all.
  • The rules read like a sentiment dictionary. The most common Positive rules are good (×9, matching 50 Positive and 16 Negative training sentences), great (×7, 40 and 0) and amazing (×7, 15 and 0). The most common Negative rules are not (×8, 9 and 73) and bad (×5, 0 and 13). A refined rule says "not" AND NOT "great" AND NOT "over": it matches 7 Positive and 73 Negative sentences, two fewer Positive ones than plain not.
  • Some rules are leftovers. With seed 1 a few Positive rules memorized words such as waiting or barely, which only occur in Negative training sentences. Reject Feedback memorizes a word that is absent from the sentence it fired on wrongly, and sometimes the word it picks happens to be a negative one. They cost a few wrong votes; the majority outvotes them. Reading the rules is how you find them.

docs.title: Step 4 — Reading the rules, and what a set of words cannot see
docs.text:
Because every vote is a rule, you can explain any single prediction by listing the rules that fired, as the first widget does. Try these in it:

Sentence Vocabulary words Firing rules \(v\) Prediction The food was good but the service was slow. good, slow, but, was 9 × good for; 2 × slow, 1 × but against \(9 - 3 = +6\) Positive Not bad at all, the staff was friendly. not, friendly, bad, at, staff, was 5 × friendly, 2 × staff for; 8 × not, 5 × bad, … against \(7 - 17 = -10\) Negative ✗ Never had anything to complain about here. never, to 1 × never against \(0 - 1 = -1\) Negative ✗

(The first and second sentences are our own; the third is a Positive sentence from the test set. All vote sums use the seed-1 rules.)

The two mistakes have the same cause. "Not bad" and "never … complain" are praise built from negative words, and a set of words keeps the words but loses their order and their scope. A rule can say "not AND bad", but not "not directly before bad". The research has three main answers:

  • Add structure to the features. Yadav et al. (2021) classify the sentiment of one aspect of a review ("the price is reasonable although the service is poor"). They split each sentence at the aspect word and add features saying where sentiment words occur (before or after the aspect), plus a few features from the SentiWordNet lexicon. They also replace every word from an opinion lexicon by a common token positive or negative, which shrinks the vocabulary. They report 78.02% accuracy on the SemEval-2014 Restaurant data and 73.51% on Laptop, on par with the neural network models they compare against. Word pairs (bigrams such as not_bad) are another simple option; the TMU library's IMDb example uses words and word pairs.
  • Convolution over text. ConvTextTM (Bhattarai et al., 2022) cuts a text into a few consecutive windows and runs a convolutional Tsetlin machine over them, with thermometer-coded window positions, exactly as over image patches. Each window is a set of words over BERT's fixed vocabulary of word pieces, so new words and misspellings still map to known pieces. A rule can then say where in the text its words must occur.
  • Better words. Combining the vocabulary with word similarities (GloVe synonyms, or Tsetlin machine word embeddings; see Autoencoders & embeddings) lets a rule about excellent also cover superb.

What to notice

  • An explanation is not a justification. The second sentence is classified Negative for a perfectly readable reason: 17 rules about not, bad and at outvote 7 about friendly and staff. The model is wrong, but you can see exactly why, which is the point of interpretability.
  • The vocabulary decides what can be learned. complain was not among the 150 words, so no rule could use it. In a clinical setting, building the vocabulary (spelling variants, abbreviations, negation cues like denies) is half the work.

docs.title: Step 5 — Images as Boolean features
docs.text:
An image is a grid of numbers: grey levels, or three colour channels per pixel. Like text, it needs Booleanizing. The papers use a small toolbox of methods; Grønningsæter et al. (2024) collect seven of them for colour photographs:

Method One pixel (or region) becomes… Keeps Fixed threshold 1 feature: grey level ≥ \(t\) shape of dark strokes Thermometer (as for positions) \(t\) features: level ≥ \(t_1\), ≥ \(t_2\), … the order of grey levels; a range is an AND Adaptive threshold (mean or Gaussian) 1 feature: brighter than the local average minus \(C\) local contrast, robust to lighting Otsu's threshold 1 feature per channel, threshold chosen per image object vs background Colour thermometers \(t\) features per colour channel colour Canny edges 1 feature: is this pixel on an edge? outlines Histogram of oriented gradients (HOG) features from thresholded gradient-direction histograms of small cells local edge directions

The convolutional Tsetlin machine paper (Granmo et al., 2019) Booleanized MNIST-style digits with adaptive Gaussian thresholding (window 11, threshold value 2), leaving just 1 bit per pixel. The toolbox paper's best single machine on CIFAR-10 used a colour thermometer on 5×5 convolution windows.

Our image example is the scikit-learn digits dataset: 1,797 handwritten digits of 8×8 pixels with grey levels 0–16 (a small cousin of MNIST). We split it 1,347 / 450 and compare three Booleanizations:

  • threshold: ink ≥ 8 → 64 features (20.6 True per image on average);
  • thermometer: ink ≥ 4, ≥ 8, ≥ 12 → 192 features;
  • adaptive: brighter than the Gaussian-weighted mean of the 3×3 neighbourhood, minus 2 → 64 features. (On 8×8 images this marks smooth background and the light inside of strokes as True, and the darkest ink as False, so the True pixels are now mostly background.)

For each, we trained a multi-class Tsetlin machine (one team per class, as in Classification, Step 8) with 50 rules for and 50 against each digit, \(T = 15\), \(s = 4\), memory depth 100, 30 epochs, seed 1. The widget shows the Booleanized image, every team's vote sum, and the rules that fired for the winner. Its accuracy readout is computed in your browser from the learned rules, which we exported from the Python run.

🖼️ Interactive: Booleanize a digit and read the rules that recognise it

What to notice

  • The Booleanization matters as much as the machine. Test accuracy: 95.1% with the threshold, 96.9% with the thermometer, 89.8% with the adaptive threshold (seed 1; the means over seeds 1–3 are 95.3%, 96.9% and 90.9%). The thermometer keeps the most information about grey levels. Adaptive thresholding was designed for bigger, unevenly lit images and wastes the tiny 8×8 ones.
  • The rules are pictures. A thermometer rule shows three stencils, one per level. A memorized "≥ 4" pixel with a ring on its "≥ 12" plane means some ink, but not dark: a grey-level range written as one AND, as in the convolutional lesson. Rules are short: on average 11.9 memorized literals per thermometer rule and 7.4 per threshold rule, out of 384 and 128.
  • Blank space is evidence. With the threshold, 71% of the memorized literals are "must be blank" (5,304 of 7,424): a 0 is recognised as much by its empty centre as by its ring. With the adaptive threshold the roles flip: True mostly means background, and 82% of its memorized literals are plain ones. Whether a rule talks in literals or negated literals depends on which value is rare, just as with words.
  • Press "next mistake". The thermometer machine gets 14 of the 450 test digits wrong. On those, the winning team fires on average only 6.9 of its 50 rules for the digit and wins by 4.9 votes over the runner-up; on the 436 correct ones it fires 17.7 rules and wins by 22.1 votes. The vote sums double as a confidence score.

docs.title: Step 6 — From small digits to real photographs
docs.text:
The digits above fit a standard Tsetlin machine because they are tiny and centred. Real images need the convolution window: rules become patch patterns that may fire anywhere, optionally restricted to a region by thermometer-coded positions. The papers then add two ideas.

  • Look at the image in several ways at once. No single Booleanization keeps everything: thresholds keep shape, colour thermometers keep colour, HOG keeps edge directions. A TM composite (see Confidence & composites) trains one machine per view, a TM specialist, normalises each machine's class sums by its own range, and adds them. Grønningsæter et al. (2024) built 22 specialists from 7 Booleanizations for CIFAR-10 (60,000 colour photos of 10 kinds of objects). With 64,000 rules each, the best specialist (5×5 colour thermometers) reached 75.4%, HOG 67.5%, adaptive Gaussian thresholding 70.2% and Canny edges 60.6%; added together they reached 82.8%.
  • Train with fewer rules at a time. Drop clause (Sharma et al., 2021) ignores a random share of the rules in each epoch, like dropout in neural networks. On CIFAR-10 it took a convolutional Tsetlin machine from 69.3% to 75.1%, and the authors show its pixel-level explanations become more object-like.

What the learned patterns look like is the same as in our widget, only bigger. The convolutional Tsetlin machine paper prints 10×10 rule patterns for MNIST in which 1 is must-be-ink, 0 must-be-blank and * don't-care, each with the window positions where it may fire; patterns labelled upper-left, upper-right, lower-left and lower-right of the digit 0 jointly make up its shape.

What to notice

  • The history of CIFAR-10 accuracy for Tsetlin machines, as told by the toolbox paper: about 61% in 2020, 75.1% in 2023 with drop clause, 82.8% in 2024 with composites. Progress came mostly from better Booleanization and teams of machines, not from changing the learning rule.
  • On medical images we did not find a published Tsetlin machine study when writing this lesson. The toolbox paper names high-stakes medical applications as the motivation; the methods above are what such work would start from.

docs.title: Step 7 — An honest comparison with neural networks
docs.text:
First our own numbers, all on the same data splits:

Task (ours) Tsetlin machine Classic baselines Neural network Yelp sentences, 150-word set of words 75.0% ± 1.9 (10 seeds) logistic regression 76.7%, naive Bayes 77.0% — 8×8 digits, thermometer Booleans 96.9% (seed 1) logistic regression on the same Booleans 96.7% — 8×8 digits, raw grey levels (needs Booleans) logistic regression 97.3%, SVM 99.3%, 3-nearest-neighbours 99.1% one-hidden-layer MLP 98.4%

And results reported by the papers (accuracy unless noted; each from its own setup, so compare within a row only):

Benchmark Tsetlin machine Neural networks in the same paper Source IMDb movie reviews (F-measure) 89.1 LSTM 85.6, LSTM-CNN 88.1, Bi-LSTM-CNN 87.9 Berge et al., 2019 Hospital notes, drug allergy (F-measure) 69.3 MLP 67.2; naive Bayes 69.9, logistic regression 69.6 Berge et al., 2019 R8 news topics ConvTextTM 96.32 BERT 97.8, XLNet 98 Bhattarai et al., 2022 BBC Sports topics ConvTextTM 96.78 BERT 99, XLNet 98 Bhattarai et al., 2022 MNIST digits CTM 99.33 (mean), 99.4 (peak) simple CNN 99.06, PreActResNet-18 99.56 Granmo et al., 2019 Fashion-MNIST CTM 91.18 (mean), 91.5 (peak) simple CNN 90.7, PreActResNet-18 92.00 Granmo et al., 2019 CIFAR-10 CTM with drop clause 75.1 Maxout network 86.8 Sharma et al., 2021 CIFAR-10 composite of 22 specialists 82.8 (Vision Transformer 99.9, cited by the authors) Grønningsæter et al., 2024

How to read these tables

  • Our runs are tiny: 300 test sentences and 450 test digits, one fixed split each. Differences of a point or two are within the noise.
  • The papers' numbers are their own, with their own preprocessing, tuning effort and ways of averaging (mean over late epochs, peak, or best run). Berge et al. note that their IMDb numbers are means over 100 runs, which is lower than reporting the best run.
  • The pattern across all of them: Tsetlin machines are competitive with classic methods and with small neural networks, especially on binary-friendly inputs (digits, short texts), and fall clearly behind large pre-trained models (BERT, XLNet, Vision Transformers) on harder tasks. The papers' authors argue that the price buys interpretability and very cheap inference; you have to decide whether that trade is right for your application.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is the whole text pipeline in numpy: Booleanize the Yelp sentences, train the machine of Step 3, and print the most common short rules. It uses numpy's random numbers and its own split (default_rng(0)), so its numbers differ a little from the widget's. It needs yelp_labelled.txt from the UCI dataset in a data/ folder, and runs in about 10 seconds.

import re

import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_selection import chi2

# ---- 1. Booleanize: a set of words. One feature per vocabulary word: is it in the sentence?
rows = [line.rstrip("\n").rsplit("\t", 1) for line in open("data/yelp_labelled.txt", encoding="utf-8") if line.strip()]
words = [set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+(?:'[a-z]+)?", text.lower())) for text, _ in rows]
y = np.array([int(label) for _, label in rows])
order = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(rows))
train, test = order[:700], order[700:]

candidates = sorted({w for i in train for w in words[i]})
X_all = np.array([[w in words[i] for w in candidates] for i in range(len(rows))], dtype=np.int8)
keep = X_all[train].sum(0) >= 2                                  # words seen in 2+ training sentences
score = np.where(keep, np.nan_to_num(chi2(X_all[train], y[train])[0]), -1)
vocab_idx = np.argsort(-score, kind="stable")[:150]                # the 150 most class-related words
vocab = [candidates[k] for k in vocab_idx]
X = X_all[:, vocab_idx]


class TsetlinMachine:
    """Two classes, as in the classification lesson. memory[c, j, k]: c = 0 votes Negative, 1 votes Positive."""

    def __init__(self, n_features, rules_per_class=100, T=15, s=8.0, depth=100, seed=1):
        self.T, self.s, self.depth, self.half = T, s, depth, depth // 2
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.memory = np.full((2, rules_per_class, 2 * n_features), depth // 2)

    def fires(self, lits, training=False):
        memorized = self.memory > self.half
        ok = ~np.any(memorized & (lits == 0), axis=2)
        return ok if training else ok & memorized.any(axis=2)      # empty rules stay silent when classifying

    def predict(self, x):
        f = self.fires(np.concatenate([x, 1 - x]))
        return int(f[1].sum() - f[0].sum() > 0)                     # tie → Negative

    def update(self, x, y):
        lits = np.concatenate([x, 1 - x])                           # words, then NOT words
        f = self.fires(lits, training=True)
        v = np.clip(f[y].sum() - f[1 - y].sum(), -self.T, self.T)
        chosen = self.rng.random(f.shape) <= (self.T - v) / (2 * self.T)
        u = self.rng.random(self.memory.shape[1:])
        own, other = self.memory[y], self.memory[1 - y]
        rec = (chosen[y] & f[y])[:, None]                           # Recognize Feedback
        own += rec & (lits == 1) & (u <= (self.s - 1) / self.s) & (own < self.depth)
        own -= rec & (lits == 0) & (u <= 1 / self.s) & (own > 1)
        own -= (chosen[y] & ~f[y])[:, None] & (u <= 1 / self.s) & (own > 1)   # Erase Feedback
        other += (chosen[1 - y] & f[1 - y])[:, None] & (lits == 0) & (other <= self.half)  # Reject

    def rule(self, c, j):
        m = self.memory[c, j] > self.half
        n = len(vocab)
        return [vocab[k] for k in range(n) if m[k]] + ["NOT " + vocab[k] for k in range(n) if m[n + k]]


tm = TsetlinMachine(len(vocab))
for epoch in range(1, 41):
    for i in tm.rng.permutation(train):
        tm.update(X[i], y[i])
    if epoch in (1, 10, 40):
        acc = np.mean([tm.predict(X[i]) == y[i] for i in test])
        print(f"epoch {epoch:2d}: test accuracy {acc:.3f}")

memorized = tm.memory > tm.half
print("memorized literals: plain words", memorized[..., :150].sum(), "· NOT words", memorized[..., 150:].sum())
for c, name in ((1, "Positive"), (0, "Negative")):
    rules = [tuple(tm.rule(c, j)) for j in range(tm.memory.shape[1])]
    common = sorted({r: rules.count(r) for r in rules if 0 < len(r) <= 3}.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])[:5]
    print(name, "  ".join(f"{' AND '.join(r)} (x{n})" for r, n in common))

epoch  1: test accuracy 0.563
epoch 10: test accuracy 0.757
epoch 40: test accuracy 0.767
memorized literals: plain words 191 · NOT words 526
Positive great (x8)  delicious (x6)  nice (x4)  amazing (x4)  awesome (x4)
Negative don't (x6)  disappointed (x5)  not (x4)  no (x3)  bad (x3)

The same picture as in the widget: about three quarters of the memorized literals are NOT-words, the short rules form a small sentiment dictionary, and the accuracy is close to logistic regression's. For images, replace the first block by a Booleanization ((images >= 8), or a thermometer np.concatenate([images >= t for t in (4, 8, 12)])) and use one team of rules per class.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"A Tsetlin machine needs special learning rules for text or images.\"

It doesn't. Every result in this lesson uses the same Recognize, Erase and Reject Feedback and the same Voting Margin as the classification lesson. What changes is the Booleanization in front of it (and, for images, the convolution window). Most of the progress reported on CIFAR-10 came from better Booleanizations and teams of machines.

\"Rules full of NOT-words are a bug.\"

They are a consequence of sparse data: a sentence contains a handful of the vocabulary's words, so almost every "NOT word" literal is True, and Recognize Feedback memorizes True literals. A rule like "NOT any of these 144 words" means "none of the warning signs appear", which can be a sensible description of a class (Sharma et al. found the same in movie reviews). Very long NOT-lists can also signal a rule that has memorized a few training sentences, so check its coverage.

\"A set of words understands negation.\"

It keeps the word not but not what it applies to. "Not bad at all" contains not and bad, and our machine called it Negative with \(v = -10\). Word pairs, position features (Yadav et al.) or windows over the text (ConvTextTM) give the rules some word order back.

\"Readable means right.\"

Readable rules let you audit a model: you can spot a Positive rule built on waiting, or a vocabulary that misses complain. They do not make the model correct, and on hard tasks Tsetlin machines are still clearly behind large neural networks.

\"A threshold at mid-grey is all an image needs.\"

On our digits the choice of Booleanization moved accuracy from 89.8% (adaptive threshold) to 96.9% (thermometer), with the same machine. For colour photos the toolbox paper's single specialists ranged from 60.6% (Canny edges) to 75.4% (colour thermometers). Try several, or combine them in a composite.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. A vocabulary has 2,000 words. How many literals does each rule choose from, and roughly how many of them are True for a 40-word clinical note with 30 distinct vocabulary words?

2 × 2,000 = 4,000 literals. 30 plain-word literals are True (the words present), and 2,000 − 30 = 1,970 negated literals are True (the words absent): 2,000 True literals in total, as always one of each pair. Almost all of the True ones are negated, which is why text rules collect so many NOT-words.

2. A rule for Allergy is \"penicillin\" AND \"rash\". It fires on a note that says \"no rash after penicillin\". Which feedback does it get when this note is labelled not-Allergy, and which literal might fix it?

It fired on the wrong class, so if it is selected it gets Reject Feedback: every forgotten literal that is False in this note moves one step towards Memorized. "NOT no" is False here (the note contains no), so it may cross first, giving penicillin AND rash AND NOT no, just like Berge et al.'s ¬not. It is a blunt fix: the rule now also rejects "rash after penicillin, no fever".

3. Why did our text machine need 100 rules per class when the breast-cancer machine managed with 10?

A typical sentence contains only 3 of the 150 vocabulary words, and most learned rules are built around one word. A rule can only vote on sentences that contain its words, so many rules (about different words) are needed before most sentences receive any votes. With 20 rules per class the test accuracy dropped to 68.7%.

4. Write the thermometer literals that say \"this pixel has some ink but is not dark\" for our digits (planes ≥ 4, ≥ 8, ≥ 12).

\(x_{\ge 4} \wedge \lnot x_{\ge 12}\): at least level 4, below level 12. A single AND expresses the range, which a single threshold feature cannot.

5. The toolbox paper's composite reaches 82.8% on CIFAR-10, and its best single machine 75.4%. Where does the gain come from, given that the learning rule is the same?

From different views of the same image: each specialist Booleanizes the image differently (colour thermometers, adaptive thresholds, Canny edges, HOG, …) and so makes different mistakes. The composite normalises each machine's class sums and adds them, so a confident specialist can outvote an unsure one (Confidence & composites).

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Ole-Christoffer Granmo, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines (free online). Ch. 10, Natural Language and Image Processing, is announced but not yet published; this lesson uses the vocabulary of the published chapters.
  • Geir Thore Berge, Ole-Christoffer Granmo, Tor Oddbjørn Tveit, Morten Goodwin, Lei Jiao and Bernt Viggo Matheussen, Using the Tsetlin Machine to Learn Human-Interpretable Rules for High-Accuracy Text Categorization With Medical Applications, IEEE Access 7 (2019), 115134–115146. The set-of-words representation, negated words, the Allergy walk-through (our Step 2 diagram), and results on 20 Newsgroups, IMDb and hospital notes.
  • Rohan Kumar Yadav, Lei Jiao, Ole-Christoffer Granmo and Morten Goodwin, Human-Level Interpretable Learning for Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis, AAAI 2021. Booleanizing aspect, position and lexicon information for sentiment towards one aspect of a review.
  • Bimal Bhattarai, Ole-Christoffer Granmo and Lei Jiao, ConvTextTM: An Explainable Convolutional Tsetlin Machine Framework for Text Classification, LREC 2022. Convolution over text windows with BERT's vocabulary.
  • Jivitesh Sharma, Rohan Yadav, Ole-Christoffer Granmo and Lei Jiao, Drop Clause: Enhancing Performance, Interpretability and Robustness of the Tsetlin Machine (arXiv, 2021). Dropping rules during training; the observation that text rules are mostly negated words; CIFAR-10 at 75.1%.
  • Ole-Christoffer Granmo, Sondre Glimsdal, Lei Jiao, Morten Goodwin, Christian W. Omlin and Geir Thore Berge, The Convolutional Tsetlin Machine (arXiv, 2019). Adaptive Gaussian thresholding, MNIST / Fashion-MNIST / Kuzushiji-MNIST results, printed rule patterns.
  • Ylva Grønningsæter, Halvor S. Smørvik and Ole-Christoffer Granmo, An Optimized Toolbox for Advanced Image Processing with Tsetlin Machine Composites (arXiv, 2024). Seven image Booleanizations, 22 specialists, CIFAR-10 at 82.8%.
  • The cair/tmu library: its examples/classification folder has the IMDb text example (words and word pairs, χ² feature selection) and MNIST convolution examples.
  • Data: Dimitrios Kotzias, Misha Denil, Nando de Freitas and Padhraic Smyth, From Group to Individual Labels using Deep Features, KDD 2015: the Sentiment Labelled Sentences dataset (CC BY 4.0). The 8×8 digits are scikit-learn's load_digits (UCI Optical Recognition of Handwritten Digits).
