docs.title: Regression with Tsetlin Machines
docs.text:
TL;DR

A regression Tsetlin machine predicts a number instead of a class. The change is small. All rules vote the same way (there are no rules "against"), the vote sum \(v\) is simply the number of rules that fire, and it is scaled to the target's range: \(\hat y = y_{\min} + \tfrac{v}{T}(y_{\max} - y_{\min})\). Here \(T\) is the resolution: the number of votes that covers the whole range. Training compares \(v\) with the target written in votes, \(\tau\). The sign of the error picks the kind of feedback (too low: Recognize or Erase, so that more rules fire; too high: Reject, so that fewer fire). Its size sets the probability, \(|v - \tau|/T\). With thermometer-coded inputs every rule becomes an interval such as "2 ≤ dose < 5", and the prediction is a staircase built from these intervals. We train our own small version on an invented dose–response curve and on a simulated points score. For the score it recovers the published points table exactly, as nine readable rules.

Level: intermediate · Prerequisites: Classification by voting (the vote sum \(v\), the Voting Margin \(T\) and how feedback is handed out) and thermometer encoding from lesson 1. The math is fractions and absolute values.

Beyond the book

The book's chapter on this topic (An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines, Ch. 3, "Regression") has not been published yet. This lesson is based on the research papers listed under Further reading, mainly Abeyrathna et al. (2020) in Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A, its arXiv preprint and the integer-weighted follow-up. We use the book's vocabulary from the earlier lessons and give the papers' terms in brackets once. All numbers not attributed to a paper come from our own small numpy/JavaScript implementation, described in Step 4.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
Many clinical questions want a number, not a yes/no:

  • How much? A drug response at a given dose, a length of stay, a lab value a few hours ahead, a risk score.
  • Ranked outcomes. A classifier treats "score 3" and "score 4" as unrelated classes. A regression model knows that 4 is closer to 3 than to 9, and is penalised less for being off by one.
  • Readable formulas. Clinicians already use additive points scores, such as CHA₂DS₂-VASc for stroke risk in atrial fibrillation: one point per risk factor, add them up. A regression Tsetlin machine produces exactly this kind of model, a sum of AND-rules, and learns it from data.

The papers report that this simple machine is competitive with regression trees, random forests and support vector regression on several small real datasets (Step 5 quotes the numbers). Our job here is to understand how it works and what its rules look like.

docs.title: Step 1 — From a vote count to a number
docs.text:
In the classification lesson, rules voted for or against a class and the sign of the vote sum \(v\) was the prediction. For a number, two things change (Abeyrathna et al., 2020, §4):

  1. No more "against". Every rule votes the same way: when its condition is True it adds one vote. (In the papers: the clause polarity is removed.) So \(v\) is just the number of rules that fire, between 0 and the number of rules.
  2. Scale the votes to the target's range. Choose a whole number \(T\), the resolution (the papers call it the threshold or resolution \(T\)). Then \(T\) votes means "the largest value", 0 votes means "the smallest":
\[ \hat y \;=\; y_{\min} + \frac{v}{T}\,\bigl(y_{\max} - y_{\min}\bigr), \qquad v \text{ clipped to } [0, T], \]

where \(y_{\min}\) and \(y_{\max}\) are the smallest and largest targets in the training data. The output can only take \(T + 1\) different values, spaced \((y_{\max} - y_{\min})/T\) apart. A larger \(T\) gives a finer output but needs more rules to fire.

The clearest example is a points score. In our simulated version of CHA₂DS₂-VASc, a patient gets 1 point each for heart failure, hypertension, diabetes, vascular disease, female sex and age 65–74, and 2 points for a prior stroke or TIA and for age 75 or older. The maximum is 9. Write each point as a rule ("IF prior stroke/TIA THEN +1", twice; "IF age ≥ 65 THEN +1" plus "IF age ≥ 75 THEN +1" for the two age points), set \(T = 9\) and the range to 0–9, and each vote is worth exactly one point.

🧮 Interactive: a points score as rules that add up

What to notice

  • The default patient (78 years old, hypertension, female) fires four rules: hypertension, female, age ≥ 65 and age ≥ 75. So \(v = 4\) and the output is \(0 + \tfrac{4}{9} \times 9 = 4\) points.
  • A 2-point item is two rules with the same condition. Duplicated rules act as a weight, exactly like the duplicated R1 and R2 in the classification lesson.
  • Age is thermometer-coded. A 78-year-old has "age ≥ 65" and "age ≥ 75" True, so the two age rules together give 2 points; a 70-year-old fires only the first.
  • Switch the rules to "learned by a regression TM". These nine rules were learned from 600 simulated patients (Step 6 shows how). Click next simulated patient a few times: the learned rules give the same score as the table for every one of the 600 test patients.

docs.title: Step 2 — Numbers in, intervals out: the staircase
docs.text:
For a numeric input such as a dose, use thermometer encoding from lesson 1: one Boolean feature per threshold, "dose ≥ 0.5 mg", "dose ≥ 1.0 mg", …, "dose ≥ 9.5 mg" (19 features, 38 literals). A rule is an AND of literals, and with thermometer literals that AND is always an interval:

dose ≥ 2.0 AND dose ≥ 1.5 AND NOT dose ≥ 5.0 AND NOT dose ≥ 6.5 → fires for 2.0 ≤ dose < 5.0

The largest memorized "≥" threshold is the lower end, the smallest negated one is the upper end. (If the lower end is not below the upper end, the rule can never fire.) The regression output is therefore a sum of intervals, each adding one vote over its own range of doses: a staircase.

Our example is an invented dose–response curve: a benefit score that rises quickly with the dose, levels off around 3–5 mg and falls at high doses (as if side effects took over). We drew 300 training doses at random between 0 and 10 mg and added noise to the benefit. The widget shows the 40 rules that a regression TM learned from these points (the run of Step 5).

🪜 Interactive: interval rules stack up to a staircase

What to notice

  • Each rule is one bar. At dose 3.65 mg, 17 of the 40 rules fire, so \(v = 17\) and the output is \(-0.66 + \tfrac{17}{20} \times 8.87 = 6.88\) (the true curve is at 7.31). The training targets ran from \(-0.66\) to \(8.21\), so each vote is worth \(8.87/20 = 0.44\).
  • Overlapping intervals make a smooth-ish shape. The 40 rules form 27 different intervals, between 2 and 5.5 mg wide, that overlap like roof tiles. Where many overlap (around 3–5 mg) the output is high; at the edges few do. At dose 0.25 mg, 5 rules fire (output 1.56, true 1.71).
  • The edges are hardest. At 9.75 mg only 3 rules fire (output 0.67, true curve 1.84). Few training points lie there, and every interval has to end somewhere.
  • No rule is "the" answer. Unlike the points score, the curve has no true list of rules. The machine finds a set of intervals whose sum fits the data. The bars are the whole model.

The original paper booleanizes a little differently: it uses every distinct value of a feature in the training data as a threshold, with bits "\(x \le v_i\)" (Abeyrathna et al., 2020, §3). That keeps all the ordering information, at the cost of many more literals. Fixed, evenly spaced thresholds are a simpler choice that works well for a toy.

docs.title: Step 3 — Feedback: the error's sign picks the kind, its size the probability
docs.text:
Training has to answer the same two questions as in classification: which kind of feedback does each rule get, and how often?

First, write the target in votes. A target \(y\) corresponds to

\[ \tau \;=\; \frac{y - y_{\min}}{y_{\max} - y_{\min}}\, T \]

votes. During training, compute \(v\) (with empty rules counting as True, as before, and clipped to \([0, T]\)) and the error \(v - \tau\).

The sign picks the kind (Abeyrathna et al., 2020, Eq. 4.2):

  • Too low (\(v < \tau\)): more rules should fire. A picked rule that fired gets Recognize Feedback (it memorizes the True literals, so it becomes a better description of this example). A picked rule that stayed silent gets Erase Feedback (it forgets literals, so it becomes broader and starts to fire on more examples). Together these are the papers' Type I feedback.
  • Too high (\(v > \tau\)): fewer rules should fire. A picked rule that fired gets Reject Feedback (Type II): it memorizes a Forgotten literal that is False for this example, so it stops firing on it. Silent rules are left alone.

The size sets the probability. Each rule is picked independently with probability

\[ p \;=\; \frac{|v - \tau|}{T}. \]

A prediction that is off by a quarter of the range gives each rule a 25% chance of feedback; a perfect prediction gives none. Compare the classification rule, \(p = (T - v)/2T\): there, examples already safely won by \(T\) votes stopped asking for feedback. Here, examples already predicted correctly stop asking. In both cases the feedback goes where the machine is still wrong, which is the resource allocation from the classification lesson: rules that are not needed for well-predicted examples are free to fix the others.

🎚️ Interactive: how the error hands out feedback

What to notice

  • A V shape. The probability is zero at the target and rises linearly on both sides. The green side (too low) leads to Recognize and Erase; the red side (too high) to Reject.
  • With the defaults (\(T = 10\), target 6.5 votes, \(v = 3\)) the prediction is 3.5 votes too low, so each rule is picked with probability \(3.5/10 = 0.35\).
  • Raising \(T\) lowers every probability for the same error in votes. A finer resolution also makes learning more cautious.
  • The dashed line is the version in the cair/tmu library, which squares the probability, \((|v - \tau|/T)^2\): small errors get much less feedback, so a nearly right prediction is disturbed less often. The papers use the linear version (with an extra scaling constant \(K\) that we set to 1).

The versions in the literature

The first preprint (arXiv 1905.04206) scales the votes by \(y_{\max}/T\) only and uses one rule per vote (\(T\) = number of rules). The journal version adds \(y_{\min}\) (our formula above) and the probability \(K\,|y - \hat y|/(y_{\max} - y_{\min})\), which in votes is \(K\,|v - \tau|/T\). The integer-weighted follow-up writes it as \(|y - \hat y|/T\). The TMRegressor in cair/tmu rounds the target down to a whole number of votes, clips \(v\) to \([0, T]\), keeps the number of rules separate from \(T\), and squares the probability. We use the journal version with \(K = 1\), a separate number of rules, clipping, and a target that is not rounded.

docs.title: Step 4 — The complete learning step
docs.text:
Put the pieces together. Every rule starts empty, with every literal at the top of the Forgotten half of its memory. Then, for each training example in turn:

Our implementation (in the widgets and in the code at the end) follows this diagram. Its details:

  • Memorize Value 1, Forget Value \(1/s\), the convention the book uses from Ch. 2 on and the default in cair/tmu. (The journal paper's feedback tables use \((s-1)/s\) for memorizing, like our classification lesson.)
  • Memory depth 100 (positions 1–100, Memorized above 50).
  • Empty rules fire while training and stay silent when predicting, as in the earlier lessons and in cair/tmu.
  • A seeded random number generator, so the widgets reproduce the numbers in this lesson exactly.

What to notice

  • Only one number is shared: the error \(v - \tau\). As in classification, no rule knows about any other; the vote sum coordinates them.
  • The two directions balance each other. Recognize and Erase push the vote sum up, Reject pushes it down. A rule that fires on examples whose targets are too low for it gets rejected there, so it narrows to the range of inputs where its vote is wanted.

docs.title: Step 5 — Training on a noisy curve
docs.text:
Now the full run on the invented dose–response data: 300 training and 300 test points, the same curve with independent noise. The settings, fixed in advance:

  • 19 thresholds (dose ≥ 0.5, 1.0, …, 9.5 mg), so 38 literals;
  • 40 rules, resolution \(T = 20\) (so one vote is worth 0.44 benefit points), Forget Value \(1/s\) with \(s = 2.5\);
  • 60 epochs, seed 1 for the machine's random choices.

We measure the error with the mean absolute error (MAE): the average distance between prediction and target, in benefit points. That is the measure the papers report. The widget trains this machine in your browser; change the knobs and it retrains in a second or two.

🏋️ Interactive: train a regression Tsetlin machine on a dose curve

What to notice

  • With the defaults the machine ends at a test MAE of 0.660 (train 0.606). The green dashed line is the error of the true curve itself, 0.472: that much is pure noise, which no model can predict. The machine is about 0.19 points above that floor.
  • The test curve jumps around. Between epochs 11 and 60 the test MAE moves between 0.568 and 1.216. Each Reject Feedback switches a rule off for a range of doses at once, so a single unlucky example can move the staircase by a step for a while. Don't read much into one epoch.
  • Rules and resolution must fit each other. With 20 rules and \(T = 20\) the machine never gets near the peak (test MAE 3.307): every one of the rules would have to fire at the top of the curve. With 80 rules and \(T = 20\) there are too many: 22 rules end up unable to fire, 8 stay empty, and the MAE is 3.206. Twenty rules with \(T = 10\) (0.703) or 80 rules with \(T = 40\) (0.645) work as well as the default. In our runs about twice as many rules as \(T\) worked best on this curve.
  • Specificity matters too. \(s = 1.5\) gives 1.976 (rules too broad), \(s = 4\) gives 0.787, \(s = 6\) gives 3.000 (rules too narrow).

docs.title: How good is that, honestly?
docs.text:
On the same 300 test points, same data:

Method (fitted on the same 300 training points) test MAE Always predict the training mean 1.625 Straight line (least squares) 1.557 Regression tree, depth 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 0.777 / 0.660 / 0.534 / 0.544 Regression TM, defaults, seed 1 0.660 Regression TM, defaults, seeds 1–10 0.595 to 0.874, mean 0.693 The true curve (noise floor) 0.472

So our toy machine is clearly better than a straight line, about as good as a depth-3 regression tree, and a bit worse than a depth-4 tree on this one-input problem. It is a small, untuned implementation. The papers tune \(T\), the number of rules and \(s\) by grid search for each dataset.

What the papers report on real data (not rerun by us): Abeyrathna et al. (2020, Table 3) compare the regression TM with a regression tree, a random forest and support vector regression on five public datasets (six target series), averaging 20 runs. The regression TM had the lowest MAE on four of the six, for example 5.160 against 7.769, 9.122 and 5.305 on dengue incidence in the Philippines, and 0.487 against 0.598, 0.563 and 1.155 on the heating load of buildings. On aerofoil noise the random forest was best (1.921 against the TM's 2.206), and on annual stock return the support vector regression was (0.073 against 0.078).

docs.title: Step 6 — Reading the rules: rediscovering a points score
docs.text:
A model you can read is most convincing when you know the right answer. So we generated 1,200 simulated patients (600 to train, 600 to test): each condition is present at random with a fixed, invented prevalence (heart failure 20%, hypertension 60%, diabetes 25%, prior stroke/TIA 15%, vascular disease 20%, female 45%), and age is uniform between 45 and 90. The target is the patient's points score from Step 1, so there is no noise: the exact answer is a sum of nine rules.

Age is thermometer-coded with 8 thresholds (age ≥ 50, 55, …, 85), so the machine has to find out which thresholds matter. Settings: 9 rules, \(T = 9\) (so one vote = one point), range 0–9, \(s = 2\), 40 epochs. After 16 epochs (seed 1) the test MAE is 0.000: every one of the 600 test patients gets exactly the right score. The learned rules (the "learned" option in the Step 1 widget):

Learned rule (each +1 point) how many IF prior stroke/TIA 2 IF age ≥ 60 AND age ≥ 75 (that is: age ≥ 75) 1 IF age ≥ 65 1 IF heart failure / hypertension / diabetes / vascular disease / female 1 each

That is the points table: two rules for a stroke, two age steps at exactly 65 and 75, and one rule for each other risk factor. One rule carries a redundant literal (age ≥ 60 is implied by age ≥ 75); merging literals of the same property, as in the classification lesson, removes it.

How robust is this? Over 10 seeds of the machine (same data), with \(s = 2\):

Rules (resolution \(T = 9\)) exact on all 600 test patients mean test MAE 6 0 of 10 0.971 9 10 of 10 (after 3 to 25 epochs) 0.000 12 1 of 10 1.025 18 0 of 10 1.345 always predict the training mean 1.191

With \(s = 1.5\), 8 of 10 seeds were exact; with \(s = 3\), only 4 of 10. Raising the resolution to \(T = 18\) with 18 rules (two votes per point) gave MAE 0.654 on average, with no exact run.

What to notice

  • Nine rules for nine points is a perfect fit, the same observation as the paper's artificial datasets: with \(T = 7\) rules, an output of \(100 \times\) (a 3-bit number) is learned exactly by four copies of "bit 1", two of "bit 2" and one of "bit 3" (Abeyrathna et al., 2020, §5).
  • Too many rules hurt more than too few here. Extra rules have no place to go: every vote they cast is a point too many. With 18 rules the machine was worse than predicting the mean. Integer weights (next step) are one fix.
  • The rules are checkable. A clinician can compare each rule with the published score and see at once that it is right. On a real outcome (say, actual strokes) the data would be noisy, and the rules would be a hypothesis to check, not a rediscovered truth.

Simulated, not clinical

The patients, prevalences and the independence between risk factors are invented for this exercise, and the target is the score itself, not an outcome. The point is to show that the machine can find thresholds and point values that are really there, not to build a risk model.

docs.title: Step 7 — Weighted rules: one rule instead of many copies
docs.text:
In Step 6, a 2-point item needed two identical rules, and in Step 2 several intervals appeared twice. The resolution is tied to the number of rules: to output 7 the machine needs 7 firing rules. Abeyrathna, Granmo and Goodwin (2020, arXiv 2002.01245) therefore gave each rule a whole-number weight \(w_j \ge 0\):

\[ \hat y \;=\; y_{\min} + \frac{1}{T}\sum_j w_j\, C_j\,\bigl(y_{\max} - y_{\min}\bigr). \]

The weight is learned with the same feedback, by counting: when a rule is picked, fires and the prediction was too low, its weight goes up by 1; when it is picked and the prediction was too high, its weight goes down by 1 (never below 0). A weight of 0 switches a useless rule off, which also deals with the "too many rules" problem above.

The paper reports, on its 3-bit dataset with \(T = 7\): the plain machine needs 7 rules (4 × "bit 1", 2 × "bit 2", 1 × "bit 3"), the integer-weighted one needs 3 rules with weights 4, 2 and 1, and both reach MAE 0. Real-valued weights, learned with a learning rate, did not reach zero error (MAE 1.857 on training and 1.799 on test) (Table 1). The authors argue that integer weights are also easier to read, because a weight of 4 simply means "four copies of this rule".

Weights are the subject of the next part of the book; see Weighted clauses and clause sharing. We did not include them in our implementation. A quick test of the update above on the points score was much less reliable than the plain machine: with 9 weighted rules, none of 10 runs was exact (test MAE 0.318 to 1.368); with 18 weighted rules, 2 of 5 runs were. The paper's results come from a tuned implementation; tuning ours is beyond this lesson.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is the complete regression machine in numpy, about 60 lines, trained on the simulated points score of Step 6. It follows Step 4 line by line, vectorised over rules and literals. It draws its own patients and uses numpy's random numbers, so its numbers differ slightly from the widgets'.

from collections import Counter

import numpy as np

# ---- 1. Simulated patients and a points score modelled on CHA2DS2-VASc (invented prevalences, not real data)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 1200
yes_no = rng.random((n, 6)) < [0.2, 0.6, 0.25, 0.15, 0.2, 0.45]   # CHF, hypertension, diabetes, stroke/TIA, vascular, female
age = rng.uniform(45, 90, n)
score = yes_no @ [1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1] + (age >= 65) + (age >= 75)   # 0 … 9 points

AGE_CUTS = [50, 55, 60, 65, 70, 75, 80, 85]                       # thermometer: "age ≥ 50", "age ≥ 55", …
X = np.hstack([yes_no, age[:, None] >= AGE_CUTS]).astype(np.int8)
names = ["heart failure", "hypertension", "diabetes", "stroke/TIA", "vascular", "female"] + [f"age ≥ {a}" for a in AGE_CUTS]
train, test = np.arange(600), np.arange(600, n)


class RegressionTM:
    """memory[j, k] = position (1 … depth) of literal k in rule j; memorized if > depth / 2."""

    def __init__(self, n_features, n_rules=9, T=9, s=2.0, depth=100, y_min=0.0, y_max=9.0, seed=1):
        self.T, self.s, self.depth, self.half = T, s, depth, depth // 2
        self.y_min, self.y_max = y_min, y_max
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.memory = np.full((n_rules, 2 * n_features), depth // 2)  # top of Forgotten

    def fires(self, lits, training=False):
        memorized = self.memory > self.half
        ok = ~np.any(memorized & (lits == 0), axis=1)
        return ok if training else ok & memorized.any(axis=1)     # empty rules stay silent when predicting

    def predict(self, x):
        v = min(self.fires(np.concatenate([x, 1 - x])).sum(), self.T)  # vote sum, clipped to [0, T]
        return self.y_min + v / self.T * (self.y_max - self.y_min)

    def update(self, x, y):
        lits = np.concatenate([x, 1 - x])
        f = self.fires(lits, training=True)
        v = min(f.sum(), self.T)
        target = (y - self.y_min) / (self.y_max - self.y_min) * self.T  # the target, in votes
        error = v - target
        if error == 0:
            return
        chosen = self.rng.random(len(f)) <= min(abs(error) / self.T, 1.0)  # error size -> feedback probability
        u = self.rng.random(self.memory.shape)
        m = self.memory                                            # changes go straight into self.memory
        if error < 0:                                              # too low: Recognize / Erase (Type I)
            rec = (chosen & f)[:, None]
            m += rec & (lits == 1) & (m < self.depth)              # Memorize Value 1
            m -= rec & (lits == 0) & (u <= 1 / self.s) & (m > 1)   # Forget Value 1/s
            era = (chosen & ~f)[:, None]
            m -= era & (u <= 1 / self.s) & (m > 1)
        else:                                                      # too high: Reject (Type II) for firing rules
            rej = (chosen & f)[:, None]
            m += rej & (lits == 0) & (m <= self.half)

    def fit(self, X, y, epochs):
        for _ in range(epochs):
            for i in self.rng.permutation(len(X)):
                self.update(X[i], y[i])
        return self

    def rules(self, names):
        lits = names + ["NOT " + n for n in names]
        return [" AND ".join(l for l, m in zip(lits, rule) if m > self.half) or "(empty)" for rule in self.memory]


tm = RegressionTM(X.shape[1], n_rules=9, T=9, s=2.0).fit(X[train], score[train], epochs=40)
pred = np.array([tm.predict(x) for x in X[test]])
print(f"test MAE {np.abs(pred - score[test]).mean():.3f} · always predicting the mean {np.abs(score[train].mean() - score[test]).mean():.3f}")
for rule, count in Counter(tm.rules(names)).most_common():
    print(f"{count} × IF {rule} THEN +1 point")

test MAE 0.000 · always predicting the mean 1.147
2 × IF stroke/TIA THEN +1 point
1 × IF hypertension THEN +1 point
1 × IF vascular THEN +1 point
1 × IF diabetes THEN +1 point
1 × IF age ≥ 60 AND age ≥ 65 THEN +1 point
1 × IF heart failure THEN +1 point
1 × IF female THEN +1 point
1 × IF age ≥ 65 AND age ≥ 75 THEN +1 point

It runs in about a second. Again the nine rules are the points table, with redundant age literals (age ≥ 60 AND age ≥ 65 is just age ≥ 65). We also tried machine seeds 2–6: seeds 2–5 were exact too, and seed 6 ended at a test MAE of 0.638.

Piece What it does Book term (research term) Rule AND of memorized literals; adds one vote when True rule (clause \(C_j\), no polarity) Vote sum \(v\) number of firing rules, clipped to \([0, T]\) vote sum (\(\sum_j C_j\)) Resolution \(T\) number of votes for the full target range (threshold / resolution \(T\)) Output \(y_{\min} + \tfrac{v}{T}(y_{\max} - y_{\min})\) (normalised vote sum) Target in votes \(\tau\) \(\tfrac{y - y_{\min}}{y_{\max} - y_{\min}}T\) — Feedback probability \(\lvert v - \tau\rvert / T\) (activation probability \(P_{act}\)) Too low / too high Recognize or Erase / Reject (Type I / Type II feedback) Rule weight \(w_j\) whole-number number of votes per rule (integer-weighted clauses)

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"A regression Tsetlin machine is just a classifier with many classes.\"

No. A multi-class machine would treat each output value as an unrelated class, with its own team of rules. The regression machine has one team whose votes add up, so one rule can contribute to every output value in its interval, and being off by one vote is a small error, not a wrong class.

\"T is the Voting Margin, so it only matters during training.\"

In classification, \(T\) was used only during training. In regression, \(T\) is also part of the prediction: \(\hat y\) uses \(v/T\). It fixes the size of one output step, \((y_{\max} - y_{\min})/T\), and with it how many rules must fire to reach the top of the range.

\"More rules can only help.\"

Not without weights. Every firing rule adds a vote, so surplus rules must learn to never fire. On the points score, 18 rules for \(T = 9\) did worse (MAE 1.345) than predicting the mean (1.191). On the dose curve, 80 rules for \(T = 20\) gave 3.206 against 0.660 for 40 rules.

\"The output is a smooth curve.\"

It is a staircase with at most \(T + 1\) levels, changing only at the thresholds you chose for the inputs. Finer thresholds and a larger \(T\) make the steps smaller, at the cost of more rules and more training.

\"Zero training error means the machine found the truth.\"

On the points score it did, because the data were generated from that score with no noise. On real data, a perfect training fit usually means memorized noise. Always compare the test error with simple baselines and, when you can, with the noise floor.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. A regression TM has T = 10 and was trained on targets from 20 to 70. Six rules fire on a patient. What does it predict?

$\hat y = 20 + \tfrac{6}{10} \times (70 - 20) = 20 + 30 = $ 50. One vote is worth 5 units, so the machine can only output 20, 25, 30, …, 70.

2. Same machine, the target for this training example is 38. What feedback happens?

In votes, \(\tau = (38 - 20)/50 \times 10 = 3.6\). The prediction is \(v = 6\), too high by 2.4 votes, so each rule is picked with probability \(2.4/10 = 0.24\). Picked rules that fired get Reject Feedback: each memorizes a Forgotten literal that is False for this patient, so it stops firing on it. Silent rules are left alone.

3. A rule has memorized 'dose ≥ 2.0', 'dose ≥ 3.5', 'NOT dose ≥ 6.0' and 'NOT dose ≥ 8.0'. When does it fire?

For \(3.5 \le\) dose \(< 6.0\). The largest "≥" threshold sets the lower end, the smallest negated threshold the upper end; the other two literals are implied and can be dropped.

4. Why does the probability of feedback shrink as the prediction gets closer to the target?

So that the machine settles instead of oscillating. If every rule got feedback on every example, the vote sum would overshoot back and forth around the target (the papers introduce the probability for exactly this reason). With \(p = |v - \tau|/T\), well-predicted examples leave the rules alone, and the feedback goes to the examples that are still wrong. It is the regression version of the Voting Margin's resource allocation.

5. A points score has items worth 1, 2 and 3 points (maximum 6). How would a plain regression TM represent it, and what changes with integer weights?

With \(T = 6\) and the range 0–6, each vote is one point, so the plain machine needs 6 rules: one copy of the 1-point rule, two of the 2-point rule and three of the 3-point rule. With integer weights it needs 3 rules, with weights 1, 2 and 3. Same model, fewer rules, and each weight can be read directly as points.

docs.text:

The main source for this lesson: the output formula, the feedback rule and its activation probability, the threshold booleanization, and the comparison on real datasets (we read the accepted version in the University of Agder's open archive).
  • K. Darshana Abeyrathna, Ole-Christoffer Granmo, Lei Jiao and Morten Goodwin, The Regression Tsetlin Machine: A Tsetlin Machine for Continuous Output Problems, arXiv 1905.04206, 2019. The earlier preprint, with output scaled by \(y_{\max}/T\) and experiments on six artificial bit datasets.
  • K. Darshana Abeyrathna, Ole-Christoffer Granmo and Morten Goodwin, A Regression Tsetlin Machine with Integer Weighted Clauses for Compact Pattern Representation, arXiv 2002.01245, 2020. Integer weights for the regression machine (Step 7).

Darshana Abeyrathna, Ole-Christoffer Granmo, Xuan Zhang and Morten Goodwin, A Scheme for Continuous Input to the Tsetlin Machine with Applications to Forecasting Disease Outbreaks, arXiv 1905.04199, 2019. The threshold booleanization for continuous inputs, applied to dengue outbreak forecasting.

docs.title: Weighted Clauses and Clause Sharing
docs.text:
TL;DR

A trained Tsetlin machine often holds several copies of the same rule, and each copy is just one more vote. A weighted Tsetlin machine keeps one copy and gives it a weight \(w\): when the rule fires, it casts \(w\) votes. The weights are learned alongside the rules with two tiny updates: +1 when a firing rule gets Recognize Feedback, −1 when it gets Reject Feedback. A rule that is right most of the time it fires climbs to a large weight; one that is right only half the time sinks to 0 and is switched off. Clause sharing goes one step further: instead of a separate team of rules for every class, all classes share one pool of rules, and each rule has a signed weight for every class (positive: it votes for that class, negative: against). On a toy task with ten classes and a budget of only 20 rules, our runs give 74.4% for the plain machine, 81.1% with weights and 85.8% with a shared pool, close to the 87.3% that is the best you can do on this data.

Level: intermediate · Prerequisites: Classification by voting (rules voting for and against a class, the vote sum \(v\), the Voting Margin \(T\), and multi-class teams). Convolutional Tsetlin machines is useful background but not needed.

Beyond the book

Chapter 5 of Ole-Christoffer Granmo's book, Pattern Weighing and Sharing, is not published yet. This lesson is therefore based on the research papers listed under Further reading: the real-valued weighted Tsetlin machine (Phoulady et al., 2020), the integer-weighted Tsetlin machine (Abeyrathna, Granmo and Goodwin, 2021), the coalesced Tsetlin machine with clause sharing (Glimsdal and Granmo, 2021), and the open-source TMU library that implements them. It uses the book's vocabulary from the earlier lessons. All the experiments are our own small runs, made for this lesson.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
In the classification lesson, two things kept happening:

  • Rules came in copies. The book's example used two identical rules, R1 and R2, so that their two votes could outvote R3. The trained breast-cancer machine had four identical rules memorizing "Inv-nodes 24-26". Every copy costs memory and computing time, and makes the model longer to read, without saying anything new.
  • Each class had its own team. A three-class machine trains three separate teams. If two classes share a useful pattern, each team has to discover it on its own.

Clinical reasoning works differently on both counts:

  • Findings carry different weights. Many clinical scores give some findings two points and others one. A weight says "this rule counts more" directly, instead of through copies.
  • Findings are shared between diagnoses. Fever is evidence for several infections and against others. One rule, "if fever", can serve all of those diagnoses at once, with a different weight for each.

The payoff reported in the papers is large. Phoulady et al. (2020) report that a weighted machine matched the accuracy of a standard Tsetlin machine with only 1/4 of the rules on MNIST, 1/3 on IMDb and 1/50 on Connect-4. Abeyrathna et al. (2021) report that integer weights needed, on average over their datasets, 6.5 times fewer literals than the standard machine. Glimsdal and Granmo (2021) report that a shared pool helps most when rules are scarce.

docs.title: Step 1 — Copies are weights
docs.text:
Look at the book's example again: R1 and R2 are the same rule, "Deg-malig 3 and not Menopause lt40". When it fires, the vote sum gets +2. You could just as well keep one copy and say that it is worth two votes. That number is the rule's weight \(w_j\).

With weights, the vote sum becomes a weighted vote sum (Phoulady et al., 2020):

\[ v \;=\; \sum_{j \,\in\, \text{for}} w_j \, C_j(x) \;-\; \sum_{j \,\in\, \text{against}} w_j \, C_j(x), \]

where \(C_j(x)\) is 1 if rule \(j\) fires on example \(x\) and 0 otherwise. (In the papers the rules are clauses \(C^+_j\) and \(C^-_j\) of positive and negative polarity, and the machine is a Weighted Tsetlin Machine.) Everything else stays as it was:

  • Prediction: the sign of \(v\) for two classes, the class with the highest \(v\) for several.
  • Training: \(v\) is clipped to \([-T, T]\) and every rule is picked for feedback with the same probability \((T - v)/2T\) as before. Recognize, Erase and Reject Feedback change the rules' memories exactly as in the feedback lesson.

The papers differ in what a weight can be:

Real-valued weights (Phoulady et al., 2020) Integer weights (Abeyrathna et al., 2021) Start value 1.0 1 Rule fires and gets Recognize Feedback multiply by \(1 + \gamma\) +1 Rule fires and gets Reject Feedback divide by \(1 + \gamma\) −1, never below 0 Extra hyperparameter learning rate \(\gamma\) none Reading a weight "this rule counts 2.37 times" "this rule counts as 3 copies"

This lesson uses integer weights: they need no extra hyperparameter, they read as a number of copies, and a weight of 0 switches a rule off. (The TMU library's weighted classifier also uses integer weights but keeps them at 1 or more.)

What to notice

  • A weight changes how much a rule's vote counts, never when it fires. The rule's literals decide when; the weight decides how much.
  • The Voting Margin still works on the vote sum, which is now weighted. A rule with weight 8 can reach a margin of \(T = 8\) on its own.

docs.title: Step 2 — How a rule earns its weight
docs.text:
The integer-weight update is two lines (Abeyrathna et al., 2021). A weight only changes when its rule fires and is picked for feedback:

  • Recognize Feedback (the rule fired on an example of the class it votes for, a true positive): \(w \leftarrow w + 1\).
  • Reject Feedback (the rule fired on an example of the other class, a false positive): \(w \leftarrow w - 1\), but not below 0.
  • Erase Feedback leaves the weight alone: the rule did not fire, so it cast no vote.

(In the literature: Type Ia feedback raises the weight and Type II lowers it.) Which weight does a rule end up with? Take one rule on its own and let it fire on a stream of examples. Call \(q\) the rule's precision: the share of the examples it fires on that belong to the class it votes for.

  • On an own-class example, the rule's \(w\) votes are on the right side, so \(v = w\) (clipped at \(T\)) and the rule is picked with probability \((T - w)/2T\). Then \(w\) goes up.
  • On an other-class example, those same \(w\) votes are on the wrong side, so \(v = -w\) and the rule is picked with probability \((T + w)/2T\). Then \(w\) goes down.

On average the weight drifts by

\[ \frac{q\,(T - w) - (1 - q)\,(T + w)}{2T} \;=\; \frac{(2q - 1)\,T - w}{2T} \]

per example. That is positive below \(w = (2q - 1)T\) and negative above it, so the weight is pulled towards the resting point

\[ w^\ast \;=\; T\,(2q - 1). \] 🎚️ Interactive: how a rule earns its weight

What to notice

  • Precise rules get big weights. With \(q = 0.9\) and \(T = 10\) the formula says 8, and the weight averages 7.72 over examples 1001–2000 of the run. A rule that is nearly always right ends up close to \(T\) and can almost reach the margin alone. Abeyrathna et al. describe this as high-precision rules "operating more independently".
  • Coin-flip rules are switched off. At \(q = 0.6\) the resting point is 2.0 (the run averages 2.25) and the weight sits at 0 for 20% of those examples. At \(q = 0.4\), below one half, the resting point is negative, so the weight hugs the floor: it is 0 for 50% of the examples and averages 0.80. Rules like that only add votes when, now and then, a lucky streak lifts them off 0.
  • \(T\) sets the unit. With \(q = 0.9\) and \(T = 20\) the weight averages 15.28 (formula: 16). Doubling the margin doubles every weight, so weights only mean something compared with \(T\) and with each other.
  • This is a simplification: a real rule shares the vote sum with other rules, so \(v\) is not just its own weight. The direction is the same: precise rules gain weight until the examples they cover reach the margin.

docs.title: Step 3 — One shared pool of rules
docs.text:
Weights also make a second idea possible. In the classification lesson, a machine for \(m\) classes trains \(m\) separate teams; a rule in the team for Car votes for or against Car and nothing else. But many patterns are useful for several classes at once. In a seven-segment display, "the top-right segment is off" is true for exactly two digits, 5 and 6: it is evidence for both, and against the other eight.

The coalesced Tsetlin machine (Glimsdal and Granmo, 2021) therefore keeps one pool of rules for all classes, and gives every rule \(j\) a signed integer weight for every class \(i\), \(w_{ij}\). Together they form a weight matrix \(W\) with one row per class and one column per rule. Each class reads the same rule outputs through its own row:

\[ v_i \;=\; \sum_j w_{ij} \, C_j(x), \qquad \text{prediction} = \text{the class with the largest } v_i . \]

A positive \(w_{ij}\) means rule \(j\) votes for class \(i\) with \(w_{ij}\) votes; a negative one means it votes against class \(i\) with \(|w_{ij}|\) votes. Sharing rules this way is called clause sharing, and the machine is coalesced because the separate teams have merged into one.

What to notice

  • The pool is evaluated once per example, not once per class. With many classes that is a large saving in computation.
  • A shared rule needs a weight for every class. The weights are small integers, so they are cheap compared with a rule's literal memories, but the matrix grows with classes × rules.

docs.title: Step 4 — How a shared pool learns
docs.text:
Training a coalesced machine combines the multi-class training of the classification lesson with the weight updates of Step 2. Take a training example of class \(y\):

  1. Its own class, as "yes". Compute \(v_y\), clip it to \([-T, T]\), and pick each rule with probability \((T - v_y)/2T\). A picked rule with \(w_{yj} \ge 0\) is on the example's side: Recognize Feedback if it fired, Erase if not. A picked rule with \(w_{yj} < 0\) that fired voted wrongly: Reject Feedback. Every picked rule that fired gets \(w_{yj} \leftarrow w_{yj} + 1\).
  2. One other class \(k\), chosen at random, as "no". Pick each rule with probability \((T + v_k)/2T\). Now the rules with \(w_{kj} < 0\) are on the example's side (Recognize or Erase), and those with \(w_{kj} \ge 0\) that fired get Reject. Every picked rule that fired gets \(w_{kj} \leftarrow w_{kj} - 1\).

The weights start at random values of \(+1\) or \(-1\), so at first every rule is randomly for or against each class. There is no floor at 0: a weight can pass through 0 and change sign, and the rule then switches sides for that class. Glimsdal and Granmo describe this as rules being repurposed.

Versions of the algorithm

The coalesced paper writes the update for every output at once, for problems where an example can have several outputs (multi-output, or multi-label), and scales Reject Feedback by \(1/(m - 1)\) for one-hot classes. The TMU library's TMCoalescedClassifier, and this lesson, instead update the true class and one randomly chosen other class, like the multi-class machine of the classification lesson. Also note that \(w = 0\) counts as "for" (\(w \ge 0\)), as in the paper and in TMU.

What to notice

  • Nothing in the rules says which class they belong to. A rule ends up "about" digit 5 only because its weight for 5 grew.
  • The feedback a rule's memory gets now depends on the sign of its weight for the class being trained. That is how one rule can be refined by digit 5's examples and rejected by digit 3's.

docs.title: Step 5 — Inside a trained pool
docs.text:
Time for an example. The data is a toy task we made for this lesson: noisy seven-segment digits. Each digit 0–9 is drawn with the seven segments of a calculator display, named a (top), b (top right), c (bottom right), d (bottom), e (bottom left), f (top left) and g (middle), so there are 7 features and 14 literals. Each segment is flipped with probability 5%, so about 70% of the examples are noise-free (0.95⁷ = 0.698) and the rest have one or more wrong segments. There are 500 training and 1000 test examples.

Even a perfect model makes mistakes here: a 6 whose segment e flipped off looks exactly like a clean 5, and an 8 that lost segment e looks exactly like a clean 9. The best you can do is to pick the digit whose clean pattern is nearest (fewest differing segments), which scores 87.3% on our test set.

The widget below shows a coalesced machine with a pool of 20 rules trained on this data (\(T = 128\), \(s = 3\), 40 epochs, seed 1). Each row is one rule; the ten cells next to it are its weights for digits 0–9.

🧩 Interactive: one shared pool of rules, a weight for every digit

What to notice

  • Every rule is shared. All 20 rules have a positive weight for at least two digits. R1, "e ∧ g" (bottom-left and middle on), has weights +46 for 2, +29 for 6 and +15 for 8, and negative weights for everything else. Those are exactly the three digits whose clean pattern has both segments.
  • Rules found the digits' defining gaps. Four rules contain ¬b (top-right segment off): R11, R19 and R20 are just "¬b", and R18 is "f ∧ ¬b". All four vote for 5 and 6, the only digits without segment b (R19 also gives 3 a small +4). R4 and R14 are both "¬a", and vote for 1 and 4, the only digits without a top segment. Duplicates still happen in a pool, but the weights now tell you how much each copy counts for which digit.
  • Click "5". The clean 5 fires five rules (R11, R13, R18, R19, R20). Digit 5's column adds up to +154, and the runner-up is 6 with +35: the ¬b rules push both 5 and 6 up, and R13, "d ∧ f ∧ ¬e", separates them because a 6 has segment e.
  • Edit the input. Switch segment e on in the 5 and it becomes a clean 6: the ¬e rule stops firing, R1 "e ∧ g" and R10 "a ∧ e ∧ f" start, and the prediction flips. Then try "next test example" to step through noisy test digits and see which ones the pool gets wrong.
  • The weights are large (up to 89 in size) because the margin is large, \(T = 128\). As Step 2 showed, weights only mean something compared with \(T\) and with each other.

docs.title: Step 6 — The same budget, three machines
docs.text:
Now the comparison the papers make: give three machines the same number of rules and see what they do with them.

  • Plain: one team per digit, half the rules for and half against, every weight fixed at 1 (the classification lesson's machine).
  • Weighted: the same teams, with integer weights (Step 2).
  • Coalesced: one pool shared by all ten digits, with signed weights (Steps 3–4).

With a budget of 20 rules, the plain and weighted machines get one rule for and one against per digit; the coalesced machine gets a pool of 20. With 60 rules: three for and three against per digit, or a pool of 60. All use \(s = 3\) and memory depth 100 and train for 40 epochs.

⚖️ Interactive: the same rule budget, three machines

What to notice

  • With 20 rules (seed 1), the plain machine is stuck at 73.6% from early on. The coalesced machine ends at 86.9% (mean of epochs 31–40: 86.7%), within half a point of the 87.3% ceiling. The weighted machine is in between but restless: it ends this run at 75.1%, while its mean over epochs 31–40 is 81.4%, with single epochs anywhere from 71.5% to 85.1%.
  • Why the plain machine is stuck. Show the plain rules: each digit's single "for" rule memorized the digit's complete clean pattern, like "a ∧ b ∧ c ∧ d ∧ e ∧ f ∧ ¬g" for 0. Such a rule only fires on noise-free examples, about 71% of the test set. With one vote per rule there is no way to say "most of these segments".
  • Weighted rules are short. Show the weighted rules: digit 6's rule "e ∧ ¬b" (bottom-left on, top-right off) with weight 13 is exactly what separates a 6 from every other digit. Digit 0 has "e ∧ f ∧ ¬g" with weight 16. The weighted machine memorized 39 literals in total, the plain one 108.
  • Switch to 60 rules. Now the plain machine has enough rules to cover noisy variants, and all three end within a few points of each other (seed 1: plain 82.9%, weighted 87.4%, coalesced 85.2% in the last epoch). Weights and sharing pay off most when rules are scarce.

One run is not enough, so we repeated it for machine seeds 1–5 on the same data. To keep the comparison fair, each machine got its own Voting Margin, chosen from \(T \in \{2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128\}\) on a separate validation set of 1000 examples. Test accuracy, averaged over epochs 31–40 and then over the 5 seeds:

Machine 20 rules 60 rules Plain (\(T\) = 32 / 2) 74.4% ± 1.1 83.2% ± 1.6 Weighted (\(T\) = 8 / 64) 81.1% ± 1.1 86.5% ± 0.3 Coalesced (\(T\) = 128 / 128) 85.8% ± 0.7 87.2% ± 0.3 Nearest clean pattern (the best possible on this data) 87.3% 87.3%

The pattern matches what the papers report on real benchmarks. Glimsdal and Granmo (2021) report, for convolutional machines on MNIST with 50 rules per class, 97.86% for the weighted machine against 98.33% for the coalesced one, and similar accuracy for both (99.33% and 99.29%) at 8000 rules per class. Their largest gap is on Kuzushiji-MNIST with 50 rules per class: 71.99% weighted against 89.66% coalesced (their abstract attributes these two numbers to Fashion-MNIST; we quote their Table 4).

A toy, not a benchmark

The seven-segment task is tiny and was made to fit this lesson: its classes really do share sub-patterns, which is exactly where sharing should help. The ranking of the three machines can be different on other data, and the best Voting Margin was at the edge of our grid for two of the machines, so they might do slightly better with an even larger \(T\).

docs.title: Step 7 — Reading weighted and shared rules
docs.text:
Weights change how you read a trained machine, mostly for the better.

Seed 1, 20 rules literals memorized what you read Plain 108 20 long rules, mostly complete digit pictures Weighted 39 20 short rules, each with a weight (some 0) Coalesced 40 20 short rules, each with a row of 10 signed weights

Some habits for reading them:

  • Read an integer weight as copies. "e ∧ ¬b, weight 13" means the same as thirteen copies of that rule in a plain machine. Abeyrathna et al. (2021) chose integer weights for exactly this reason.
  • Compare weights with \(T\), and within one machine. By Step 2, a weight close to \(T\) marks a precise rule; a weight near 0 marks a rule that is right about half the time it fires. A weight from a machine with \(T = 8\) can't be compared with one from \(T = 128\).
  • Ignore rules with weight 0. They cast no vote. In their bankruptcy example, Abeyrathna et al. (2021) report that integer weights switched one rule off, leaving the single readable rule "Bankruptcy if Negative Competitiveness".
  • Read a shared rule column by column. In a coalesced machine, ask "which rules vote for digit 5, and with how much?" by reading digit 5's column of weights, and "what does rule R1 mean?" by reading its row: e ∧ g is evidence for 2, 6 and 8.
  • Watch for empty rules. In the weighted run, several "against" rules ended empty, with weights of 6 or 7. During training an empty rule fires on every example, so it acts as a fixed offset; when classifying it stays silent, as in the earlier lessons. It is a reminder that the weights were learned with the training-time behaviour.

Interpretable is still not the same as correct

The weighted machine above reads beautifully and still had epochs at 71.5%. The weights make the model shorter to audit, not automatically right. Check accuracy over several runs, as in Step 6.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is a complete coalesced Tsetlin machine in numpy, about 70 lines including the data. It follows Step 4 line by line, vectorised over the rules and literals. It uses numpy's random numbers and its own data, so its numbers differ a little from the widgets'.

import numpy as np

# ---- 1. Data: noisy 7-segment digits (segments a-g; 5% of segments flipped)
SEGMENTS = {0: "abcdef", 1: "bc", 2: "abdeg", 3: "abcdg", 4: "bcfg", 5: "acdfg", 6: "acdefg", 7: "abc", 8: "abcdefg", 9: "abcdfg"}
PATTERN = np.array([[s in SEGMENTS[d] for s in "abcdefg"] for d in range(10)], dtype=np.int8)

def make_data(n, rng, noise=0.05):
    y = rng.integers(0, 10, n)
    X = PATTERN[y] ^ (rng.random((n, 7)) < noise)
    return X.astype(np.int8), y

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
X_train, y_train = make_data(500, rng)
X_test, y_test = make_data(1000, rng)


class CoalescedTsetlinMachine:
    """One shared pool of rules. memory[j, k] = position (1 … depth) of literal k in rule j.
    W[i, j] = signed integer weight of rule j for class i (> 0: votes for i, < 0: votes against i)."""

    def __init__(self, n_classes, n_features, n_rules=20, T=128, s=3.0, depth=100, seed=1):
        self.T, self.s, self.depth, self.half = T, s, depth, depth // 2
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.memory = np.full((n_rules, 2 * n_features), depth // 2)          # top of Forgotten
        self.W = self.rng.choice([-1, 1], size=(n_classes, n_rules))          # random sides to start

    def fires(self, lits, training=False):
        memorized = self.memory > self.half
        ok = ~np.any(memorized & (lits == 0), axis=1)
        return ok if training else ok & memorized.any(axis=1)                 # empty rules stay silent

    def predict(self, x):
        return int(np.argmax(self.W @ self.fires(np.concatenate([x, 1 - x]))))   # class sums v_i = W_i · c

    def update_class(self, lits, c, i, is_class):
        v = np.clip(self.W[i] @ c, -self.T, self.T)
        p = (self.T - v) / (2 * self.T) if is_class else (self.T + v) / (2 * self.T)
        picked = self.rng.random(len(c)) <= p
        own = (self.W[i] >= 0) == is_class                                    # rule is on the example's side
        u = self.rng.random(self.memory.shape)
        mem = self.memory
        rec = (picked & own & c)[:, None]                                     # Recognize
        mem += rec & (lits == 1) & (u <= (self.s - 1) / self.s) & (mem < self.depth)
        mem -= rec & (lits == 0) & (u <= 1 / self.s) & (mem > 1)
        era = (picked & own & ~c)[:, None]                                    # Erase
        mem -= era & (u <= 1 / self.s) & (mem > 1)
        rej = (picked & ~own & c)[:, None]                                    # Reject
        mem += rej & (lits == 0) & (mem <= self.half)
        self.W[i] += np.where(picked & c, 1 if is_class else -1, 0)          # weights: toward this example's side

    def fit(self, X, y, epochs):
        n_classes = self.W.shape[0]
        for _ in range(epochs):
            for e in self.rng.permutation(len(X)):
                lits = np.concatenate([X[e], 1 - X[e]])
                other = (y[e] + self.rng.integers(1, n_classes)) % n_classes   # one random other class
                for i, is_class in ((y[e], True), (other, False)):
                    self.update_class(lits, self.fires(lits, training=True), i, is_class)
        return self

    def rules(self):
        names = list("abcdefg") + ["NOT " + s for s in "abcdefg"]
        return [" AND ".join(n for n, m in zip(names, r) if m > self.half) or "(empty)" for r in self.memory]


tm = CoalescedTsetlinMachine(n_classes=10, n_features=7).fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=40)
acc = np.mean([tm.predict(x) == t for x, t in zip(X_test, y_test)])
nearest = np.mean(np.argmin((X_test[:, None, :] != PATTERN[None]).sum(2), axis=1) == y_test)
print(f"test accuracy {acc:.3f} · nearest clean pattern {nearest:.3f}")
for j, rule in enumerate(tm.rules()[:5]):
    print(f"rule {j + 1}: IF {rule:<16} weights per digit 0-9: {tm.W[:, j].tolist()}")

test accuracy 0.835 · nearest clean pattern 0.874
rule 1: IF c AND e AND f    weights per digit 0-9: [29, -48, -50, -52, -23, -81, 20, -66, 52, -15]
rule 2: IF a AND b AND NOT e weights per digit 0-9: [-8, -81, -62, 35, -70, -39, -32, 48, -63, 67]
rule 3: IF NOT a            weights per digit 0-9: [-18, 41, -13, -23, 34, -21, -14, -49, -23, -18]
rule 4: IF NOT a            weights per digit 0-9: [-23, 41, -12, -29, 34, -10, -10, -53, -23, -26]
rule 5: IF b AND c AND g    weights per digit 0-9: [-43, -31, -82, 27, -64, -11, -30, -39, 56, 17]

It takes about 7 seconds. Rule 1, "c ∧ e ∧ f", votes for 0, 6 and 8, the three digits that have all three segments; rule 2, "a ∧ b ∧ ¬e", votes for 3, 7 and 9. Turning it into the weighted machine of Step 2 takes three changes: keep a separate pool per class, fix each rule's side by its position instead of the sign of its weight, and replace the last line of update_class with \(+1\) on Recognize and \(-1\) (not below 0) on Reject.

Piece What it does Book term (research term) Weight \(w_j\) how many votes a firing rule casts weight (clause weight) Weighted vote sum \(v\) sum of the weights of the firing rules, for minus against vote sum (\(\sum_j w^+_j C^+_j - \sum_j w^-_j C^-_j\)) Weight learning +1 on Recognize, −1 on Reject (not below 0); rests near \(T(2q - 1)\) (integer-weighted TM; SSL automaton with step 1) Shared pool one set of rules for all classes (clause sharing; coalesced TM) Weight matrix \(W\) signed weight \(w_{ij}\) for every class and rule; may change sign (clause-output weight matrix) Class sum \(v_i\) \(\sum_j w_{ij} C_j\); the highest wins (class sum, \(v = Wc\))

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"A rule's weight is the probability that it is right.\"

No. In Step 2 the weight rests near \(T(2q - 1)\), so it depends on the Voting Margin as much as on the rule. A rule with precision 0.9 rested near 7.7 with \(T = 10\) and near 15.3 with \(T = 20\). Weights rank rules within one machine; they are not probabilities.

\"Weights make the model harder to read.\"

Integer weights are just copy counts: "weight 13" reads as thirteen copies of the rule. And with the same budget, the weighted machine in Step 6 memorized 39 literals against the plain machine's 108, because short rules with big weights replaced long exact ones.

\"A weight of 0 deletes the rule.\"

It silences the rule's vote, but the rule still fires, still gets feedback and can earn its weight back. In the Step 2 run with \(q = 0.6\), the weight sat at 0 for 20% of examples 1001–2000 and kept coming back.

\"In a shared pool, every rule votes for every class.\"

Every rule has a weight for every class, but most of them are negative. In the trained pool of Step 5, each rule voted for between two and three digits and against all the others. To see what a rule is for, read its row; to see what votes for a class, read the class's column.

\"Clause sharing is always better.\"

In our runs it helped most with 20 rules (85.8% against 74.4% for the plain machine) and much less with 60 (87.2% against 83.2%, with the weighted machine at 86.5%). Glimsdal and Granmo report the same: large gains with few rules per class, similar accuracy with thousands.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. A weighted machine has the rule \"Deg-malig 3\" voting for Recurrence with weight 3, and \"Inv-nodes 0-2\" voting against with weight 2. A patient matches both. What is v, and what is the feedback probability with T = 4 if the patient did recur?

\(v = 3 - 2 = +1\), so the machine predicts Recurrence. For a patient with recurrence, \(v = +1\) is already from the patient's own side, so each rule is picked with probability $(4 - 1)/8 = $ 0.375.

2. A rule fires on 400 examples of its own class and 100 of the other class. Where does its integer weight settle with T = 10?

Its precision is \(q = 400/500 = 0.8\). The resting point is $T(2q - 1) = 10 \times 0.6 = $ 6: high enough to matter, but well short of reaching the margin alone.

3. Why does Erase Feedback leave the weight unchanged?

Erase Feedback goes to a rule that did not fire on an example of its own class. The weight measures how much the rule's vote is worth, and here it cast no vote, right or wrong. Only firings (true positives and false positives) carry information about the vote's value.

4. In a coalesced machine, rule j has weight w = −1 for digit 3. It fires on a training example of digit 3 and is picked. What happens to the rule and to the weight?

With \(w_{3j} < 0\) the rule is against 3, and it fired on a 3, so it voted wrongly: it gets Reject Feedback, and its weight goes up by 1 to 0. Since \(w \ge 0\) counts as "for", the next time it fires on a 3 and is picked it gets Recognize Feedback and its weight rises to 1. The rule has been repurposed to vote for digit 3.

5. With one rule for and one against per digit, the plain machine scored about 74% while the best possible is 87.3%. Why couldn't it do better, and how do weights fix it?

Each "for" rule memorized its digit's complete clean pattern, which fires only on noise-free examples (about 70% of them, \(0.95^7 = 0.698\)), and every rule has exactly one vote, so it can't express "most of these segments". With weights, short rules that capture one distinguishing feature (like "e ∧ ¬b" for 6) earn large weights, and a few of them together tolerate a flipped segment.

Darshana Abeyrathna, Ole-Christoffer Granmo and Morten Goodwin, Extending the Tsetlin Machine With Integer-Weighted Clauses for Increased Interpretability, IEEE Access 9, 8233–8248 (2021); preprint arXiv:2005.05131. Integer weights (+1 / −1) learned by a stochastic-searching-on-the-line automaton; the weight update used in Step 2, and results on breast-cancer, liver-disorder, heart-disease and bankruptcy data.
  • Sondre Glimsdal and Ole-Christoffer Granmo, Coalesced Multi-Output Tsetlin Machines with Clause Sharing (arXiv preprint, 2021). The shared pool with a signed weight matrix used in Steps 3–6, with results on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, Kuzushiji-MNIST and imbalanced IMDb and CIFAR-10.
  • CAIR, Tsetlin Machine Unified (TMU): the open-source library with TMClassifier(weighted_clauses=True) and TMCoalescedClassifier, which we read to check the details of the update rules.
  • Ole-Christoffer Granmo, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines (free online). Chapter 5, Pattern Weighing and Sharing, is announced; the vocabulary of this lesson follows the published chapters.
